div.head: MGDOUGALLS SELF-RAISING FLOUR I NIVIEGEESIM
div.p: MGDOUGALLS SELF-RAISING FLOUR I NIVIEGEESIM
PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE. REV. H. OGDEN AND THE LABOUK WAR.
THE CHARGE OF " SETTING CLASS AGAINST CLASS."
I
I
I
!:;ik
II

The Progressive Labour League brought its campaign on behalf of the National Insurance Act to a close on Monday evening with a meeting in St. Barnabas' School, Bostock-street. There can be no doubt that the League has rendered a very useful service in counteracting the effects of Tory misrepresentations of the measure, and many oi the electorate will have a firmer grasp of its provisions in consequence of the meetings held in all parts of the town. There was a good attendance at the concluding meeting, the Rev. H. Ogden presiding. Mr. T. H. Garside, of Manchester, was the principal speaker. The CHAIRMAN said the statesman who was responsible for the Insurance Act had been charged in the House of Commons with setting class against class. Mr. Austen Chamberlain in one of his latest utterances declared that the present strike and the unrest in the industrial world was the outcome of Limehouso and Newcastle and of wild and lurid language. He (the chairman) did not want even to attempt to rebut that charge. One remembered that Mr. Austen Chamberlain still had a father living, and that there was a time in the history of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain when he was regarded as a politician and agitator who was setting class against class and whose advanced revolutionary ideas were such as to make him a dangerous member of society. But supposing Mr Austen Chamberlain's charge were true, if a statesman had made a body of men discontented with living in tubs and boxes—and that was the description given to the housing accommodation for the miners in South Wales —if he had been the indirect means of moving the miners to fight to the last, ditch and to the last drop of their blood for a living wage—that stately sum of ss. or s. per day— MR. LLOYD GEORGE HAD DONE A SERVICE TO MANKIND

by resurrecting the man'W-fiblti.--the man End enabling him to stand upon his feet. (Applause.) A great portion of the community wad suffering great inconvenience and others were enduring fearful privations, but he had yet to learn that those who were suffering most were making the loudest wail about the miners' struggle. With regard to the Insurance Act, when the measure came into operation in July it would be its own best advocate and lecturer. It appealed to him for the glorious things it attempted to do for the man wbo had hitherto not been considered and who had to battle for the mere necessities of daily bread. It would give a fighting chance to the consump- tive and, by its maternity benefits, it would confer at any rate a modicum to enable the wife and family to tide over times of exceptional difficulty. As to the position of the domestic servant, he had in mind a case, not five miles from Warrington, of a servant girl who toiled and slaved in a house until rheumatism grew upon her. Although she had given something like twelve years' service in that family, the mistress found it was an inconvenience to have the girl in the house. Her home was some dis- tance away and one hardly dare prophesy what would have happened if there had not been a kindly friend near at hand to take her in. There seemed to be no home for her but the poor house. Would it not have been a blessing if she had been entitled to medical attendance and 7s Gd a week? She would have felt she was not placing herself on the kindness and charity of anybody. In conclusion Mr. Ogden said he supported the Act, not because he was concerned with the political or party side of it, but because it would do something for the " bottom dog "—for the man who was at tee bottom rung of the ladder of human society. Surely no man with a heart, no women with feeling, who realized the humanitarian vein which ran through the Act, could fail to rejoice that such a chance was being given to the lowest, the most obscure and the most forgotten of human Society. (Applause). Mr. GARSIDE dealt at considerable length with the friendly society aspect of the measure. He said the greatest difficulty that any organization of a friendly society character had to meet to-day was that they could not get young lives to join. The majority of YOUNG MEN WERE TOO DENSELY STUPID and careless of their own interests to make any provision even for next week, let alone for next year. Trade unions had to beg of them to join their ranks—in I fact there were thousands of young men who would not I have been members of their unions if they were not flogged into joining them, and there was a still greater' number who had had the opportunity in bygone days of joining sick societies but refused to do so. Mr. Garside showed how the Act placed every insured person between the ages of 16 and 69 on an equal footing with regard to contributions and benefits and said the reserves accumulated for each man must be precisely the amount it was needed to meet his particular age. Mr Harold Smith—they must not I think for a moment that he said it uncharitably—would do well to read a little more before he talked. (Hear, hear). If he would read the Act carefully there would be no necessity for anybody to write a line as to the disposition of reserves. Mr. Smith said that the Government was paying nothing, that really they (the working classes) were paying everything that was paid. Well, he was right but he was telling a great deal more of the truth than he intended to tell. "If we reason it out" continued Mr Garside" is it notcorrect to say that every penny of taxation that Mr Harold Smith gets the receipt for, is paid by you? Of course it is. He pays income tax. Who finds the money? You. Every solitary copper of every tax that is paid in this or any other country is TAKEN DIRECTLY OUT OF THE PCCKET OF LABOUR. (Hear, bear.) There is not a solitary copper of taxation that is paid from any other source. Adam Smith laid that down over 100 years ago and it is an economic axiom that is just as true to-day as it was then." But Mr Smith would tell them that the people had to pay, that the Government paid nothing. What did the Act say about contributions? A young man paid 4d., and the employer 3d. The benefit that a young man of 18 got under the Act cost exactly 5A., so that there was a margin of 1 kci out of his own and the employers' contributions and the Government contribution was apparently not needed. Mr. Harold Smith chimed in " There you are robbing the young man in order to benefit the old man." That was exactly where Mr. Smith had forgotten to read the Act. Otherwise, he would know that from the contributions of the employer and employed and by the State credit was created a reserve which was increased as the days went by,solhat by the time the young man joining at sixteen reached the age of forty, the amount of reserve taken from his contributions would be practically nothing, but all that had been taken from his contributions in years gone by would be standing to his credit, and would be applied to his benefit when the amount of his contribution plus the State contribution would not be sufficient to pay for the benefits he was receiving. The Government said it would give credit to every man and woman insured under the Act for the full amount of the reserve value required, plus two-ninths of the actual cost of administration. Instead of robbing the young man, the Act was the hest safeguard he could possibly have, because it placed him as a unit in a condition of absolute solvency. (Applause.) Dealing with the position of the Post Office contributor, Mr. Garside said he challenged any friendly society representative to tell him of any organization in the world that would admit is man who was known to be diseased and give him fall medical benefits for a contribution of 4d. a week. They could not do it. The Act, concluded the lecturer, was an honest, well-meant and carefully thought-out endeavour to meet a great need and he I appealed to the workers to help to make it run smoothly to suggest any wise changes, to help to re-model it where necessary and in a thousand ways to make it what it was intended to be—a great measure for the uplifting of men and the betterment of our common humanity. (Applause). Several questions were then put to Mr Garai& and lucidly answered. Mr. J. ELWELL, in moving a vote of thanks to the speaker, said he admired the Act as one of the best attempts ever made to alleviate mauy of the burdens under which the workingman laboured. It would greatly encourage the worker in the practice of thrift. At the present time there were only about 3,000,000 people insured with friendly societies, but the Act proposed to bring within its benefits about 1.5,000,000 people. It would compel the improvident to prepare for sickness and other forms of distress. If the workers were to obtain the fullest advantages from the Act, they must use their intelligence and take care that they drew their benefits through the best sources. Ten shillings • per week for 26 weeks VMS not all that the Act gave. At the end of three years a valuation must take place, Ind those societies who had been moat economical in their working would be able to give superior benefits to their members. If there was one thing he deplored at the present time, it was MAN'S INHUMANITY TO MAN 9 and the way in which those in authority treated those who, through no fault Of their own, had to seek help Only that day he was told of a young MO with a wife and family who applied to the Union Authorities for relief and was informed that all they could do for him was to' tell him to "come insida. " It was a disgrace that such a state of things should exist in this country in the twentieth century. (Hear, hear.) If workingmen wanted their children to be provided with a mid-day meal at school, they had to submit to the most degrading questions. They ought to rise against such a state f affairs. When distress arose through causes, over which men had no control, they ought not to be insulted in that way. They must try and culti- vate a better spirit towards thhir fellow men, and see that those in authority used their powers in a more humane manner. (Applause). Mr. J. MORTON seconded, and the vote was heartily passed.

had been nationalized and a profit of £9,000,000 was expected from them in the coming year. The payment of M.P.'s salaries and election expenses and the opera- tions of the National Health Act were also allowed for. All the taxes on tobacco, sugar, tea, cocoa, coffee, and dried fruits would be remitted. They had long been told that they were food taxers but he hoped the Ceposition would take note of the fact that the total amount of the food taxes which were to be abolished was £9,750,000, as against £52,000,000 derived from things which were absolute luxuries and not necessaries of life. The proposed remission of stamp duties, which last year brought in £9,500,000 would be a great relief to the commercial part of the community. The land taxes and house duty had been diverted to the local authorities who were benefiting considerably from them. The £9,500,000 paid last year in relief of local taxation would no longer be required and, as all import duties would be abolished,they did not intend to pay an army of customs officials to do nothing. There would be a reduction of £4,000,000 in the expenditure on the navy, as we had, practically speaking, arrived at a definite understanding with Germany. An additional £3,000,000 would be devoted to old age Pensions. Taking everything into account, they were faced with a deficit of about £102,500,000. In deciding upon the taxation which would be necessary to meet it, he had taken into account now the income of the country was derived. In the years 1904-9 there were 62,309 estates which averaged at the death of the owners only a trifle over £3OO each, while 4,000 estates aversged over £50,000. They proposed to remedy that unequal distribution of the wealth of the country by a drastic graduation of the income tax. It was not, how- ever, intended to leave the death duties out of account, in fact they hoped to receive an increased revenue from them. The income of the country amounted, in round figures, to £2,000,000,000. Of that sum, 5,000,000 people received half, while the other half was divided among the remaining 40,000,000—n0t a very fair propor- tion. The Government thought that a person who had any means at all within reason should contribute towards the upkeep of the country. It was therefore proposed that a person in receipt of a weekly wage of 15s. to 20s. should pay one penny per week income tax. For the recipient of a wage of from 20s to 40s the tax would be twopence per week; while a wage of 40s to GOs would carry a tax of threepence per week. From those small amounts they would raise about £12,000,000 equal to Gs per head as against 303 charged under the existing direct and indirect methods of tixation. It was proposed to add 3d in the £ of taxation for each £l5O or part thereof to £9OO per annum and Gd in the £ on each £5OO or part thereof to £3,500 per annum' with a super tax on all over that amount. When we had to incur such heavy expenditure on the army and navy it was only right that the man who had the most property to protect should pay for the little extra tune that was being played to him. He claimed that the Government was dealing leniently with the workers and with the professional classes. The recipient of over £l,OOO a year would probably make the most disturbance about the taxes but the Government felt that, in ordinary justice, some of the poorer people should be relieved while others should be made to pay their far quota to the revenue of the country. (Applause.) Mr G TOUMLIN (L., Abingdon) seconded the adoption of the Budget. Mr J 51cDERatna (C., Paisley) commented on the peculiarity of the situation that a representative of the Upper Chamber should be chosen to introduce the subject of finance which they held to be sacred to the House of Commons. (Laughter.) The Upper House had been reserved by the Liberal party for a considerable time as a sort of political scrap heap, and the member for Burton must have felt his consignment to it somewhat keenly. (Laughter.) It was a sincere tribute to the memory of the late member for Peters- field (Mr. F. G. Taylor) that the Chancellor should have proceeded on the lines indicated by him in his celebrated Budget. It also showed that the Government had not recovered from the effects of that measure and did not know how to grasp the situation which brought forth such a Budget from the Conservative side. The present Budget was merely a worthless imitation and indicated that the resources of so-called Free Trade finance were at an end. When they , found the Liberal party subm;tting a £300,000,000 Budget, they must come to the conclusion that the system under which such a thing was possible was no longer practicable in this country. The abolition of the duties on tea, coffee, sugar, S:o., had been part and parcel of the projected Tariff Reform Budget for years. With regard to the customs and licence ditties which now went to local authorities, he would remind them that in their Local Rating Bill the Government threw over the " bold Budget" of Mr. Lloyd Gelrge and superseded his vindictive taxes by a much milder scheme. At the same time, it had the defect of making t maintenance of hospitals and similar institutions dependent upon the capacity of the people to consume alcoholic liquors (Laughter.) The reduction of expenditure on the navy would not be welcomed by the House. Whatever differences they had on other matters,it seemed to have been generally accepted on both sides, with the excep- tion of a few extremists, that it was imperative that the navy should ha maintained at a certain standard,but it would not be continued under the new Budget. Indirect taxation was to be entirely abolished. While the theory of a single tax seemed very plausible and attractive to those who were fond of theories, the practicability of such a scheme had not been accepted by any of those who had been made responsible for the affairs of an industrial and commercial country like ours : (A Voicx : "What about your late Budget ?") It simply proved that the Govern- ment had fallen into the trap which the Conservatives set for them. (Laughter.) If the nationalization of railways in other countries was anything to go by, continued Mr. McDermid, the Chancellor would have to face a deficit rather than a surplus from that source. A great deal of the money that was being expended on

landlords, hut they had gradually shifted their respon- sibilities on to the shouldefs of the rest of the com- munity. It was the policy of tariff reformers to extend the system of indirect taxation. The present Budget, he claimed, would prove the salvation of the working clruses.

-------- Mr. C. PLINSTON (C., Darlington), maintained that a reduction of the duties on footstuffs had been part of the policy of tariff reform ever since Mr. Chamberlain took it, up. He entirely disagreed with the Government in imposing income tax on anybody whose wages were less than 25s per week. It was unjust that anyone who was not receiving a living wage should be taxed to any extent at all.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
LIBERAL BUDGET DISCUSSED.
A UNIVERSAL INCOME TAX.

With the vote on the Budget on Tuesday evening next the Warrington Parliamentary Debiting Society will bring the session of 1911-12 to a close. Although the attendances on the whole have been somewhat dis- appointing, the work of the session has not fallen short of its predecessors in interest, debates having waged round some Of the most keenly contested questions of the day. The Budget, which was introduced on Tuesday, by the Lord Chancellor (Mr. J. Jarman), proposes to levy a universal income tax, beginning with the earner of 15s weekly, and ..o establish the " free breakfast table. " The LORD CHANCRLLoR mentioned that last year the Conservatives, instead or bringing in the Tariff Reform Budget for which their opponents were longing— (laughter)—introduced a system of graduated income tax. He supported that measure and did not propone to go back on the attitude he then took up. With regard to the sources of revenue, the proceeds of the customs and excise duties had been allocated to local authorities under the recent Local Rating Bill and therefore nothing would he available from those sources for the Imperial funds. Several sessions ago the Liberal Government passed an Education Act which placed the whole of the cost of education on the National Exchequer, and there would be an increased liability under that head of .C 32,000,099. The railways

education was absolutely thrown away. The results did not prove that we were getting value for money. Our most highly paid teachers who, from their ripe experience and ability, ought to be capable of impart- ing information to the scholars, had to devote most of their time to clerical work for central departments, preparing returns about slate pencils, &c. (Laughter.) Considerable retrenchment, with increased efficiency, was possible in that department.

Councillor HAWTHORN (Chancellor of the Exchequer,' said he was glad the Conservatives now appreciated that the House of Commons was the proper Chamber to discuss finance. It had been a hard lesson for them to learn, but now they had admitted that the Liberals were right in their contention that the Lords were not entitled to interfere with the Bodget. (Laughter ) It was late in the day for the tariff reformers to pose as pioneers of reduced taxation of food, especially when the great apostle of that policy had told them that they could not have Colonial preference without a tax on wheat. The statement of the member for Paisely that in their last Budget the Conservatives were setting a trap for the Liberals to fall into, was an admission that the Opposition had been playing with finance. With regard to the railways, it was reasonable to anticipate a profit for, under a sstem of nationalisa- tion, they would do away with expensive boards of directors, while the strike had shown that tickets could be interchangeable on the various lines and some trains could be dispensed with. The increased expenditure on education was not due so much to officialism as to the placing of new liabilities, such 'is the feeding and medical inspection of school child -en, on the local authorities. Under the new Budget the workingman would know exactly how much he had to pay to the upkeep of the State and it would a'so make the " free breakfast table" an accomplished tact. There was a tsme when the whole of the taxes were paid by the

div.head: Mr. WATSON (Socialist) : Is 255. a living wage?
div.p: Mr. WATSON (Socialist) : Is 255. a living wage?

Mr. PLINSTON : lam prepared to say a higher figure than that; but I only gave it as a figure of speech. Continuing, he said he agreed with the principle of a graduated income tax. An inquiry into the expendi- ture on education would be beneficial, as there was undoubtedly a great deal of waste going on. As to the supposed " undtratanding " with Germany, be was somewhat sceptical, as the first Lords of the Admiralty of Liberal Governments had previously been deceived on that point. Tbere was nothing in the Budget to show the expenditure in connection with national insur- ance.

The LORD CHANCELLOR said it was included under the heading of " National Health." Mr PLINSTON : Then you are giving the Insurance Act a new name. You should not try to quibble. Let us understand in plain English what you really do mean. Continuing he said the Bill did not indicate whether Ireland was going to contribute anything to imperial expenditure or how much it was going to cost this country to set her up in business. He contended that the Government ought to put some taxes on the luxuries of the rich over and above the tax on income. Those who indulged in champagne, expensive cigar?, and foreign motor cars, at enormons expense, should be taxed on those things.

Mr Durigs (Soc., West Ham) supported the Budget but said he was entirely opposed to the taxation of any- one whose income was less than £2 a week. At the same time they bad to be thankful for all mercies, and the Budget was a decided improve- ment on the present conditions. The under- lying principle was that men should be taxed according to their income and not according to what they consumed. Luxury did not lie in the com- modity itself but in the ability to obtain it. Conse- quently all taxation should be derived from income. The worker was taxed in the workshop and should not be taxed anywhere else. With regard to the estimated profits from railways, 33 per cent of the railway workers were earning from lis to £1 Is per week, and yet they would be taxed to the extent of 4s 9d a year on that scanty income. Lie maintained they were being robbed of the £9,000,000 which was set apart as profit. The LORD CHANCELLOR said an undertaking had been given that any profit on the zailways should go to the increase of wages and the reduction of rates. There- fore the profit was not taken into account in the estimated income in the Budget.

Mr. DUKES, continuing, said the whole of the money to be raised from the workers who earned from Iss. to 40s. could very well have been placed on those whose incomes ranged from £l5O to £OOO. He did not object to a man haying £l6O, provided he earned it. But when they considered that the man who got coal received a wage averaging 265., it was stretching things too far to say that sums of from £5OO to £5,000 could be earned income. Mr. N. NIELD (C., Newton), said he did not suppose any member was opposed to the principle of the graduated income tax. He agreed with previous speakers that a man who received less than 255. or 30s, per week ought not to pay income tax. The Govern- ment ought to protest the living wage. When one considered that, under the Insurance Act, people who had less than a living wage would have to pay 3d. or 4d. per week, it was unfair and thoughtless to call upon them for anything more. He objected to the too drastic way in which the Budget would tax those from whom the capital for the develop- ment of our industries was derived. We had already had sufficient experience of the war in which capital was rapidly leaving this country. if we were to con- tinue to pile on the load of taxation, England would soon be in a parlou state. The expenditure on the navy should, if anything, be increased,as there were signs that before many years had passed this country would be in a very critical position. He contended that the land taxes—an ingenious source of income— ought not to have been diverted from the Imperial Exchequer. Whatever Government was in power in the future, they would have to embody in their pro- gramme more and more social legislation. The railway and coal strikes and other significant incidents bad impressed on every thinking man that we could not go on ranch longer with things as they were. Assuming that the Chancellor's contention as to the probable yield of the land taxes was correct, he was throwing away a valuable asset with which be might do a great deal of good.

Mr. J. A. HEYWOOD (L., Limehouse), expressed his satisfaction at the reduction of expenditure on arma- ments. We had nothing to fear from Germany. The people of that country did not want to fight us and we did not want to fight them. It was only a fewa in yeardi - viduals with money bags who wanted to force on wars. The only blot on the Budget was the taxtation of very low incomes. Anyone receiving over £3,000 ought to pay almost lyilf of it away. (Laughter). The debate was adjourned until Tuesday next.

div.head: [BY REDCAP].
div.p: [BY REDCAP].
WYANDOTTES.

If it were possible to take a census of all the pure breeds of poultry in this country, I think you would find Wyandottes heading the list. I have before me last week's issue of the " Feathered World " and therein I find no less than eleven columns of adver- tisements devoted entirely to Wyandottes. There are a great variety of colours in this most useful breed of fowls. This week's illustrations depicts a pair of Columbian Wyandottes. In colour they are very much like the Light Brahma. A flock of Columbiana on a nice grass run, make a very pretty picture.
COIXUBIAN WYANDOTTES.

As well as being a handsome fowl, they are also an extremely useful all-round variety. They are grand winter layers, and bid fair to become keen competitors with the Whites ; they have made rapid strides this last two years, and ere long we shall see a great many breeders taking up the Columbian Wyandotte. To give you practical proof of this statement I append the following letter sent to the " Feathered World" last week by a prominent breeder of Columbians. " . . . . . From our own experience we find that in our part of the country, at any rate, they lay far better than any other Wyandotte. We have a pen of eight birds, and from November 7th to March 16th they have laid 570 eggs. As regards looks, surely the most ardent admirers of the other Wyandotte colours must admit that the Columbian runs them all very close, and when breeders can get the hackle in the cocks a little deeper it will improve the general appearance of a breeding pen very considerably. The public, it appears, are at last beginning to recognise the sterling qualities of these really hand- some fowls, and when a bird which is good to look at manages at the same time to keep the egg-basket well filled it is bound to become popular, and popular it is becoming too, for one could not fail to notice the crowds that were continually collecting round the pens containing this breed at the Palace and the Dairy last year, and the remarks that were passed about them. For any one requiring a useful all-round bird com- bining beauty and utility, they are second to none." Amongst the other varieties we have the Whiten Blacks, Buffs, Blues, Silver Laced, Black Laced, Buff Laced, Silver Pencilled, Partridges, and Blue Laced. There are also quite a number of other colours, but these are more or less in their infancy. To mention them they include : White Laced Blacks, Spangled Reds, Piles and Cuckoos. What an army ! I really think that the Wyandotte has now passed the Old English game for variety in colours. I will refrain from mentioning the individual qualities of the different varieties. This I can do when the different illustrations appear in due course.

TABLE I. OW LS. Do they pay? Whatever branch of poultry farming you take up, this vital question should be asked and answered before making a start. And so I would point out. When one has to sell a good fat table bird for about from 3s. to 3s. 6d., and taking into considera- tion the fact that you have them to feed for something like four months, there is not much margin left for profit. The rearing and feeding of table poultry cannot be made to pay in a small way. Those who are best able to make this branch of poultry farming pay,are farmers and small holders. Because they have almost unlimited accornodation. And unless you are able to forage the young stock until-the time for fattening off arrives, you cannot make it profitable. In a small way and where your operations are limited, you have every scrap of fond to purchase, For instance, supposing you rear a fowl from the shell up to four months old, at the rate of 11 per week for food. What does it mean? Bow does it work out? Sixteen weeks at Id. per week, amounts to a coat of 2s. Very well then. If you reckon labour and loss of stock at another Gd. per head, the total cost of production is 2s. Gd. So that if you sell the dead stock at 3s. each or even 3s. Gd. (which is considered a good price) it only leaves you at the latter price, is. per head profit. So that again if you must make £5O per annum you would have to get rid of 1,000 fat birds. Then look at the labour involved in rearing and feeding 1,000. The only way the small farmer can make this branch pay, is by purchasing young stags and topping ' them up. This is undoubtedly a paying system. Providing you have good

As a matter of fact, from two to three weeks good feeding and they are ready. It is a good plan to fix a few contracts with local farmers for the purchasing of all the young cockerels bred. been semi-finalists. There was only a minute to go when Wakefield got to the other end. Scrummages were keenly fought out until the interval was clearly in arrear. thomas got penalised for rushing round the pack, and Newbould kicked a goal with the last kick of the first half, fully four minutes after time. Wakefield : one g0a1,2 points; Warrington, nil. Warrington were unfortunate in resuming a goal to the bad, and they seemed to have a tea porary fit of despondency. Wakefield attacked desperately and Dickenson's kick was charged down near the line, Tilley saving pluckily. Newbould passed to Kershaw, who made a big effort, bat was pulled down under the posts. From the next scrum Newbould again got the ball and kicked across for Simpson to field smartly and race over at the corner, as Mclntyre knocked him out of play. The try was made safely, and Taylor had a try for goal, which failed. Warrington could not get going, and again was a kick charged down, and the Wakefield men estab- lished on the line. Warrington's forwards I were beaten in scrum work,and the ever-busy Newbould secured the oval and rushed to the line. Tilley and Mclnlyre both went for the big half back who handed the ball to Simpson to touch down easily at the corner. This time Taylor goaled, and Warrington had suffered eight points to be scored in as many minutes since the resumption. The Wirepullers showed true Lancashire doggedness and gradually improved the position, Skelhorn dribbling cleverly to the home quarter. creevey got few passes from the scrum—where Warrington failed to heel three times out of four—but he broke through once and gave Woodbnrn a wide pass which the wing man failed to take on the run. In the loose the Warrington men were great, and a forward rush beat the home backs. Thomas picked up and kicked to the line, where Skelhorn and Trantor both had a certainty but for a frightfully unlucky screw- bounce by the ball, which went in touch at right-angles. This was a cruel disappointment to the plucky visitors. Creevey again bluffed his opponents and found an open- ing for a well-judged kick to the corner. Woodburn raced up and beating Land got R try far out. Renwick took the kick and landed a lovely goal from touch. Play became very exciting after this, and Warrington were continually in the home half but were unable to get possession from the scrums, if the backs could have handled oftener they might have equalised, but Wakefield managed to secure the ball and kept the lead to the end. Final : Wakefield Trinity, 2 goals, 2 tries, 10 points ; Warrington, 1 goal, 1 try, 5 points.

div.head: CUP-TIES.
div.p: THE CUP-TIES.
Warrington's Duel With Wakefield.
A DRAW AT HOME AND DEFEAT AWAY.

On Saturday for the third time Warrington made a draw in their cup-tie struggles of the season, but the performance was inferior to the previous ones at Nor- manton and Hull because it took place on the Warrington ground, where victory should have been assured. ‘Vakefield Trinity brought a strong team, but owing to the disorganisation of the railway service by the strike, only a handful of supporters accompanied them. War- rington had to rely on the same side as in the previous rounds, Brooks and Bradshaw being still hors de combat. The weather was bad, a heavy drizzle of rain prevailing throughout the match, but fully 9 000 spectators assembled, and the receipts were £lB7 Iss 91. Naturally the ground was greasy, and favoured the heavier York- shire forwards. The teams and officials were : Warrington : Mclntyre, back ; %Voodburn, Renwick Dickenson and Waywell, three-quarter backs ; Jordan and Daintith, half backs ; Shugars, Thomas, Fearnley, Chesters, Tranter and Skelhorn, forwards. Wakefield Trinity : Smith, back ; Fellowes, Poynton, Lynch and Simpson, three-quarter backs ; Slater and Newbould, halt backs ; Taylor, Anton, Crossland, Walton, Beattie and Kershaw, forwards. Referee : Mr F Renton, Hruoslet. Touch judges : Messrs W McGowan, Broughton Rangers, and G Robinson, Runcorn. cvarrington had the wind to begin with, but a piece of misflelding by Dickenson from the initial kick-off gave the visitors an early advantage, and Mclntyre was hard pressed to clear his line. Jordan broke through from the serum and punted well up the field, and the forwards following at a great pace prevented Smith making any reply. Tnere was some lively work in the visitors' quarter until a penalty drove Warrington back. Newboule set his backs going at half-way and there was some smart handling by the three-quarters, Poynton being eventually grassed by Renwick in good style. The visitors showed up prominently at this stage, and Simpson was nearly over after smart work by Slater and Poynton. Short kicking by the Warrington halves and last forward play drove Wakefield back, and Newbould was lucky to clear under difficulties. Warrington were playing with great dash, though it was noticed that Fearnley had gone lame. The Trinity backs handled better, but met a grand defence. Woodburn got a chance on the right, and kicking over the full hack's head, appeared a likely scorer until Slater raced up and sent the ball dead. Then Treater charged a punt by Smith near the line, but the ball glanced into touch—bad luck for Warring- ton. The VVirepullers were very energetic at this st•lge, and Waywell forced the ball past the custodian, but could not get up in time. Interval : No score. Wakefield resumed in confident style with the wind in their favour, and for some minutes the home line was in great danger, but Reowick tackled Slater, and broke up a dangerous move by the Trinity backs. Once clear of the line, the home forwards rose to the occasion and overplayed the opposition in brilliant style. Smith was caught in possession by Skelhorn and Warrington pressed hotly. Newbould got possession and ran to half way, before passing wide to Poynter'. The ball fell short and Renwick dashing up got his toe to the ball and dribbling grandly past the full back sent it over the line. A groat race ensued but the Colonial kept his advantage and opened the score with a brilliant try near touch. The cheering was loud and long, for points were obviously very precious under the condi- tions. Mclntyre took the kick at goal, but made a poor attempt with a wet ball. The home side were now all over" the Wakefield men and there was a thrill of excitement when Woodburn was seen to race away from centre and repeat Renwick's feat, the full-back having no chance. Unfortunately the referee detected some infringement and brought the wing man back. The game seemed well won until five minutes from the end, when Crossland made a strong burst from his own half to the Warrington quarter before passing to Slater. The latter crossikicked, and Wood- burn saved right on the line. Unfortunately he played the ball before his own men were up, and Poynton got hold and rushed over with an equalising point exactly It minute from time. G. Taylor made a fine attempt for goal, and the match was drawn—a bitter disappoint- ment to the Warrington men, who had shown great superiority till the last movement. Score, one try each.

div.head: RE-PLAY AT WAKEFIELD.
div.p: RE-PLAY AT WAKEFIELD.
Warrington's Game Struggle.

Warrington turned up at Wakefield on Wednesday with any amount of confidence in themselves. Owing to injuries and other causes, changes bad been made in the team, but they were looked upon as an advantage. Tilley, Creevey and Arnold were introduced after some weeks absence' Jordan acting as reserve man, while Mclntyre played on the wing in place of Waywell. The train service was not at all bad, though full fares prevented more than a score of supporters making the journey to the cathedral town. The Trinity men were also compelled to make changes in their team, Kershaw taking the place of Lynch at centre, and Land, the "A " team custodian displacing Smith. The weather was brilliant and the ground in perfect order for a fast game, while the crowd rolled up in such force that at 4 o'clock when operations commenced there were eleven or twelve thousand people present. Some 'hundreds rushed one of the gates but the receipts totalled the fine sum of £234.

Mr B Ennio"), Wigan, was the referee. The home side won the toss, and had the advantage of a strong breeze for the opening stages. Thomas set the hall in motion, and a poor reply being made, Warrington were soon busy in the borne quarter. Finally Slater punted well down the field, and Creevey dropping the catch, the scene was changed in a twinkling. The Wakefield forwards raced up, and Crossland set the backs going speedily on the right. A score seemed probable, as Woodburn bad three men to deal with, but he shunted tle man with the ball into touch ten yards from the goal-line. Daintith relieved from the next serum in clever fashion and, found touch at centre. Wakefield got going again and Simpson made a dash down the wing, until Mclntyre barred progress, while a cool mark by Renwick under the posts further checked the borne lot. Warrington were kept on the defence, and Taylor had a penalty shot at goal which went wide. Dickenson attempted to run the ball out, but his kick was short, and Crossland marked in front of goal. New- bould took the kick, but missed an easy chance. War- rington had made little headway no fat, but 'Dickenson now shone with an ?Id-time rush through the home centres, which carried play to the Wakefield quarter. Here Renwick bad a try for a goal from a penalty, and a fine shot fell just under the bar. Woodburn improved his tide's position by a run and punt which found touch near the line. Dickenson again dodged his way through and gave Woodburn a chance, but Fellows downed the winger a yard short. Warrington were playing aggres- sive football at this stage, but a floe break-away by Poynton changed the scene. The tall centre eluded the Warrington backs and worked a tine opening for New- bould, who tried to double in with the wing open, and was promptly smothered by Shugars and Skelhorn. It was a fine chance missed by the homesters, and War- rington showed their appreciation by their best display of passing, Creevey and Renwick each bluffing the opposition in a run over half the length of the field. Tranter followed up finely and charged Land's kick near the line, being all over a scorer when Slater got tip and tackled the young Warrington forward a yard from the line. The pressure was maintained by the active Wire- pullers, and Tilley took a drop at coal which was only inches out. Again Warrington passed across, Mclntyre reaching the corner flag before being checked. Wakefield had many anxious moments until Crossland found touch in the Warrington quarter from a penalty kick. Dickenson inter- cepted a passing movement by the home backs and raced clear away with Skelhorn alongside. On reaching Land he tried a kick, which was luckily charged down, and Warrington's best chance went awry. A pass to Skelhorn, or a long punt, and Warrington would have

div.head: WARRINGTON OF THE FUTURE.
div.p: WARRINGTON OF THE FUTURE.
A TOWN PLANNING SCHEME.
ALDERMAN BOLTON'S OPPOSITION.

The Warrington Corporation is preparing to take advantage of the powers conferred by the Town Planning Act and a scheme for the development of the town on attractive and conve lent lines is already well advanced. On Tuesday afternoon the landowners of Warrington and district were invited to meet the members of the Street Improvement Committee in con- ference at the Town Hall and there was an encouraging response. The discussion also disclosed a general dis- position to co-operate with the Corporation in working the Act in the most efficient way. The Mayor (Coun- cillor Dr. Joseph) presided and was supported by Alderman Bennett (chairman of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee) and the Town Clerk (Mr J Lyon Whittle). The MAvoit, in welcoming the landowners, said it was to the mutual advantage of landowners and those interested in land that they and the Corporation should have an understanding upon the general principles of the Town Planning Act, which placed within the power of the Corporation the laying out of undeveloped land. They all knew of the waste of public money that had taken place in the past aed landowners had also become embroiled in uncertain law suits to protect their property against ill-advised schemes of neighbour- ing owners. With the assistance of landowners they could avoid these evils and see that those who bad laid out a good scheme should not find their efiorts ruined by an adjacent owner putting up a factory or some cheap cottages. (Hear, hear.) The object of the Act was to prevent a waste of public money, and it was in the interests of landowners that they should make the most of their land. The Actwas also intended to promote the health and happiness of those who lived in the district. The Town Council bad passed a resolution to apply to the Local Government Board to carry out the provisions of the Act, and they now asked the land-

scheme would be the allocation of separate areas to separate purposes. It was indesirable that unpleasant or injurious business operations should be carried on in residential quarters. The works should naturally be allocated to the vicinity of the Ship Canal and the railways, leaving the other areas for residential purposes. There aught to be some sub-divisions of the various classes of house , property ; they did not want to mix mansions and artisan dwellings promiscuously while, on the other band, tbey did not wish to fix too great a gulf between them. From the health point of view, the most important of all was the limitation of the number of houses to the acre; they wanted to

div.head: BOAT RACE.
div.p: THE BOAT RACE.

The University Boat Race will take place on March 30th, over the Thames champion- ship course—Putney to Mortlake. Cam- bridge spent last week-end at Brighton, and since Tuesday have been given an easy time. Much interest centres around Mr. R. O. Bourne, the Oxford stroke. If Oxford win—

and experts say that if the fine power and determination shown by the crew at practice is kept up they should—Mr. Bourne will create a new record, by stroking the winning crew four successive years. Oxford have won thirty-seven 'times to Cambridge's thirty.

At Heatley. These teams met in their return engage- ment and were well represented. Invariably there is little between these two clubs when they meet. Saturday% game was a fair and even one all through, and the result, a draw of one goal each, was a fair indication of the game. BowDoN VALE V. ALTRINCIIAM LADS.

-- At Vicarage-lane, Bowdon. The game opened even and fast, both ends being visited in turn. Coombes put in good work on the visitors' left but Potts cleared his Huse?, whilst at the other end Mackennall put over. The Lads were now having the best of matters and, follow- ing pressure on the home goal, C Johnson opened the score with a good effort. This roused the Vale, who quickly retaliated in a very short time, Morgan succeeded in equalizing the scores. Once more on level terms the game became highly interest- ing but both defences were sound. Hassell was penalized, but from this consequent free kick, Cash cleared when hard pressed, whilst Goulden failed to improve a capital centre by Coombes. As the result of an individual effort by Johnson (Vale) the latter player got completely through the Lads' defence and placed his side in front. Half-time: Bowdon Vale, 2 ; Altrincham Lads, 1. Resuming, the Vale had slightly the best of matters and Johnson with his second goal placed his side further ahead. Hassell (Bowdon Vale) came uuder the ban of the referee and retired. Final: Bowdon Vale, 3 ; Altrincham Lads, I. ST. CROSS v. LATCHFORD.

At Knntsford. In the opening stages of the game, St. Cross held the advantage but found the visitors' defence in good trim. As they settled down Latchford improved and the game became more even. Taking the game all througb, St Cross showed vast improvement on former games, and in the end suffered a narrow defeat with the score : Latchford, two goals ; St Cross, one. LYIII3I V ATOMIERLEY. . .

At Lymm. For this important game at Lymm neither teams were at full strength. Seeing that both teams are in the running for the Championship plenty of interest was taken in the game. Taking the game all through, Mobberley deserved their victory on one point only. Both attacks were equal, but the " Dockers" showed by far the better defence, inflicting upon Lymm their first home defeat with the 'core : Mobberley, two goals; Lymm, nil„ SECOND DIVISION. PADGATE UNITED V. ROBERTSON'S. This game took place at Pialgate in miserable weather. The visitors won the toss and were the first to press but could make no impression on the home defence. The game became more even, neither side claiming any advantage. Both defences held out and the interval arrived with the score sheet blank. Upon resuming the pace increased and through a blunder by the visitors custodian, Pedgate opened their account. Stung by this reverse Robertson's fought keenly but the home custodian cleared finely on several occasions. Just before the call of time Robertson's caught the home defence in two minds and equalized matters, the game ending with the score one goal each. ST. VINCENT'S V LOSTOCK GRALAM. On Stamford Park, Altriocham, on Saturday. Result: Lostock Gralam, 3 ; St. Vincent's, 1.

owners to co-operate with them. (Hear, bear, and applause.) Alderman BENNETT then gave an interesting explana- tory address, in which he first of all touched upon the need for a town planning scheme. It was, he said, imperatively necessary on the ground of health. Under the existing conditions as many as 46 houses had been built to the acre in various parts of Warrington, and there were whole wards which had not an open space. The result was at once reflected in the health conditions of the town and neighbourhood. While these doubtless compared favourably with other towns of a similar I character, they compared very unfavourably with the general standard of health in the country and particu- larly with those which had been laid out on better lines. Tee general infantile mortality of the whole of the country was 10G per thousand, and in Letchworth, I the garden city, it was only 36.54. The general death- rate over the whole of the country was 13.4 ; at Letch- worth it was only 6.3. Letchworth was, in fact, believed to have the lowest death-rate in England. Then there ; was the question of economy. The existing state of things was absolutely fatal to true notions of economy. They were all convinced of the need for more open spaces, but they could not afford to buy them, because it would involve the acquisition .of a considerable amount of property. Looking at it from the broad standpoint of the town as a whole, any economist would realise the absolute waste of money in widening Bridge-street, Horsernarset-street, Buttermarket-street and Sankey-street—which had been caused through the want of foresight on the part of our forefathers—the cost was a ouarter of is million pounds already ; what it would be by- the time they had finished he did not know. From the standpoint of convenience town planning had an unanswerable case. At the present moment there was no convenient road between Wilde spool Causeway and Latchford and a great sacrifice of time was also involved by the absence of any outlet from Lancashire to Cheshire between Warrington Bridge and Warburton Bridge. Dealing with the question of amenity, Alder- man Bennett said that was perhaps his particular fad, but the fact remained that the pleasantness and attractiveness of the town had been very little con- sidered in the past. Let them take Winmarleigh-street for instance. It was blocked up by other buildings and was much narrower than it ought to be, and the result was that all that charming view of Cheshire was shut out because their forefathers did not make the street wider,and plan it on sufficient and adequate lines. (Hear, hear.) There was nothing to be said for the haphazard and chsotic way in which things had been allowed to develop in the past. Desirable property could be ruined by the proximity of unsuitable buildings. A man might spend a large amount on erecting a beautiful house, but there was nothing to prevent anyone building a bc.neworks opposite to it. (Laughter.) Inferior cottage property could be thrust into a high-class residential district, thereby causing a deterioration in the letting value of the locality. At present the property owner was saddled with the enormous and often ruaneces sary expense of making streets 40ft wide and paving them with flags and setts, when probably the only traffic was the milk cart and the bread van. Under the Act the Corporation would have the power to relax such bye- laws. (Hear, hear.) There was hardly a country in Europe which had not possessed all the powers of the Town Planning Act—in some cases for several genera- tions. We were almost the last in the field in that respect. Outlining the scheme which the Town Council had in mind, Alderman Bennett explained that the area which it would embrace included all the por- tions of the borough which were not already developed. It was their ultimate intention to work on broader lines in co-operation with the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council, and the Runcorn Rural District Council, and he was elad to say that each of those authorities had signified its willingness to co-operate. Having explained that the conference was not intended to commit those present to any specific scheme, the Alderrran pointed out that the first principle on which the committee proposed to act was the provision of thus opening , AIORE MAIN ROADS, up large areas of land which under the existing conditions were practically incapable of development. It had been suggested tliat they should link up Walton New-road with Wilderspool-causeaay ; make a direct avenue from the Town Hall into Cheshire; construct a road through a tract of land belonging to the Manchester Ship Canal Company and develop it for houses or industrial purposes ; connect Wilderspool- causeway, by a direct road, with Latchford ; make a ne-v road, starting from Forest-street,Latchford passing over the river to a point opposite Manor Locks and continuing to Manchester-road, opposite King Edward-street ; make a river embankment from Howley to Debby's Locks; and provide better communication between Winwick-road and Orford and Fearnhead. It vas also proposed that there should be more direct roads to St. Helens and Sankey. Another feature of the

LIMIT THE NUMBER OF HOUSES

as much as they could with fairness to the landowner and builder. The question of open spaces was linked up with that, and in every reasonable area there ought to be an open space. They could give to landowners and builders substantial concessions for the advantages they asked from them in return. They all realized the absurdity of a uniform standard for all streets and back passages, and another principle on which the Council could act was that more houses par acre should be allowed where open spaces were provided. The alder- man showed bow sedulously careful the Act was of vested interests and concluded by asking the land- owners to assist in trying to evolve out of the chaos which had disgraced and hampered the community so long, a well-ordered, healthy and even beautiful and attractive town. (Applause). Discussion haying been invited Alderman BOLTON said the scheme was designed to make the out-lying districts satisfactory at the expense of those who had to pay rates in the Borough. The question had been kept to the fore by deputations at the Council's expense. The mountain had been in labour and had brought forth a mouse. (Laughter.) The landowners would think "If you develop the roads we shall receive a certain amount of money " Councillor PEMBERTON : I rise to a point of order. Is Alderman Bolton speaking as a member of the Town Council or as a landowner ? This has unanimously passed the Council and I don't think it is a proper position for him to take up. Alderman Bovrox : lam speaking as a landowner. Councillor PEMBERTON : Then you ought to confine your remarks to bow the scheme will affect you. Alderman BOLTON : If you don't want criticism I will sit down. lam a landowner and a ratepayer. The MAYOR : I regret your remarks should be in such a strain.

Aldermen BOSTON : These things ought to have a finality before they are brought up for the confirma- tion of the people who are interested. The MAYOR : There cannot be finality at this stage. Alderman BOLTON : It is practically a scheme ior developing Padget e at the expense of Warrington. Councillor BlnmEs : I must object to those remarks I live at Padgate, and there is no intention, in any shape or form, to bring in Padgate at all. It is outside our boundary. Alderman BOLTON : It is using the ratepayers' money to develop witside districts. Councillor PEMBETtTON : lam sorry to object but I ask the ruling of the Town Clerk as to whether Alder- man Bolton must object only in respect of any land of his which will be affected by the scheme. Alderman BOLTON: I object to the ratepayers' money being used to develop the land of landowners by schemes which are the result of dreaming and that sort of thing. (Laughter.) They
WANT THE MILLF,NNIUM, BUT THEY WILL PAY NOTHING FOR IT. . .

(Laughter.) The MAYOR: I agree that Alderman Bolton has a right to speak as a landowner, but I regret that he does not confine his remarks to the strict argument of the debate. We want fair criticisms. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BOLTON : I have opposed it in the Town Council and said it was a waste of the ratepayers' money to send deputations to London and Germany, just to provide a cheap trio for half a dozen. (Laughter.) The MAYOR : You ought to say this in the Town Council. This is not aTo s n Council meeting. It is a conference. What you have to say, you must say as a landowner.

Alderman lior.ToN : As a land and property owner, I object to having to pay rates to develop land that belongs to somebody else, unless lam perfectly satisfied that it is required. I object to putt:ng fewer houses per acre for some particular fad and then leaving back passages unpaved. I also object to byelaws being framed which are different from those which have already brought the sanitation of the town to its present standard. We don't want dwellings in blocks on the London tenement principle. If that is a development of town planning I am out of it. (Laughter). Councillor PEMBERTON : You are very much out of it. (Laughter.) Mr. H. BRRESFoRD MELVILtE said that without going into details they could support Alderman Bennett in the general scheme. When they went into details they could settle what would affect the landowners of the town.
The MAYOR: You will be consulted from time to time,

Alderman BOLTON: lam only sorry the landowners don't pay the rates. In answer to Mr. Wilding, the MAYOR said the meet- ing would not he committed to a scheme that afternoon. Alderman JAMES EVANS said the Council were com- pelled in some form or other to consider the Act. The Local Government Board would expect from an important borough like Warrington some report on the Act. (Hear, hear.) They could not proceed with the scheme without the co-operation of the interests that would be involved. This meeting was more of a con- sultative character than anything else. They had met to confer with each other.

_ Mr J E SECKER asked what would be the next stage? Alderman BENNETT replied that if any landowner had any serious objection to what was raised, he could put it down in writing and submit it to the Town Council, who bad to consider the objections. If the Town Council again passed a resolution in favour of the scheme they would go to the Local Government Board. In the meantime the various interests would be consulted again. Mr WILDING : Suppose the roads are made, will it be at the expense of the rates? Alderman BENNETT : No. That is purely a matter of bargaining. We can go to the landowner and make some arrangement for give and take.. .

Mr. PETTSR LAWTOZ said he understood that corn- pensation was payable to owners whose property would be adversely affected by the scheme. On the other hand, was it not a fact that where an open space improved the value of land, the owner could be charged on the increment? Alderman BENNETT : But we can only claim half, whereas we have to pay compensation in full. Mr SECKER said he represented several owners who owned a large portion of Warrington, and he should like to propose that so far as they were concerned they gave their co-operation to the rough scheme which practically meant that the Council came before them asking whether they agreed to the boundaries of the borough being the land they would adopt under the Act So far as the landowners were concerned they would raise no opposition to that being the portion of land they would adopt under the Act. Speaking personally he agreed with a great deal of the excellent speech which had been made by Alderman Bennett. He did not agree with many of the details, but he did with the general principle, reserving his absolute right to criticise minutely and carefully and possibly with some opposition. He thought the scheme of town planning would not be very succesaful unless the byelaws were not only relaxed but the almost,impossible byelawswhich existed to-day absolutely removed. Many of the bylaws were absolutely absurd and should be removed before they proceeded to further extension. Alderman JAMES EVANS said there must be a thorough consideration of the byelaws with reference to undeveloped land and street making. The resolution was not put to the meeting, as it was explained that it was not necessary to do so. Mr. DuNLor (on behalf of the Manchester Ship Canal Company) said he had bad the opportunity ot seeing several town planning schemes, but he did not think one had been so carefully thought-out as the Warring- ton scheme. He only wondered at their moderation in stopping at the borough boundary. He however, repre- sented certain lands which were held for statutory purposes and he could not acquiesce in any town planning scheme being considered in respect of them at the present time. . . . .

1.43 AIAYOR : I take it that there are no objections except those which have been already mentioned. We know Alderman Bolton. (Laughter.) Mr. MELVILLE : I take it that Air. Dunlop does not object to the general principle, but that he is not pre- pared to pledge the Ship Canal Company to the scheme. The MAYOR : That is so.

Councillor PEMBERTON' : At this stage. Alderman BENNETT said he was very delighted with the result of their first conference. It augured extremely well for the future. "As to Alderman Bolton," he continued, "I won't trust myself to say any- thing. It has been said with a great deal of truth that 'speech is silvern but silence is golden' sometimes, and I am sure I shall consult my own dignity and the general feeling of the meeting if I say nothing about it." (Ifear,liesr.) The other gentlemen who had spoken, said the alderman, bad intervened in a friendly spirit and with a desire to help the Corporation in the scheme. It was quite clear that on the broad prin- ciples of the scheme, they were practically unanimous. On the motion of Alderman .13F.NsErr, seconded by ' Mr. SECKER, the Mayor was thanked for presiding.

div.head: "GOOD LITTLE STEPHEN WALSH."
div.p: "GOOD LITTLE STEPHEN WALSH."

Mr Melville, the Conservative member for Wigan, speaking in Wigan on Wednesday, in reference to the coal strike, said be did not think there was any man in the whole country who had done such signal service in this crisis as " good little Stephen Walsh." On every ocmision during the last fortnight Mr. Walsh had spoken out like a man, and had shown splendid courage 'in most difficult and trying situations. All Wiganers were proud of the manner in which he spoke in the 1 House of Commons on Tuesday evening.

NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Mr. J. H. Smethurst, who was yesterday elected chairman of the Board of Manage- ment of the Infirmary, has graduated for the position by years of hard work on behalf of the institution, latterly in connection with the Million Penny Fund, and his appoint- ment will give general satisfaction. He succeeds Mr. W. Peter Rylands who has guided the dr.stinies of the committee during the critical time associated with the extension of the Infirmary and the raising of £16,000 to meet the cost of the scheme. - * * *

The general rise in prices that is taking place all over the world is further illustrated by the official figures published by the German Imperial Statistical Office. These show that January's prices topped December's in 21 articles out of a list of 33 ; and com- pared with 12 months earlier the January figures showed increases in no fewer than 30 out of the 39 articles listed. The general level of German prices is now higher than at any time since the Government began to keep its records. What has Protection done for the German consumer? • •

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell was, for once, caught napping at the meeting of the Board of Guardians on Wednesday. It was reported that twelve pigs bred at the Workhouse were ready for killing and the Board had given orders for them to be sold, when Mr. Mitchell interposed with the suggestion : They would be a nice gift to the suffering poor." The Chairman promptly retorted: "1 am very glad to hear you advocating a good feed of pork "—and the Board laughed when it remembered what a staunch advocate of vegetarianism the militant Vicar of Burtonwood is. *

We regret to have to hold over the report of the 103rd annual meeting of the governors of the Infirmary, held on Thursday after- noon. A reference was again made to the Insurance Act and its possibly harmful effect upon the revenue of the institu- tion, and Councillor Roberts characterised the predictions of Mr. W. Peter Rylands, as unduly pessimistic. He, for one, did not share in any degree the Chairman's fears that the Institution was likely to suffer from any want of practical interest on the part of the workingmen, whatever it might lack in financial support from other sections 'of the community. * * * _

Mr. B, S. Townroe was on Saturday form- ally adopted as Conservative candidate for the Middleton Division. He went " the whole hog" very thoroughly by declaring himself an opponent of Home Rule, Welsh Disestablishment, and "for the last ten years a strong believer in a revision of our fiscal system." As this is the first intima- tion we have had of Mr. Townroe's deep-rooted and long-standing fiscal convictions, though he has loomed large in local public prints, we can assume, without doing him any injustice, that they have taken an uncommonly long time to mature. What we always thought was his life's work—the furthering of national military service--seems already to have been choked, either by the free air of Middleton or the rank internal growth of Tariff Reform. * *

People so fond of percentages, as are many of our Tariff Reformers, should be asked to work out a little sum relating to the British motor car industry. We are asked to believe it is in the hands of foreigners. Well, the official figures show that, compared with 1910, our last year's purchases from abroad increased less than 17 in a hundred; while our British sales to foreigners increased more than 28 in a hundred. British quality is gradually but surely overhauling the market. Foreign competition, said the Protectionist Lord Tullibardine the other day at the Scottish Motor Show, " had been the means of making the British motor trade what it was. It had knocked out all the bad cars and rotten businesses, and the result was that, now they had left, we had the very best cars in the world and the most reliable soundest business concerns."

The Town Council. The monthly meering of the Town Council will be held on Tuesday, at the Town Hall. Socialist Lectures. The Warrington Socialist Society has arranged a series of scientific lectures to be delivered in the Co-operative Hall on Monday, Tuesday and Wednes- day next, by Mr. Henry F. Nortlicote.

Hearts of Oak Society. Under the auspices of the Hearts of Oak Benefit Society, a public meeting to explaitt the provi•ionq of the National Insurance Act will be held in Bold-street Wesleyan School on Wednesday evening next The speakers will include Mr. It. Green (Sherringham), president of the society.

An intimation has bet-n received from the Board• of Education that on the results of the science and art examinations held last year, Sydney W Clatworthy has been awarded two Iting's prizes in principles if ornaments and painting of ornaments, and Charles If Price a King's prize in practical mathematics. Rink Hockey. An exciting hockey match betwren Northwich and Warrington Palatine on the rink of the latter club on Saturday evening resulted in the Palatine team being the victors by seven goals to two. The scorers were: Whittaker 5, Cook 2 ; and for the visitors, Morgan 1 and Jones 1.

At a meeting or the Warrington branch of the National Union of Dock Labourers on Saturday, the following resolution was passed unanimously : "That this meeting of the Warrington Branch of the National Union of Dock Labourers of Great Biitain and Ireland wish to enter our emphatic protest against the authorities in arresting Mr. Tom Mann, and the vindictiveness displayed in refusing to grant bail during his remand." . _ _ _ . . .

Warrington Sunday School Union. The inaugural meeting of the Primary Teachers Training Class was held last Friday evening in Friars' Green Sunday School. Miss V. M. Taylor presided. - Miss Porritt delivered a very able and lucid address on The organisation of a primary department." A criticism lesson was given to a group of childien by Miss Winstanley in a highly creditable manner. After the children had been dis- missed, the lesson was criticised and discussed. This was followed by an address on' Reasons for criticism lessons " by Mr. 0. Sinclair.

Railway Ambulance Challenge Cup. The annual competition of the Cheshire Lines Ambulance Corps was held at Liverpool on Friday of last week. The Warrington team (Engineers `Depart- mod) carried off the honours cf the day, being successful with 272 points out of a possible 300. The Engineers have tried bard for the coveted trophy for 19 years, and this is the first time it has been brought to the Warrington Works. Each man was also the recipient of a handsome dinner service. The team which will now represent the Cheshire Lines in the Inter-railway Competition to be held at St. John's Gate, Loudon, in April next, was composed ( f the following: —J Gibson, F Broadhurst (leader), James Dimelow, Jos. Smith and J Wilson. The Late Mrs. Bowden.

In the churchyard at Grappenball the funeral took place at noon on Wednesday of the late Mrs W Bowden, " Clunteif," Victoria-road, Grappenhall (mother of Dr E E Bowden). The Rev H V Pigot officiated. The chief mourners were : Mr W Bowden, Dr and Mrs Bowden, Miss Bowden, Mr W L Bowden, Mr and Mrs G F F White and Dr Langdale. Wreaths were sent by Mr and Miss Bowden, Ernest and Katie," " Billy and Cyril," "Harold," "Ted and Minnie," " George and Dora," " Will, Polly and Children," Mrs Hibbert and Ellen, "Strathmore House," Heaton Moor ; Dr and Mrs Peacock, Miss Bancroft and Mrs M A Braid. The funeral arrange- ments were carried out by Messrs J and NV Dutton, Warrington. Church Lads' Parade. . _ .

A Church parade is an ever popular fixture with the members of the Church Brigade and on Sunday morn- ing there was a good muster of members of the St. Paul's, St. Elphin's and St. Clement's Co.'s on the occasion of a visit to St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, where an eloquent sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Willis. Starting from Arpley Cannons the lads, headed by the St. Paul's Band, marched down the principal streets to the church. Their appearance was the cause for much comment of a complimentary nature; their bearing and conduct whilst on parade being irreproachable. The officers who were in charge of the companies expressed their pleasure at having such a fine set of youths under their care. The members meet on Thursday evenings in Kendrick-street and all intending members are cordially invited. The Gymnasium. There was a large attendance at the Gymnasium on Monday. to witness the annual display by the pupils, who acquitted themselves most creditably in nn interesting series of drills and competitions. The Mayor presided and the prizes were distributed by the Mayoress (Mrs. A. Nield). The champion of the first eight, in the men's section is T. Main, a post office official, of Oxford-street, who carried off the coveted gold medal on the retirement of O. C. Sinclair, who has held the championship for eight years. A silver medal with gold centre was presented to S Woods, the next in order of merit, and the other prize-vvinners were:-3, H Sisson; 5, L Collier; 5, Sanders; 6, R Sisson; 7, 3 BOSCONV S, A Lloyd. The champion of the boys' class is Reginald Hewitt, aged 13 years and 5 months, a scholar at Arley-str.eet school. The other medallists were: 2, J Morns ; 3, A Cade. Miss Amy Grounds, of Grapprhall•road Latchford, has earned the title of champion of the girls' class, and the other medal winners were : 2, A Tyrer ; 3, E C Ward. The Igx.aminer, Saturday, March, 30. 1912.

Town Planning has been brought a sted nearer activity, as far as Warrington is con- cerned, by the conference between the Street Improvement Committeeland the landowners. Warrington may yet become beautiful, if the scheme which the Corporation has in view is allowed to develop on broad and systema- tic lines. There was a distinctly hopeful and encouraging note about Tuesday's conference and, with the promised co-operation of those interested in the land, we may be sure that none of the egregious blunders of the past, for which this generation has had to pay so dearly, will be repeated in the laying out of new areas; but that full regard will be paid to symmetry and attractiveness as well as to the mere utility and convenience of the moment.

United Irish League. A meeting of the John Magion branch was held in the Clubs Rooms, Winwick-street on Thursday evening. Mr D Currie president occupied the chair. The Vice-President (Mr D P Mahoney), commented briefly ,on the great success of the recent St. Patrick's Day dance, and suggested that the Parr Hall be secured for 17 March, 1913. The Chairman spoke of the hopeful outlook for the Home Rule cause, and appealed to those present, and the Irishmen of War- rington generally to do everything in their power to assist the Irish party with funds, so that the shameless campaign of misrepresentation and calumny that was going on all over the country, could be effectively met. Mr. Edward Kelly proposed that the Home Rule Fund 1912 be opened. Mr. William Quinn seconded, and it was supported by Messrs M Conroy and D P Mahonv the latter of whom suggested that the appeal of the National Trustees be cent out without delay.

There is a pleasant story told about Mr. Healey (says the "Yorkshire Observer" London correspondent). Everyone knows his reputation as a member of no party but his own—an Ishmaelite whose hand more often than not is against every man, and every man's hand against him. It is only a couple of days since he was denouncing the Treasury as a thing that he hated and loathed and held in contempt. On Tuesday night, in the closing division, shortly before three in the morning, a Liberal Member sup- porting the Government ran across Mr Healy in the Lobby, and expressed a very natural surprise at finding him there. " Well," said Mr. Healey, "the fact of the matter is that the Prime Minister's speech the bravery and honesty of it—so strongly moved me that I will give that man any vote he asks me to give in support of the policy he thinks necessary to meet the present crisis." No more remarkable tribute could well be paid to the impressiveness of Mr. Asquith 's appeal.

A fire, the cause of which is as yet unknown, occurred shortly after 7 30 ( n Monday evening at the lock-up premises of the Arpley Brush Company, at the river end of Barbauld-street. The Superintendent and Deputy-Superintendent and a good number of firemen were soon on the spot with reel cart, ladders and the steam fire engine the latter, however, not being used. On their arrival the firemen found that a large crowd had assembled, but excellent order was kept by the police, under the direc- thmt of the Chief Constable, and operations were in no way hampered. The premises were blazing furiously, and it was evident that they could not be saved—as a matter of fact they were entirely destroyed, as well as the contents —and an effort was made to prevent the flAttleS spreading to the shop of Mr Acton, plumber, in which was stored a quantity of petrol. In this they were successful and several spectators complimented the brigade upon their excellent stoppage of the outbreak. The adjoin- ing bill-posting station suffered, however, as well as Mr. Boothroyd's shop, a number of valuable musical instruments being damaged. A good supply of water was obtained from the Appleton and Winwick mains
