Rechabltes and the Insurance BM. We would call the attention of our readers to a public meeting and concert to be held at half-past seven this evening in the Friars' Green Suurray school, to be presided over by Mr. J. Jarman. The programme will be provided by the following artists, viz, Miss Elsie Hewitt and Mr G H Gough, soloists, Miss Jarman pianist, and Mr David Sutton, the well- known Lancashire humorist. During the evening an address will be delivered on the State Insurance Scheme, by Mr. J. H. Lear Caton, secretary of the Birmingham Temperance Association, and member of the Board of Directors of the Order of Rechabites. This is the second visit paid ti Warrington by Mr. Caton, and those who had the privilege of hearing him on his former visit will remember him as an exceedingly able and interesting speaker. Mr. Caton comes fresh from the deliberations of the Board of Directors, who are engaged in the task of amending old rules and where necessary formulating new ones, t) be submitted for consideration at the forthcoming special conference to be held at Leicester in Whit-week. In addition to the public meeting, there will be a tea at five o'clock, to be followed at six o'clock by a conference; to these two meetings every Ilechabite is urged to attend. Mr. Richardson Campbell, the high secretary of the Order is expected to attend an afternoon meeting.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"The Witness for the Defence."

Modern " Society" problem plays are somewhat rare attWarrington, which ought to provide an addi- tional reason for generous Dublin appreciation, somehow or other "The Witness for the Defence ' has not drawn large audiences at the Court Theatre this week. The Warrington public is becoming notori- ousl• fickle, and moreover shows a tendency to appreciate the most what is least worthy of aporecia- ,tion.Here we have a play from the pen of Mr. A. E.W. 'Maslen, one of the most brilliant of present-day writers, Ind a play moreover which Sir George Alexander 'made memorable in London. Yet our local 'theatre-goers have scarcely awakened to the fact that an exceptional treat is afforded them by Mr. Alban Limpute Company. "The Witness for the Defence' is an absorbingly interesting study of the mental processes and conduct of ordinary educated people faced with emotional and tragic situations. A drunken, sneering, violent brute of a husband is shot by his wife in a fit of very natural terror and hysteria; he meets with his deserts and passes from the story. But the legacy he leaves is the trial for her life of the widow, who is only saved at the last moment by the coloured evidence of a friend and former lover who knows what lead up to the crime and was present a moment or two befote it occurred. His view is that justice was done when the husband met his death, and that nothing is required of the law but an acquittal of the lady who WAR guilty in deed but not in intention. Subsequent develop- ments shift the scene from India where the tragedy occurs, to Little Beding in England. The lady falls in love, becomes engaged and deems the secret neo she is not called upon to tell to even her affianced husband. Henry Thresk, the champion of the early days and at the trial, thinks differently, and a very strong and dramatic scene between the two focuses the deepe4 attention en Act 3. There is an unexpected denouement, but in the long run everyone earns the justification of all concerned and the lady wins a long- delayed peace and happiness. Mr. Mason' has presented a very strong play, ingeniounly constructed and written with a forcefulness and intensity which are made apparent by the sustained interest of various scenes when only two people are on the stage at once. No ordinary playright can make' the dialogue of two persons suffice for the absence of nearly the whole company for lengthy periods and Mr. Mason's success in this respect is a testimony to his powers of characterisation and genius for writing words, phrases, and arguments which make an appeal to the intelli- gence. The company, as a whole, presents the play most effectively and artistically. Miss Barbara Everest, as Stella Ballantyne, bears off the palm for a dramatic, yet skilfully restrained presentment of a very emotional role. She was, perhaps, a little weak in the first scene when living "under the terror" of a bully, but in the succeeding scenes her acting was full of charm and dramatic power. Mr. J. Herbert Beaumont was quietly effective and forceful in the truly Alexander-like part of Henry Thresk, and filled a big nlace in the pro- gress of the play. The clever light comedy of Mr. Ardene Linden was frequently delightful in the character of Harold Hazlewood, the humanitarian, whose principles require such a lot of consideration and oft-times- fall foul of the dictates of ordinarS common sense. In the part of the lover, Mr. Chas. Mansell was a little deficient in lover-like ardour, and has not quite got the knack of infusing the necessary realism into a stage embrace. The various scenes were skilfully presented, but we fell foul of the " curtain " to Act I. when the tragedy misses fire to some extent (like the gun), and the dead man makes a prosaic bow to the audience within five seconds after being well and truly murdered. This was the only inartistic detail in the whole of Mr. W. J. Butler's fine presentment of all the naked devilry that can be seen through the cracked veneer of a gentleman addicted to cocktails and cursed with a vile temper.,, NEXT WEEK, PICTURES.

Next week, by way of variety, the Royal Court Theatre management have arranged with Mr. Will Onda to present an exceptionally interesting series of pictures, which include the greatest "Problem " picture ever shewn, "Retaliation," an absorbing modern drama. Reproducing scenes from the social and theatrical worlds with all the realism of actual life. The vividly pictured story of a life commencing in humble surroundings and proceeding to wealth and power through a remarkable series of adventures, which are illustrated in scenes which increase in interest and dramatic power right up to the end. Mr. Onda holds the exclusive rights in Lancashire of this film. Other dramatic and comic pictures, will be shown. The Court Theatre orchestra will, under tha direction of Mr. Tom Boothroyd. play suitable music. and Miss Sara Silcock, the popular local singer, will appear at each performance. In all there will be three hours' entertainment at prices varying from is. to 2d. There will be two matinees, Thursday and Saturday, at 2 o'clock with full programmes as at night.

div.head: THOSE CLOCKS.
div.p: THOSE CLOCKS.
MR. ENGLAND BEATING ABOUT THE BUSH.
To TIIE EDITOR " EXAMINER."

Sir.—Your further article on" The Clocks," like its predecessors, was undoubtedly interesting and was I venture to assert put together by a journalist whom the Yankees would call " smart." The dishes have been specially prepared and spiced to suit most of your readers and I have no hesitation in saying most of them were appetising and palatable to the majotity, and no doubt they enjoyed the feast thus set before them.

I should not have attempted to interfere with their digestion if I had not felt that some of the courses were quite out of season. Let me remind you of one. You say "The failure of the Prescot Watch factory has been hinted at in Mr. England's letter in which a doleful extract is given from a pamphlet by a Prescot watchmaker. We have no desire to bring into the glare the commercial and financial reasons for the failure of the Prescot Clock and Watch venture. But speaking in general terms and sustained by the ' experience of H. Williamson Ltd., we are justified in coming to the conclusion that where business enter- prise and sound finance are directed to the trade there is no reason why it should not be eminently successful."

Now, I think that was vary well put together and the remarks made by the journalist on the question would he convincing to anyone who is ignorant of the subject. Let me say first of all that the " Prescot watch- maker" so styled, I presume so as to convey that he was a man of very little weight, was as 1 stated in my letter. Mr. T. P. Hewitt, the leading authority in England in the watch trade and Chairman of the] Prescot Watchmakers' Trade Association. May I add too that he is an inventor of watch m ;vements and was the Managing Director of the Prescot Watch Factory and also who was consulted by the Govern- ment prior to the passing of the Merchandise Marks Act. At least this shows that he was considered by them to be a man of some "light and leading." In politics, as I stated also, he was a Liberal and a Free Trader, but his experience in trade caused him to I absolutely change his views on our Fiscal Policy. Now with regard to the Prescot Watch Factory, sound finance and business enterprise were directed, in its management. It was equipped with the most modern machinery that could be obtlined. What was its history ? The first six years of its existence the factory was enlarged from time to time and profits were made and dividends of 6 per cent paid on both preference and ordinary shares. The output was con- stantly increasing and the prospects most encouraging. At one time over 1,000 employes were at work. Shortly after this Mr. Hewitt in his pamphlet says "The Americans by their hostile tariff system were enabled to thrust the English and Continental makers out of their country. Our trade subsequently began to decline. It decayed in London and Liver pool to such an extent that it might be said to be almost gone—House after House failed and some capitulated by simply shutting their doors Eventually the result was that thousands were thrown out of work—some to-day to be found sweeping the streets and others in the vvorkhouse." You have mentioned Williamsons Ltd. as a success. It is one of the few survivors and happens to be an exception and one of those exceptions which does not prove the rule—for ths rule has been proved otherwise as the watch and clock industry is practically in the hands of the foreigners. No one acquainted with the trade will seriously dispute this statement. With regard to Lady Greenall having purchased foreign clocks, she distinctly states in her letter that it came about through our so-called Free Trade system. She says in her letter "The clocks in ques- tion were supplied by one of the leading firms in the country, and were purchased in a Warrington shop and a good price paid for them." I gather from this that the Warrington firm either had no British clocks or considered the forego clocks superior. The latter is probably the case, for it is common knowledge that the Britisher is losing the art of making clocks, from the obvious reason that he is being unfaiity ousted out of the trade. The consequence is that there are far too few British clocks " ticking " in British homes to-day. And the British workman, like the clock, goes on " strike" and on " tick."- —Yours truly. E. ENGLAND.

Mr. England has gone to a lot of trouble to demonstrate that the failure of the Prescot Watch Factory is an argument for lariff Reform, but that the success of H. William- son, Ltd.. has no bearing on Free Trade. While he probably has a full understanding of the adage that "two blacks do not make one white," he cannot see that a black on one side and a white on the other neutralise each other. To Mr. England, William- sons' success is "one of those exceptions which does not prove the rule," while the Prescot failure is a complete, unanswerable demonstration of the need for a revised fiscal policy. Tariff Reformers have a knack of putting the blind eye to the telescope, and deluding only themselves. This is a case in point. . Other presumptions by our correspondent are equally fallacious and founded on that modicum ot knowledge which is so often a dangerous thing for its possessor. He remarks with an air of finality that
"the watch and clock- industry is practically in the hands of the foreigners. No one acquainted with the trade will

seriously dispute this statement." As a matter of fact "no one acquainted with the trade" would have made so sweeping and foolish an assertion. There are plenty of English makers of high class watches and clocks. The trade that the foreigner holds is the cheap trade, especially as regards the trade in clocks, and—(this is a fact that Mr. England needs thoroughly to assimilate)— it is a trade which we have never held and have therefore never lost.

But the whole point of our argument re clocks was based upon the specific charge that Lady Greenall bought " dumped " foreign clocks as prizes for aa exhibition designed to discourage the purchase of" dumped" foreign goods. That she could have bought English- made clocks cannot be denied. Mr. England says "I gather . . . . that the War- rington firm either had no British clocks, or considered the foreign clock superior."

Mr. England is wool-gathering, if he will I excuse our saying so. The foreign clocks are infinitely inferior to the English clocks, and only worth about one-third the money. If Mr. England will really consult someone "acquainted with the trade," he will not need to " gather " anything but hard facts. Should it be necessary we can furnish him with the name of the place where the " dumped " clocks were made, the name also of the maker, and the price to the English consumer.

Warrington Photographic Society. A large audience assembled to bear the long antici- pated lecture by Mr. G. H. Walker on the Society's summer outings of 1911. They included trips by walking or by train to Hill Cliffe and the Denna, to Pettypool and Vale Royal Parks to Dutton and along the canal at Northwich to Pickering Budge and the Devil's Garden and to Prestatyn, most of which excursions have been recorded in the weekly local pars of this newspaper. The pictures were of views, and incidents by many members, who had lent the slides and negatives to the speaker, and very pleasant it was tolive over again the scenes which made the summer of 1911 grateful to the memory of all who took part in them. Mr. Walker being a native of the Weaver Valley, was able to contribute not a few personal recollections of his own boyhood, and some of the incidents were decidedly laughable. Indeed, his quaint humour, linked with the many historical refer- ences to the places visited, completed a very enjoyable and interesting evening, and in the vote of thanks Mr. Rowlands and Mrs. Lowe expressed the unanimous hopeof the Socciety that the same lecturer will be able to make a similar evening an annual event of tha winter sessfon.

div.head: AN INCREASE OF 6d. PROBABLE.
div.p: AN INCREASE OF 6d. PROBABLE.

The Borough Budget will be submitted at the Council meeting on Tuesday evening by Councillor Wilkinson, Chairman of the Finance Committee. The utmost secrecy has been observed by members of the Com- mittee in regard to the amount of the certain increased call upon the ratepayers. We have reason to believe that an extra call of 6d. in the £, making the rates Bs. 4d. in the E, will be necessitated by the deficiency on Education (E 3,500 and an increase of sinking fund and interest charges of £3,000.

Daylight Saving sill. you permit me to draw the attention of your readers to the fact that if the Daylight Saving Bill came into operation this year, vie should rise iron' our beds and f. dlow our daily pursuits on the first in-rning on which the alteration of the clock would take place, namely, the 21st of April, at the same distance from sunrise as we did this morning, and. therefore, 83 the conditions of life in regard to the early part of the day would certainly be no worse than they were this morning, it is impossible to believe that the change could cause inconvenience to anyone. —Your faithfully,
W. WILLETT.

Sloane-squqre, Llndon, S.W. Match 23rd, 1012. "Principle" in Politics. Sir,—ls the " principle "of the minimum wage now conceded by Parliament to the miners, to be as effective in operation is the " principle " of Women's suffrage conceded by Parliament for many years ? To quote Mr. G. K. Chesterton :—" People seem to think that the conceding of a principle does not matter ; that it is something too vague even to be a pious hope ; a polite platitude before settling down to business, A " principle " binds you to do nothing, leaves you free to obstruct anything. The principle of a proposal ought to be its backbone, the hardest and most unchanging thing in it. With us it is the softest and the wo,t uncertain thing."—Yours etc., V. F. W.

Sir,—l notice that Mr Harold Smith voted against the Conciliation Bill in the House of Commons on Thursday night. As a member of the deputation (Warrington Branch N.U.W.S.S.) who waited upon Mr Harold Smith befote the last election, might I remind him:of a statement he then made. In answer toa request as to whether he would sup- port the Conciliation Bill or not, he answered thus : " I should not think of either voting for or against the Bill, without first consulting the Warrington Branch of the Women'a Suffrage Society." I should like to ask him if during his visit to Warrington this week he fulfilled the above promise?— Yours &e.,
GAL.

Mr Jarman and Endowments. Sir —Speaking at Stockton Heath last week, Mr. J. Jarm3n is reported by you to have asked: "If the Government dropped the question of Disendowment, did they think the Church would worry over Disestablisbment ? " Now I cannot say what Mr. Jarraan's audience would " think "in the event he contemplates, but I venture to assure him that Churchmen " would " worry over Disestablishment since they would regard it as an act of national apostasy. May I ask Mr. Jarman whether Disestablishers would worry over Disestablishment if Disendowment were dropped? Again. Mr. Jarman is reported by you to have said : "So far as the talk of robbery and confiscation was concerned, it should be borne in mind that the funds were not going to the endowment of Nonconformity." Does Mr. Jarman mean by this that a theft is no theft so long as the thief does not retain the stolen property for his own use? If so, this is a revised version of the eighth Commandment which is not generally recognised. Is Pontius Pilate excused because be did not actually himself carry out his sentence or benefit by the result? Further, according to the same zeport, Mr. Jarman said :

"If the Church would be satisfied with Dis- establishment without Disendowment, he would say : "By all means let them keep their endow- ments." That is to say, if the Church will consent to a decree of divorcement, she may keep the property which belongs to her! And lastly, Mr. Jarman is reported by you to have said :

"The Nonconformists had managed without the endowments up to now, and they would still be able to manage and possibly things would go on better than they had done." What does Mr Jarman mean by this? Does he claim some sort of virtue on the part of Nonconformists in that they have been able to manage without property which is not and never was theirs? And, in particular, what means he by " Possibly things would go on better than they had done?" Go on better with whom? And surely he does not mean that Nonconformists have managed without having any endowments, for this is contrary both to fact and common knowledge.—Yours H. J. WESTBROOK, Stockton Heath. March 27th, 1912.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOWLING ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOWLING ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Bowling Association was held in the Pelican Hotel on Thursday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr John Willett, and be was supported by Mr J Wood (lion secretary), G F Freeman (treasurer). and delegates from the Bull's Head Bowling Club, Warrington Liberal Bowling Club, Cemetery Hotel, }glands' Recrea- tion Club, Whitecross Bowling Club, :Junior Conservative Club, Penketh Park Bowling Club. A letter was read Irom Mr George Ball, jun., who regretted his inability to be present owing to sickness in his family. The Penketh Park Bowling Club were admitted as members and resigna- tions were received from the Western Point Bowling Club and the Egerton Arms Bowling Club. A sub-com- mittee was appointed consisting of Messrs George Ball, jun., Skelhorn. Dean and Regan and the secretary, to revise the rules.

It was decided on the proposition of Mr Gleave seconded by Mr E A Burdett, 1.13,1 t the Association join the British Crown Green Bowlitts Association. It was also decided to play home and home matches, and not to work on the knock-out "system.—Mr 0 F Freeman (the treasurer) presented the balance sheet, which showed a balance in hand of 3s Si. He explained that the small loss on the individual merit competition was accounted for by other competitions taking place at. the same time and it was hoped to have the competi- tion earlier this season. The accounts and the auditor's report were adopted on the proposition of Mr J J Critchley, seconded by Mr J Shaw. I\l r A Scott proposed and Mr A Greta ves seconded the resolution that Mr A II Crosfield be the president for the ensuing year. Both gentlemen paid tribute to Mr Crosfield for his interest in the bowling element of Warrington and district. The vice-presidents were re-elected CIL bloc and the patron list is constituted as in the past year. Mr George Ball, Jon, was re-elected chairman of the council ; Mr .1 Wood, hon secretary ; and Mr 0 F Freeman, bon treasurer. Messrs A B Burdett and Isaac Newton were re-appointed auditors. The Pelican Hotel was chosen for the keadquarters of the association.

div.head: RAILWAY DISCONTENT.
div.p: RAILWAY DISCONTENT.

Mr A J Williams, organising secretary of the Liver- pool District of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, say absolute violations are taking place of the August railway settlement, and unless cettain com- panies adopt a saner and more conciliatory attitude towards the men, he would not be surprised if there is a strike in May.

Rochford (Essex) guardians have decided to continue out-relief to a woman of 92, while entitled to an old-age pension, refused to apply for it. A Lenten service was held on Wednesday night in the assembly room of a Frensham public-h use by the village branch of the Church of England Men's Society

Arthur Barri-, a brakesman formerly employed on the London and North-Western Railway, was fined 20s and costs at Chester, on Saturday, for travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from Warrington to Chester without paying his fare and with intend to avoid payment. lair E Gardner, who prosecuted. said that on February 12th the defendant was seen at War- rington Station to enter the 11.30 a.m, train from Warrington to Chester. He was wearing the uniform cap and waistcoat of the company, which aroused the suspicion of a railwayman who was assisting in the working in the train. He told Detective Draw on the arrival of the train at Chester, and the officer saw the defendant go to the booking office sad take a ticket to Shotton. The detective travelled by the same train to Shotton as the defendant, and on arrival there stopped Barris and asked him where he had travelled from, and he replied Chester. Eventually he admitted having travelled from Warrington, and said he had a free pass. He produced this, but it, had expired in December.

div.head: EXTENSIVE RAILWAY THEFTS.
div.p: EXTENSIVE RAILWAY THEFTS.
BEAVY SENTENCES ON WARRINGTON MEN.

For some time past a series of extensive robberies have taken pace on the premises of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and on Thursday morning four prisoners appeared before the presiding magistrates in answer to charges of theft. Three of them pleaded guilty hut in the case of Archibald Edward Freeman the plea was set up that be had been persuaded into admitting the theft,and which was denied by the police.ln the first case Thomas Walton, 13,Monk- street, was charged with stealing a quantity of soap, cocoa and leather to the value of £2 6s. 6d. and was further charged with stealing from the goods yard cheese value £2 ss. The Chief Constable stated that a man named Griffiths, who was a special constable, was on duty at Froghall Sidings about 9.25 on the 20th inst. when he saw the prisoner go up to the door of a van. When the constable asked him what he was doing there, the prisoner answered" Nothing, let me go." He was taken to the pointsman's cabin and subse- quently Detective Clarke and Inspector Forster searched prisoner's house and found tall the goods and in addition a London and North-Western Railway man's cap. When charged prisoner admitted the offence. Mr If Tait, the company's fsolicitor, stated that they would see from the various charges preferred against the prisoners that morning that very extensive xohberies had taken place. Prisoner, who was formerly in the employ of the company as an engine-driver, was convicted of railway thefts in January of last year. Be now expressed his sorrow for his conduct and pleaded for leniency. He was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment— six months on each of two charges. Joseph Taylor, 7, Haydock-atreet, was charged with stealing a quantity of clothing value £1 ss. Gd.from the premises of the Railway Company. Mr Tait stated that the prisoner had been employed by the company for the past two years but had been suspended a few weeks ago on account of the coal strike. He admitted the thefts and the clothes had been found in his house. Taylor was fined £3 or one month's imprisonment, John Doodson, 8, Milner-street, was charged with stealing various goods from the premises of the company to the value of £l.

Mr Tait said that from information received from another prisoner who was in custody, Detective Sergeant Clarke and Detective Goode, of the company's police force, went to Bank Quay Station on the 23rd hlarch and prisoner admitted the offence. The goods were found in his father's house in Milner-street, and also the pawn tickets for some cloth and curtains included in the charge. Doodeon was ordered to pay .£5 or in default one month's imprisonment. Archibald Edward Freeman, 26. Ernest-street, was charged with stealing on the 6th of March two tins of 43x-tongue, the property of the London and North- Western Railway Company. Mr A Browne, who appeared for the prisoner, pleaded "Not guilty." Mr Tait said the prisoner had been in the company's service for 12 months as a temporary goods porter. on the date in question Peter Clare was on duty in Bank Quay station when he discovered the two tins partly covered under some timber. From information received from another prisoner Detectives Goode aud Holland went to the station and asked the prisoner to come with them to the police station, as a man there had accused him of stealing the ox-tongue. lie replied that he had not stolen anything. Prisoner had since admitted that he had taken one tin and hidden it and if the foreman, Clare had not found it he would have taken it away next morning. When charged he replied "The case was broken open and the tins taken out." Peter Clare gave evidence as to finding the tin. He had never heard Detective Clarke say to prisoner " If you will only admit it I will let you go." Detective Clarke said that on the 23rd March he along with Detective Reddington were in the police station when the prisoner was brought in by Detectives Holland and Goode. He said " The case was open and I took the meat." Mr Browne then called Freeman into the witness box and he stated that he was in the yard when two officers came to him and Detective Goode asked him to accom- pany him to the Police Station to make a statement. The officer bad never mentioned that be was going to be charged with the theft. He was kept in the deten- tion room for nearly three hours before he was formally charged. Prisoner alleged that Sergeant Reddington had asked him to admit the theft whilst he was in the room. He also alleged that the officer had said : " It's all right: you might as well be hung for a sheep as a lamb." He would not have admitted it if he had not been promised that he would be let off' He denied ever having even touched the tins. He said to Doodson in the Police Station " Have you had a tin of tongue; I have. " Mr. Browne urged that the prisoner would have been

div.head: CHARGES AGAINST WIFE AND FRIENDS.
div.p: CHARGES AGAINST WIFE AND FRIENDS.

At the Warrington Police Court on Wedneeday before Mr. Charles White and other magistrates Francis Charles Dixon, formerly of 1, Bostock-street, was sum- moned by his wife, Edna, for desertion and applied for an order of alimony. Mr. Browne appeared for the complainant and Mr. Steel defended. In opening his case Mr Brown said that the parties bad been married about seven years and during that time the defendant had only taken his wife out on one occasion. He was of a terribly jealous disposition and it appeared he charged two of his intimate friends with being too friendly with his wife. One of the defendant's friends was in the habit of going to his house and on Sunday night the 29th February defendant went out as usual. Between eight and nine o'clook when the wife was playing the piano in the front room, the friend of the defendant called at the house and was preparing to leave when he met the husband returning borne. The husband made a veiled allegation against his wife and on the following Friday he removed all the furniture and left nothing at ' all in the house except seven volumes of an encyclopedia. The wife had had to go out and earn her own living. Continuing Mr Browne said that the defendant had admitted to three witnesses, he proposed to call, that there was nothing whatever in the allegation. Mrs Dixon gave evidence in support of this state- ment. She denied that any mis-conduct had ever taken place between her and her husbands friends. By Mr Steel : Her husband had not had to complain about her staying out late at night, and he had not complained about men bringing her home from whist drives, dances and the theatre. The visits of the friends of her husband's were not talked about by the neigh- bours so far as she was aware. Tha friend who had come to the house had not done so without his wife's knowledge. He generally brought a message from his wife, who was a particular friend of hers. Mr Steel, continuing his cross-examination, asked if she had not told one of the gentlemen that she was very lonely when her husband was out? Complainant : Not in those words. In answer to further questions, witnees said that when her husband arrived home on the night in question there was no-one hiding behind the door. She tad not said " it was no use, he could not hide,'' unless she said it in a joke. She had told her husband she bated the sight of him because of what he had done to her. The two friends against whom defendant bad made allegations were called, and emphatically denied them Mr Steel on behalf of the defendant, said that from time to time the husband had had to complain about his wife staying out late and when be had remonstrated with her the only reply be got was that she would do as she liked. Statements had been made to the defend- ant with regard to the visits of certain friends of his to the house during his absence and on one Saturday he followed a gentleman to the house and he stayed over an hour. The wife had never informed him of those visits and his suspicions were aroused. He thought there was sufficient evidence to justify the magistrates coming to the conclusion that adultery might have been com- mitted, and the circumstances were such that the husband had reasonable cause to cease to co-habit with his wife and therefore was not called,upon to maintain her.

The defendant who said he was a cycle repairer gave evidence in support of the statements by Mr Steel. On the 25th of February he arrived home late and he saw his friend hiding behind the door. In consequence of that conduct be gave notice to the agent next morning. Cross-examined by Mr Browne : Did you tell a relation of yours that you did not think there WAS any mis-conduct between your wife and your friends? Defendant: No, I had my suspicions. He had never seen anything. He had never complained about his wife going to whist drives but he had complained about his wife going home with other men. The magistrates made an order for Bs. per week and allowed £3 3s for costs.

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Tinnion (in the chair), Councillor T Pemberton and Messrs A J Jolley and 3 Upson. NEGLECT OF CHILDREN.—JOhn Barry, labourer, Bank - street, was charged with neglecting his four children on the IGth March, and leaving them chargeable to the union.—Mr Shearer stated that the prisoner's family had been in and out of the Workhouse for a consider- able number of years. He had not given his wife any- thing since July Ioll.—Prisoner, who said he had no heart to do anything, was committed to prison for three months with hard labour.
TVESDAY:—Before Councillors Roberts (in the chair)

and Jackson Holmes, Colonel Ede'sten, and Messrs 3 Rymer Young, W Richardson and T Locker. THEFT FROM A PAWNBROKER.—Jaines Ray, of no settled abode, was charged on remand with stealing on March 18th a suit of clothes, value 12s 6d, the property of Benedict Tyrer, 100, Buttermarket-street. The prisoner pleaded guilty. Chief Inspector Williamson said the prisoner was seen by a Constable loitering about the shop at 12.30 p.m. The officer watched him and saw him go up to the doorway and take e suit of clothes, and he then arrested him. Ray was sent to prison for one month.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
LATCHFORD.

The first eleven had an exceptionally close match with Stockport in which there was a lot of good hockey. The game opened fast and a good run by Pearson and Dale ended in Travis converting a perfect centre from the latter. Stockport equalized and Fletcher put Latchford in front before the intervtl. The second half was an even struggle, first one side leading and then the other, Hackney nd Travis netting for the home team. Near time the score was 4-4 but the Stockport forwards made a great rally and notched the winning goal. The visitors are to be complimented upon a clever win thoroughly deserved and gained by good play. Their defence was sounder than Latchford's but the forward lines were about on a par. Knight gave one of his best exhibitions at left half and Brad- shaw also did well in a strange position. The second goal for Latchford was the hundredth for the season, this being the second year in succession the first eleven have earned the distinction. In the match Travis also made his personal "bag "into 51 goals which it must be conceded is capital. Since November he has played a dashing game in the exacting position of centre- forward and made good use of the many fine positions worked by the forward line as a whole and by some hard working half-backs. The club programme concludes to-day with a match with Wallasey at Latchford. H Wright, goal ; P Allanson, T Dixon, backs ; P W Isherwood, J B Wilkinson. A Knight, halves ; R A Dale, J E Pearson, H Scott, W Fletcher, C Hackney, forwards. Referee, Mr F Grounds. Bully-oft 2.15 p.m. The second eleven at Wallasey is : Three full backs, H Eccles, W Pickles, It Parkinson, H T Gibbs, A Bradshaw, T Banks, halves ; H R Colton, H Parker, E Banks, W Minutia, H Fletcher, orwards. Train from Central 12.30.

not for them, either as individuals or collectively, to undertake to settle the balance of right and wrong in the serious and difficult questions which had driven a vast number of their fellow-countrymen to the extreme step of abandoning their work and which had brought us all to a condition bordering on industrial chaos and anarchy and, worse still, productive of personal pain and misery. The sorrow of an industrial war, in which there was little or no physical violence, might be often in the end as great as the sorrow produced by a violent international conflict, That, in the present situation, violence had been the exception and not the rule was surely a cause for thankfulness, and at the same time a tribute to the ultimate sanity of our national life and character. Few nations other than our own could have borne the situa- tion of the past few weeks with such quietude and general calm, and we had cause to rejoice in the reasons which had made such a calm attitude possible. Discuss- ing the deeper meanings of the workerss' demand, Dr. Mellor said that, perhaps for the first time in the long story of social development, those dim and silent masses of mankind on whom fell the burden of the actual heavy manual toil of the world, had become excessively con- scious of the fact that the positive fruit of their labout seemed to go for the most part to these whose hands were never soiled by dirt and whose backs were never bent beneath the load. This consciousness might come in a wholly one-sided way, blinding men to all save one fixed idea; but come it did, and its coming served to throw into lurid prominence inequalities in our social existence which were really plain enough, and to reveal weaknesses in our economics organization to which only the name of injustice could be applied. Wherever and whenever it was made this demand for a guaranteed living wage as the due reward of labour pointed backward to a real, though perhaps dim, consciou.ness of fundamental social right and social justice. Beneath all the confused clamour that went on about us, it was not impossible to catch, ever and anon, the voice of a divine right, the echo of a justice that might still rule the hearts of men. Religion could not and dare not be deaf to this : she dare not and could not minimize the importance of these confused and stifled groanings and travailings of justice. Social right and social justice were great things and, in the end, were bound to prevail. The grave confusion of our life to-day meant a new awakening to the power and the possibility of that new and better order of the world, the vision, of which had so often .and so wonderfully a Inspired men since society began s course. ro him it also seemed that we were living in a period when on

necessities of health were fresh air, pure water, whole- some food, physical exercise, sufficient rest, and reason- able recreation. An these were available and within easy reach. Hut society had elected to live in conjested areas and had brought into existence conditions which rendered them inaccessible to a great many people. There was again the manifest disparity b?tween poverty and wealth and in the commercial world for many long hours and low wages, sweated and cheap labour, the unemployed and the unemployable. Theology, philosophy, science and politics had all endeavoured to find some solution to this problem, hut the Christian and especially the New Church man must believe that in the revelation of the infinite wisdom of God the true and final solution was alone to be found. One of the opening phrases of the Lord's prayer taught us to seek that the Divine will should be done on earth as in Heaven. How it was done there the Worci of God did not directly reveal, but tha doctrines received from the Lord by the New Church made it clearly manifest, and were in agreement with the Word which declared that the great need was that earth should become more like heaven. Throughout the Word its divine author insisted on the need of righteousness of fair and honour- able dealing between man and man, of just weights and measures, of considering the poor and of neither Inclining to an unjust judgment by reason of sympathy. with him, nor being blinded by the gifts of the rich. Woe was fpronounced upon those who added field to field, and house to house, who built their house by unrighteousness or their chambers by wrong and used their neighbour's service without wages. " My people " said our God " shall be all righteous." " Racept declared the Saviour " your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees ye shall in no case enter the kingdom of heaven," Righteous conduct leadini,, to centime worship and not formal worship without it was the divine demand. In the writings of Swedenborg we had shown to us how these Divine laws obtained in heaven. There were

Governments there and of them it was said : " All the forms of heavenly government agree in this that they regard the general good as their end, and in that good the good of every individual. The Doctrine of Charity or Life of the New Church again taught us that love of one's countly was the love of the neighbour in a larger form than the love of the individual, The Doctrine of Use asserted that everything was made for use and ought to contribute its use to the general good. Riches and wealth were declared to have an eternal and spiritual side as well as a spiritual and natural side. What was needed in this world was the unselfish love of heaven and removal of the selfish love of hell, all should be of use and contribute to the general good and receive support therefrom in return. Just as in a healthy body every organ lived for the whole and not for itself, so should it be in Society, and just as when an organ became diseased it impoverished the rest sl with Society, cc hen rnqn allowed self interest to stand in the way of the good of others. At the close of a lengthy exposition of these principles of these principles several questions were asked. On April 10th at Atkinson's Cafe at 8 p.m. Mr. Claxton will give an address on" The Atonement," and on the two succeeding Wednesdays on "Redemption and Salvation" and " Miracles."

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
"IDLERS, SOCIALISTS, AND SYNDTCALISTS." COLONEL WALKER ON THE DISCONTENT.

Colonel Hall Walker, M.P., declared to the Ladies' Conservative Association of the Widnes Division on Tuesday that the discontent which was spreading throughout the country must be stopped. They knew perfectly well the causes. It was not so much that individual was against individual, or that men wanted to got this wage or that wage; but it was the principle they had to find fault with and the way the Government was governing the country. The country was handi- capped and manacled, and we should never be better until we bad protective tariffs. The discontent was being fanned by dissatisfied idlers, Socialists and Syndicalists. LAND-TAX REMEDY FOR LABOUR UNREST. ADDRESS TO WIDNES LIBERALS.

Mr. P. W. Raffan, M.P for Leigh, was announced to speak at a meeting of Liberals on Monday night, on " Labour Unrest," but he sent a telegram from the Hou-e of Commons saying that his presence was requi,•ed on the coal trade crisis. Mr. Max Muspratt was also nnable to attend.

Mr. Begot. Of St7l.3.l;e's, said labour unrest was a wages question. Men were robbed of from one-half to two-thirds of their wages just as really as if a man stood at the pay-boxes at the works and collieries and extracted part of the men's takings. Was it, therefore, a wonder that there was labour unrest ? The time had come when workpeople should go strongly, energetically, and constantly until justice was done to the worker. (Applause.) The coalowners had all the forces of his Majesty's Army and Navy at theq. backs. Why was Tom Mann upon his trial ? Because he had said in effect what wit said in the churches every Sunday—" Thou shalt not kill." Thy privileged classes had become frightfully nervous, and these four words were not to be uttered outside the churches. The el ux of the labour question was that of the land, and the moment the people got hold of the correct idea a settlement was in sight. They needed to place the working men of the country in the suns position for weathering labour disputes and strikes as favourably as the masters were placed. (Hear, hear.) The only way to fight the privileged classes was Mr. Lloyd George's Id in the pound on the capital value of land— ,' principle beaten in the Cabinet and never introduced into the house—and present-day troubles would be settled for many years. The fining of enterprise which developed urban estate and provided dwellings and works was one of the sources of unemployment. Follow- ing the miners another section of the workers would come into their own. When they understood the question of economic rent they would also find the solution to the tact: that a rise in wages was always followed by a rise in the price of commodities. Mr Fox. Manchester, moved a resolution expressing hearty approval of the proposal to ttx and rate land values contained in the recent Land and Taxation Reform Memorial, and calling upon the Government to put those proposals into operation at the earliest possible moment. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. INCREASED RATES. The fortnightly meeting of this authority was held ,at IDutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr J Spruce presiding.

DISTRESS AND DISFRANCHISEMENT. A circular was read from the Local Government Board with reference to distress caused by exceptional unemployment, laying down certain rules tor the guidance of the board in giving extra grants to those in distress through the existing state of affairs. The Clerk said he was glad to say it was not neces- sary to do anything in their district up to the present time.

Mr Morris asked if those people who received tern porary relief would be disfranchised. The Clerk : lam afraid they would. I know of no law to the contrary. Mr. Morris said be had attended a meeting at Widnes the previous week where he understood it was not so. Mr. Davies : The l'rime Minister rays it does. The Clerk said he knew of nothing to the contrary. THE NEW CHAPLAIN.

A letter was read from the.ite;i; J T Harwell, of Walton Vicarage, accepting the position of chaplain to the Workhouse. He however, expressed a wish that the stipend offered had been in writing instead of figures because owing to indistinct typing he had taken it that the stipend was -.C50 per annum whereas he now found it was only .£3O. (Hear, hear.) As the travelling expense each Sunday would necessarily be very heavy he hoped they would be able to give him an increase at an early data.

div.head: SLIGHT INCREASE IN RATES.
div.p: SLIGHT INCREASE IN RATES.

The Clerk presented the .showing there would have to be an increase in the poor rate of 1,.d. in the £. lie pointed out that this was due to the County Council expecting an increased relief rate. It might have been possible to have scraped the 3d out of the poor rate had it not been for the existing state of the country at the present time and the possibility of special relief having to be given In reply to Mr. Linaker jun., the clerk said the rate- able value of the district had increased by £3,003 or £4,000 during the year.

The coal tenders were postponed for the present owing to the strike.

DELEGATES' REPORTS. The Clerk reported that along with Messrs Pilling and Mclntyre he attended the Central Poor Law Con- ference in London on February 13th and 14th. The President, who was a member of the Royal Commission on Poor Law, referred at length in his address to the minority and majority reports of the commission. He did not agree with the proposal that Poor Law Union should be swept away and the administration be referred to the County Council. He favoured the retention of the existing authorities with such modification only as might be needed for the efficient performance of their duties. He reminded the delegates that the attack upon Guardians was still strong and their position remained critical The report was adopted. - - -

COAL AND ITS SUBSTITUTES.

Bs C. E. Parker. • In coal we have the earth's great store of energy ; combustion releases this energy, man's ingenuity con- trols and makes it effective. This store, buried for ages, was brought into use and appreciation in the thirteenth century. All our heat is derived from the sun, and coal is the most useful and compact form in which the Fun's heat is conserved. Coal was naturally first used for the heat it gave forth in combustion, the conversion of heat into power came afterwards, a little more than a century ago. For ages tbe muscle of man or beast did the world's work. It was in 1781 that James Watt, thrJugh observing the steam lifting the kettle lid, realized the possibility of the power in water converted into steam and the steam engine was the result. Forty years later Stephenson gave the world the locomotive and our great railway system began. Of the sources of energy available for the generation of power coal is the most serviceable. Coal has now become one of the most important factors that govern the advance of any nation. The future may reveal other sources of ;cenergy, but for the time being the countries that have rich deposits of coal and iron command the material :future. The entire com- mercial and manufacturing system of the United Kingdom rests upon a basis ;of coal. Note how the life and activities of our countly have gathered round the coalfields—the centres of population are by the coal deposits.
PRODUCTION AND STORE OF COIL IN EUROPEAN COUNTRIES ESTIMATED ABOUT 1908.

Production Total Coal Deposits per annum. in Million of tons. Great Britain 236,130,000 140,000 Germany 119,350,000 150,000 France , 34,780,000 17,000 Belgium 21,500,000 16,000 Russia 17,120,000 20,000 Tho above figures of the amount of coal in the different countries are only rough approximations, there may be a great deal buried of which nothing is known. It is cAlculated that at our present rate of consumption British coalfields will be exhausted in about 600 years. None here present need therefore worry unless we take thought of our next incarnation, which may then be due. If economy in consumption does not keep pace and balance the ever increasing demand for coal for power purposes, our rate of progress towards exhaustion may be considerably accelerated; while on the other hand greater economy, and new methods for producing energy, may reduce our present consumption and prolong the life of our store of coal. At present economies are just about keeping pace with the increase of power production, i.e. the amount of coal used for the unit of population remains about the same, 4 tons per annum for each person. There is little doubt our best and most easily worked deposits have largely been used up, a considerable proportion of what is left is at a greater depth and in thinner seams. It is therefore probable that the cost of getting coal will increase, and this will mean an increased price for the raw material for developing energy. A Royal Commission in 1905 compiled statistics showing the percentages of our coal raised for different purposes as follows :
Per cent. Factories Domestic

Iron and manufacture 12'17 Mines Gas Works 6 50 Railways 6.53 Potteries, brickworks, glass works, chemical works 2.16 ' Metal and Minerals '43 Coasting ;learners Steamers over seas Exported 2035 It will be seen that the total amount of our coal exports is 20 per cent, of the coal raised, but a good deal of this is for coaling stations for British ships. We have doubled our exports of coal during the last sixteen years. During the first half of the last century solid fuel , only was employed for the generation of heat and I power, but during the last half of the century liquid and gas eons fuels have come to the front that is for certain purposes. Instead of the heat first converting the fuel into gas, then the gas by combustion in the flue imparting heat through boiler plates to the water, next the water being converted into steam gas ; instead of this, various fuels have been converted into gas' and the gas drawn direct to the engine cylinder and exploded by combustion, the expansion of the gases created giving the power. It is calculated by experts that the average con- sumption of coal for the proc:uction of 1 b.h.p. per hour is 51bs., but with the most economical form of boiler and engine this consumption could be reduced to 11b.This is not a theoretical figu re but is obtainable in practice. If we say that instead of it being possible to reduce the coal consumption for power to a fifth we could reduce to a fourth, we should save upon the 52,000,000 tons of coal used for power production 39,000,000 tons a year. This would prolong the life of our coal supplies for another 100 years, that is to make it last 700 instead of GOO years. It is unneces- sary to say that. In the economical power produc- tion of which I speak there would be no margin for waste in smoke, that is in the form of non-consumed carbon products. More has still to be done in the consumption or combustion of gases. This appears to be possible, and also necessary, because some of the gases which escape as the products of partial combustion are more deleterious to animal and vegetable life than the carbon products observeable to the eye. The gassification of coal and other fuel under control has been for general purposes found to be more economical than burning in an open flue where about nine-tenths of the theoretical heat is lost. I well remember when it was considerEd a good result when we could generate power at a cost in fuel of a penny per horse power per hour ; now about fifteen h orse power can be developed for a penny—that is under the best conditions. I refer here to the ordinary form of suction gas. Not only have there been great economies EffEcted in power production from the same amount and quality of fuel, but much has been done by bringing into use inferior coal and other forms of fuel by more effective utilization. Peat, spent tan, sawdust, and like things, which were useless waste, and costly to get rid of, are now used for developing gas. During the last few years several tanneries have put down producer plants and can with these, using spent tan containing 50 per cent, of moisture as the only fuel,get power enough to drive all the machinery. Other trades have got like I results from their waste materials.

There is little doubt that in the vast peat bogs of Ireland there is a reserve of wealth in this material for power production which will, I believe, in the not distant future, make Ireland almost independent of the coal which is shipped across the channel for power production. The chief disadvantage of peat as a fuel has been, first, the difficulty and expense of getting it dry, peat in the bog containing about 90 per cent, of moisture, and second, its bulk as com- pared with coal increasing its cost of transit and handling. The first difficulty is diminished by the fact that gas can now be produced from peat with 50 per cent, moisture, and the second difficulty will probably be lessened by the erection of power stations on the peat bogs developing power electrically, and conveying it to where it is required by electric cables at the same time recovering sulphate of ammonia and other bye-products. An Irish friend of the writer is driving his linen factory developing 400 h.p. by a suction gas plant from peat alone. There is in the United Kingdom (mostly in Ireland) 6,000,000 acres of peat bog. These deposits vary in depth from 16 to 25 ft. On the basis of dry peat, which could be roughly calculated as being worth half as much as common coal in calorific value, we should have a peat supply calculated on the coal basis of 7,440,000,000 tons, i.e. with a calorific value of 12,000 British thermal units per lb. when perfectly dry. Speaking of Ireland there is one feature about the effect of the present coal strike and coal prices which at first sight seems peculiar, but on consideration as found to be only natural. The price of coal comparing the same weeks, and even days, shows that coals in Ireland, where almost all is imported, was about 10s. a ton,that is contrasting the usual relative prices-10s. a tou—cheaper than in this country. The explanation of this apparently curious phenomena is to be found in the fact that the further you get from the source of supply the reserves proportionately increase. Thus we have it even in this country, the shortage has been felt most acutely nearest the coal pits where practi- cally no stocks are held. When we get across the channel to lieland reserves are always in hand to equalize the irregularities which arise in transport. In the same way it will take a long time before the effects of the coal strike are felt by Captain Scott in the region of the South Pole. On the other hand when work is returned, coal prices will probably tumble down more quickly in the ccal raising centres than in more distant parts. Next week I hope to be able to give information about the financial results of the coal mining indus tries during late years.
The Examiner, Saturday, March, 30, 1912.

EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY. The compensation cases reported in these columns last week brought to mind a very different set collected from various insurance offices and printed in a Nottingham paper a while ago. Among them were the following :.,-;—Cow, whisking her tail, causes injury to milkmaid's eye. gervant receives shock through seeing large Teddy bear when room was only dimly lighted. Barmaid severely hit by flying cork. Man- servant sprained leg through stamping on rat. Domestic, fetching coal out of cellar, collapsed from fear caused by silent appearance of washerwoman,and broke her arm. Coachman, proceeding from stable, struck on face by master's slipper, intended for sing- ing cat. Cook, breaking coal, piece went down her throat. Curate scalded through stumbling, whilst carrying tea-urn at parochial gathering. ,Travellers nose injured in collision with lamp-post. Butler's hand injured by pia in embracing patlourmaid. To the latter a contemporary added. the characteristic American ease of " severe injury to hand in endeavouring to hold tongue." FAMOUS CLOCKS.

Those Dump ' Exhibition clocks of Lady Greenall's bid fair to rival some of the historic timepieces of this and other countries. By-the-bye, what in an article in "'rho English Illustrated Magazine" has been described as "the oldest clock now existing in England" is the Wells Cathedral Clock, which was removed from Glastonbury Abbey to Wells in the reign of Queen Elizabeth. The dial plate is 6ft Gin. in diameter. The outer circle is divided into twenty-four parts, to represent the twenty-four hours of the day; the numbers are in Old English characters, and mark the hours from twelve at noon to midnight, and thence to twelve at mid-day. An inner, or second circle, gives the age of the moon, while on a still smaller circle is a female figure, having round it the motto, "Sc Peragrat Plnebe." Round a tower above the dial-plate knights on horseback

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
MR. B. S. TOWNROE.

The formal adoption of Mr. B. S. Townroe, of Warrington, as prospective Conservative candidate for the Middleton Parliamentary Division, has been finally ratified. I am well acquainted with the constituency. It acquired an unenviable notoriety for wobbling but has latterly become more stable. 'ihe neighbouring division of Sovverby has all along remained consistently and overwhelmingly Liberal ; but until the advent of the present Member, Middleton regularly alternated with each election, returning now a Liberal then a Conservative. Sir Ryland Adkins is the first representative who has succeeded in stopping this game of see-saw. Though each election since he appeared on the scene has been hotly con- tested, and guns of heavy and formidable kind (to say nothing of small " bores" innumerable) have been brought to bear upon the citadel, it has withstood the last three assaults, and of those who have led these one after another has gone for reward or consolation elsewhere. Middleton is steadily becoming the forlorn hope that Sowerby has always been, but the Tories who have so constantly fought the one are not likely to neglect any possibilities in the other. Mr. Townroe may expect a lively time among the cotton operatives of the division,for they are keen and earnest politicians, and take matters seriously. FEEDING SCHOOL CHILDREN.

I gather that, should the necessity unfortunately arise, the Local Education Committee will be in a position to provide meals for some 800 children of the town. Well, as one speaker upon the subject remaiked the other day, you cannot cram brains of school children if their stomachs are empty. I

The other evening I accompanied a friend to a meet' ing of an Esperanto group in an East Lancashire town, and I was able to follow a good deal of what was said during the conversation for practice. Two rather good stories were told, and as they were both new to me, they may interest others. A member said a friend at whose house he was spending an hour or two rose to show him something concerning which discussien had occurred. As he began his search for the article, his wife entered the room. " What are you looking for? " she asked, and he, not wishing to explain just at the moment, replied "Nothing." " Why " quietly pursued the lady, "you will find that in the whisky decanter! " The other little anecdote was perhaps more to the point. A lady friend had a smattering of French, and on a visit to Paris went into a shop to air 'it in company with one from the same town who spoke the language more fluently. Said the former to the latter, " I want to ask for some scent, but I can't for the life of me tell what's French for eau de cologne!" SPECIALLY COMMENDABLE.

I note with satisfaction that the Warrington Esperanto Society has a membership of half-a-hundred, and a most enthusiastic band of cfficers. In a booklet issued by the British Esperanto Association, I read that the new language is being taught in all kinds of schools on the Continent and in America. A large number of commercial firms in Great Britain and on the Continent use Esperanto in their correspondence with firms and individuals in other countries, and issue their trade circulars printed in that language. By special circular the Ministry for Railways in Austria has called the attention of its staff to the value of the international language and has officially recommended its employees to learn the system. This year's congress, fixed for August, is to be held in that country, and as I write I have before me a handsome, copy of a profusely-illustrated guide already issued in anticipation of the event. It consists of considerably over 100 pages entirely in Esperanto. I know several who attended the Congress at Antwerp some eight months ago.. There were 1,700 present from ail parts of the world Fourteen national Governments sent official delegates namely, Great Britain, the United States, Belgium Austria, France, Germany, Guatemala, China,Norway, Brazil, Roumania, Russia, Spain and Switzerland. Twenty-eight nations sent national delegates. As a correspondent testified at the time, it was common enough to see South Americans, who knew not a word of German, conversing eloquently with Hungarians who had no knowledge whatever of Spanish or Portu- guese. Warm friendships sprang up between persons who did not know a single word of each other's language, and yet talked with each other as freely as if they wei e using their own mother-tongue. I fear that England lags behind somewhat as to this import- ant movement. lam impressed with the evidences of its progress and extension in almout all other countries. In turning over the leaves of my Esperantist acquaint- ance's albums, I find that the Japanese are among those who have taken it up warmly, and of course it is as easy to communicate with them as it is to inter- change courtesies with Russians, Germans, French,and people of other nationalitieu who write in Esperanto. I fancy too many in this country labour under misappre- hension as to this. As I understand it—indeed, we have positive assurance on the point—Esperantists do not aim at making Esperanto a universal language to the point of crushing out; all the existing languages of the nations. They believe that every man ought to be able to speak two languages—a national language and an international language. The Russian ought still to speak Russian and the Englishman Englisb,but they ougnt at the same time to be able to converse with each other in Esperanto. That is so simple a matter through this medium that, slight as my acquaintance with the new language is, I can read post card messages in it written by any foreigner whose vocabulary is reasonably restricted.

At some distance from the clock, and at a higher elevation, is seated the curious figure of a man, in the costume of King Charles 1., which vigorously strikes every quarter of an hour with its heels against a bell, and can also be made to strike the number of the hour with a hammer. The Stras- burg Cathedral clock is still more remarkable—very much more wonderful in fact, but I must not venture upon the details here.

"-A FINE DODGER." "Uncle Caleb's" story for the children under this heading reminded me of a yarn which an old soldier who had served in India used to spin for me when I was a youngster. Put as briefly as possible' it was to the effect that he was once in a cavalry charge, had occasion to alight for a moment, sought and obtained the colonel's permission, and had no sooner left the squadron than a cannon ball took off the head of the man wbo had ridden into the position the, he had himself occupied but a moment before ! Time was when .I believed that and mary elled. Now, of course, I know it will not bear the slightest investigation, and I wonder, not so much at my childish simplicity in swallowing it at any time, but at the audacity of the narrator—and he a compositor, too! "WEATHER LORE."

During the last —keen frost, my hairdresser (he objects to the desciiption " barber ") said it meant so much loss to him. I expressed surprise, supposing that men would have to turn out to be shaved and so forth as usual. "No," said he, "it's not so. They get toasting their toes at the fire, and won't stir for anything unless forced. My receipts are already 7s. less to-day than last week at this time. I next had occasion to look in on my tailor, and be said, "Now if this weather had only come a month or so ago, there would have been a demand for overcoats ; but it's too late, now." My bootmaker guessed that a thaw would make things hum a bit, though plenty of rain was all right for his trade: The subject has been dealt with in the "Children's Corner" of late. Last Saturday's con- tribution was on " How to foretell the weather," and it was shown that animals and birds are acutely affected by atmospheric changes. Mr. Inwards, who has written a book on " Weather Lore," has the follow- ing note on this point: "The observations of naturalists, shepherds, herdsmen, and others, who have been brought much into contact with animals,have proved most clearly that these creatures are cognisant of approaching changes in the state of the air long before we know of their coming by uther signs. To many kinds of animals, birds, and insects, the weather is of so much more importance than to us, that it would be wonderful if [nature had not provided them with a more keenly prophetic instinct in this respect."

I had the prescription filled the same night, and in the morning I was up, my cold was gone, my heart normal, and though I had a little pain during the day, I have not had it since. I gave it to my mate, and he tells me that he has lost his Rheumatism and Lumbago. "The prescription was this : Go to the nearest chemist's shop and get GO grains of Kephaldol in tablet foto]. Take two tablets at once, and then one every hour until the pain is gone. I took three when I went to bed, and broke up my cold."—Mr Johnson Hicks, Newcastle.

THE GREAT INURANCE ACT.

div.head: HOW THE ACT AFFECTS FRIENDLY SOCIETIES & TRADE UNIONS.
div.p: HOW THE ACT AFFECTS FRIENDLY SOCIETIES & TRADE UNIONS.
BY L. G. CHIOZZA MONEY, M.P.

Friendly societies in the past have been too much neglected by the Legislature. The National Insurance Act gives for the first time full and proper assistance to those in- stitutions, and proper protection to their members in respect of their insurance. What has been done in the past may be gauged by the amount of the total annual vote for the negistry of Friendly Societies, including the Assistant Registries of Scotland and Ireland. It amounts to the paltry sum of £9,910 in 1912. We need not wonder, then, that the great majority of friendly societies, apart from the great affiliated orders and centralised socie- ties, are in an unsound financial condition. Millions of friendly society members are not insured for the benefits they subscribe for. It is, of course, a dangerous business to em- bark upon without expert guidance. With regard to trade unions, benefit work has been always done knowingly on a non- actuarial basis. The idea has been to make the whole of the funds of a trade union avail- able for any purposii at any moment. They have accordingly adopted the rule-of-thumb method of paying out sickness claims as they arose, accumulating no proper reserves, and relying upon levies, if necessary, to regain solvency if funds should run out. It is, of course, a most uneconomic method of con- ducting health insurance work, and for the good of trade unions themselves it ought to be ended. The National Insurance Act, by encouraging them to end it, performs a &tat service for the trade union movement.

div.head: EFFECT OF 4CT ON FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
div.p: EFFECT OF 4CT ON FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

The National Insurance Act "Interferes', with the work of friendly aocieties and trade unions by compelling workers to insure them- selves against loss of health. A worker, find- ing 4d. deducted from his wage for sickness insurance, would in many cases be compelled to give up his friendly society subscription if the State Act did not enable the friendly society to carry on the State Insurance. But that is precisely what it does. The friendly society has a constitution and rules which are of the general character required by the Act for an "approved society." A great deal of nonsense is talked about extra work thrown on friendly Societies by the Act, and as to making official returns, keeping official accounts, &c. It is forgotten that friendly societies either are now keeping proper accounts or ought to be doing so, and that, if registered, they now make returns to the Registrar of Friendly Societies, and have now, if registered, to make a periodical! valuation.

It will be understood that the members' contributions pass vi tl the employer, vi tt the Post Office, to the Insurance Commissioners. The approved society, however, shoWs by its members' insurance cards what is due to it from the State, and obtains credit accord- ingly. Out of that credit the Insurance Com- missioners, adding the proper State•contribu- tion which they have received from the Treasury, furnish them with the funds to pay benefits. It is all delightfully simple and automatic, as most things are when they are done on a big scale with proper organisation. It should be added that an approved society is allowed to invest its own members' four- pences, but I really do not know why it should want to do so; investment is much better left to the central authority. The National Insurance Act, Part 1., is concerned solely with Health Insurance; there is nothing in it, however, to forbid a friendly society from continuing funeral money benefits or any other of the proper purposes defined by the Friendly Societies Act. The society simply keeps one depart- ment for the National Health scheme, and adds to it what other departments it pleases within its existing scope. The male worker pays 4d. to it through his employer; he can pay as much more as he pleases for additional insurance.

div.head: COLLECTING SOCIETIES._
div.p: COLLECTING SOCIETIES._

Friendly societies proper should be care- fully distinguished from " collecting socie- ties." The latter are societies which employ paid collectors to gather contributions at a greater distance than ten• miles from their registered office. Their business is practically confined to funeral money benefit; in the nature of the case they cannot check sickness A collecting society can become an ap- proved society if it establishes a separate branch to work the National Health Insur- ance. Many of them doubtless will do f3O, and if this proves to be the case, so much the better, for, in effect, in each such case a col- lecting society will have established a proper friendly society branch. EXISTING FRIENDLY SOCIETY FUNDS RELEASED.

Every worker compulsorily insured by the Act enters insurance at the same flat rate of contribution, normally 4d. for a man and 3d. for a woman. Every worker aged sixteen to sixty-five is treated as though sixteen years of age, and this, is accomplished by drawing upon the entire insurance fund in order to create for each person over sixteen a reserve fund such as he would have accumulated if he had been contributing ever since he was six- teen. By this means the whole of the insured are made sixteen years of age for insurance purposes. It follows that, as a friendly society mem- ber becomes compulsorily insured under the Act, he is furnished with a new insurance re- serve, and does not need for the purposes of the National Health Insurance his existing reserve, which he has built up by his own thrift. That means, of course, that his exist- ing reserve is released. Under Section 72 of the Act his society may entirely revise its finances in view of this important fact, and may make a scheme either increasing the benefits of its members without increasing their subscriptions, or reducing their subscriptions, or combining both methods. What happens in kPalk is that under the Act the friendly societies gain- a very large sum—£lo,ooo,ooo or more.

Of course, when a friendly society is not solvent it cannot gain very much, but it must gain something. Its members are eet up with new reserves, and their old reserves are there- fore released to give them some degree of extra benefit.

THE SPECIAL CASE OF TRADE UNIONS. In the case of trade unions doing friendly society work, as has been explained, they have not hitherto built up insurance reserves, rely- ing upon their power of levy to get straight at any time. There are, therefore, no reserves to be released, as in the case of such a society as the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows. Nevertheless, let it be remembered, their members are furnished with reserves by the State scheme, and they are therefore, in re- spect of the Health Insurance, put on their feet from an actuarial point of view. That means a great accession of strength to a trade union, since it can use more of its members' contributions for the main purpose of trade union work, viz., improving the conditions ot employment of its members. Further, out of the many millions of corn- pulsorily insured persons, trade unions have the opportunity, by forming branches, to work the National Insurance Act as approved societies, to gain millions of new members. Many existing trade unions are small bodies, but they need not be shut out on that round. The Act allows small societies, whether friendly societies or trade unions, to become approved, only providing that they shall to a certain extent .pool their risks by association with other societies. For the sake of trade unionists themselves, it is earnestly to be hoped that the small trade unions will thus group themselves, for a federation of British trade unions by groups is a thing devoutly to be desired. British trade unions, indeed, have a mag- nificent opportunity in./this matter. If thex

A BOY'S ESSAY ON THE TERRIER. A boy who owns a fox terrier sends me the following amusing little essay. He is quite a youngster, having just left school and gone to his first situation as office boy. I wonder if the piece is his very own? Anyhow, here it is :

"The fox-terrierds a small black-and-white disturbance which afflicts and delights many families. He is active and beautiful, like a college sophomore, and has the sophomore's habit of starting a new variety of trouble at any time on a second's notice. The fox-terrier has thin legs, an active expressive mouth, a lean, well-shaped head, talkative eyes, and a nose which leads him swiftly from one misdemeanour to another. Originally ho had a libet,l tail, but it has been edited and revised by man into a more stump. This was done because of the fact that when the fox-terrier's tail was as active as his head it took two people to watch him with even partial success.

The fox terrier is a house pet and is clean and dainty in his habits. He lives on meat, milk, potatoes, mice, old shoes, curtains, books, mahogany table legs, opera hats, and tablecloths. In return for this diet he guards the house with unremitting ferocity. No burglar can come within a street of a fox- terrier's family without dislodging an erup- tion of barks, howls, whines, shrieks and sniffs from the faithful brute. He also guards the house against all cats, dogs, street-cars, late pedestrians, bats, owls, dead leaves, and moonbeams which may chance to pass the place at night. After a family has got used to a fox-terrier and has lost him temporarily it can sleep right through a boiler explosion and fire next door without so much as stirring. ,Losing the fox-terrier is the favourite diversion of the family which owns him, or at least pays the tax on him. The ordinary fox-terrier has a larger acquaintance around the town than the postmaster and dines in a new place everyday. Owing to his wander- ing disposition the terrier is loved twice as much as ordinary dogs. He is frantically welcomed when he returns home, and the family is grateful when he goes away again and gives it a rest. :Very few people have seen a fox-terrier die, because he almost always loses himself first.

The fox-terrier is vivacious, audacious, ingenious, mercurial, hysterical, wheedle- some, companionable, affectionate, optimistic, fickle, restless and irrepressible. AN ENGINEERING POEM. A road that leads to sure success Can anywhere be made By any one, without the need Of other people's aid; The formula is simple, too, For all to understand— The road must be macadamized With lots of grit and sand. Some try to build their roads on luck, But that's uneven stuff, It may hold out a mile or two And then turn out too routth ; Half-finished roads, begun with it, Stretched out on every hand, But the real highways that go on, Are laid with grit and sand. Some build on influence, but that Has ruined many a road; • It stands fair weather well enough, But when it's o'erflowed By winter storms, it melts away, Dissolving what was planned ; No ! roads that last through rain or shine Must be of grit and sand. Some builders think that cleverness Is certain to succeed, And some believe in taking risks, And some in making speed; But still the same plain formula Works out in every land— The roads that always reach the goal Are laid with grit and sand.
—Priscilla Leonard. THIS WEEK'S STORY. FULL OF GRIT. He: "The motor is doing fifty miles an hour. Isn't it splendid? Are you feeling afraid ?"
She: (Swallowing another mouthful of dust.) "Not a bit dear. I'm full of grit."
