She reached out her hand and touched ills arm. All the wiles of the accomplished co- quette were at her finger tips, and it was necessary to her scheme of vengeance to have this man who was passing under the name of "Smith" her willing, dazzled slave. "We are friends, you and I," she said soft- ly, "and we have one common bond of in- terest—that of Clifford Hawke."
"You have not told me why you hate him," he said suddenly. She smiled.

"We have only met twice, and in that time have talked about so many other things. But I hate Clifford Hawke because I know him to be a bad, false man, and a liar, and I should like to see him exposed for the man he is," she finished under her breath. "Now tell me what you have done," she went on. "I am longing to know." "I have already ten thousand shares in the mine that Hawke has his eye on, and I am the biggest shareholder in it now; by and bye I shall buy up the other remaining shares, and as Mr. Smith' I shall hold Hawke up financially. He has dropped a lot of money lately, besides having borrowed far more than he can pay back. I know that he is already heavily in debt, and that his credit is not so good as it was." "I am glad," she said slowly. "I want to see him down--so far down that he can never risd again. You can do this for me?" He nodded. "Yes, but one day we shall come face to face, Hawke and I, and then there will be another settling day—beyond the financial one."
"Are you quite sure that het believes you dead?" she said.

"Quite. You see my old pal Cardew stayed at Claverton-street that night, and was wearing my clothes. There was no posi- tive proof that I was not there too. I had in- tended to stay with him, but as I was going into the country for a couple of days, I could not. I suppose .he let himself in with my latchkey and the landlady never saw him

div.p: OUR SERIAL STORY.

as I told her last week to be brave. If you are not it will only be more difficult for her." "Brave!" he exclaimed bitterly. "I am to see my life's happiness filched from me by a designing scoundrel, and then grin and bear it! Of course you may depend upon me not to thrust myselt upon tier,' he went on, "but one day I shall punish Clifford Hawke for this last coward's work."
Lady Mary looked at him with startled _

"What do you mean, dear" she said quickly. "I mean that while I was lying in that hospital I have been thinking, piecing, to- gether a puzzle, and now I know that I was purposely kept away for those ten days be- fore that wedding—that I owe my detention to Clifford Hawke's evil agency." "Surely you are mistaken!" Lady Mary said quickly. "You must not let your natural disappointment and grief warp your sense of justice. I don't like Clifford Hawke any more than you do, and yet I am con- vinced he had no idea where you were." "And yet he told you and Stella that I was at Ostend, well and flourishing," he broke in quickly. "You would not tell me who gave you both that piece of lying information, but I found out that Clifford Hawke had been to Ostend during those ten days, and it did not take me long to put two and two together." "All the same," she repeated, "you must ' not accuse him without proof, Jasper, and' for Stella's sake, I hope you will remember that any public quarrel between you and Clifford Hawke would only pain her in- ' finitely more than it would him."
"Heaven knows that I would rather die than brinv any worry ilauvi hex dear bead."

div.head: BID FOR A BRIDE
div.p: A BID FOR A BRIDE
BLANCHE EARDLEY, Author of " Kitty Bell—Actress," "The Lady
Killer," &c.
CHAPTER XVI.
"FOIL HER SAKE YOU MUST NOT SPEAK."

Stella sat with a white tense face listen- ing to Lady Mary's worldly wisdom. They had driven home to Lady Mary's house, and though the servants had been too well trained to show any surprise, they were sure to express themselves freely in the w.:.rvants' hall, and it was this view that Lady Mary W3B impressing upon Stella in the drawing. room.

"It's madness, dear, sheer madness; you married the man—took him for better for worse only yesterday, and you must live with him. Think of the scandal, the awful laugh- ing stock you are making of him and your- self. You must go back." "I can't," Stella whispered hoarsely. "You blame sue now, but I did not go without a struggle; I knew it was my duty to stay, but I could not. I had a telegram from some anonymous person telling me to ask my hue- band about his first wife and child, and when I taxed, him with it he did not deny that ho had been married before. He had lied to me, cruelly lied, and when I asked him about it, he laughed and said the past was not my business, only the present!" "Of course it's not pleasant to know that he had kept it from you," Lady Mary said, "but, my dear child, that hardly constitutes a good reason for leaving him like this." Stella rose and paced the room restlessly. Her face was. flushed, and there was a look of .pain in it that made Lady Mary's heart ache with unspoken sympathy. You have not heard all," she said in a low voice; "he seemed infuriated when lie saw the telegram I had received, and all his superficial polish left him, and—and—he kicked Fifi, the dog, out of the drawing-room and then insulted me because I left the room and took her upstairs. Oh, dear Auntie," she went on, falling into the old childish form of address of years ago, "you don't know how I hated him when I saw him kick that dog." Lady Mary sighed. "It's very dreadful, dear; I sympathise most utterly, but what can you do? The man might be a scoundrel in hie home, but he probably was unstrung and excited at the thought that you were criti,lising him. Give him a trial, dear. Think of the insult you have dealt him by leaving him." "That is nothing compare a to the trap he laid for. me," she retorted tiuiekly; "he even told me that lie about Jaspar being at Os- tend! Why should he have said that? He must have guessed that I was going to try and break off my engagement to him, and he plotted to prevent me. He is cruel and bad; why, it was his car that knocked down poor Lottie that time, and he did not even step to help her or call when she was ill! I will never —never go back to him—nothing will make me!"

"Mr. Hawke," said a servant's voice at the door, and turning sharply both women saw Clifford Hawke, suave and polite. His eyes rested for a moment on Stella, then he glanced at Lady Mary. "I am sorry to intrude, Lady Mary, but I have called for my wife," he said. "I knew I should find her here."

_ "I was amazed when Stella arrived, Lady Mary said gravely. "She seems to have a good reason for running away, Mr. Hawke." Ile laughed contemptuously. She is hysterical and foolish. I punished a stupid little animal for getting in my war, and Stella immediately thought fit to run away and denounce me as a scoundrel!" You know it is not only that," Stella said quickly; "you know that von dared to cruelly kick my d 0... You ie about that even as you lied about having seen Mr. Ten- nant in Ostend!" Clifford llawke's face grew livid,'and for a moment he looked as though he would break into a raging temper, but he controlled him- self with an effort and said quietly: "I see you have met this Mr. Tennant." "I was at the hospital where he is, and Stella went with me, Lady Mary broke in hurriedly. "I don't think, Mr. Hawke, that you will do any good by hectoring Stella. I am sure she will return to you if you meet her half way." "Am I to understand that you intend to keep up. this ridiculous attitude?" he said, turning to Stella abruptly. "I may be rough and clumsy in my manners, but that does not prevent mt from loving you. I have never cared about a woman really till I met you; my other attachment was a calf love episode. You are the love of my manhood." He had dropped for the moment the bully and become again the man who had wooed her, and for the first time since then Stella felt sorry for him. Sorry that she was so in- different to him, and far, far more sorry that he cared as he said he did. She turned to him wearily. "You protest a great deal of affection, but I don't see how you can explain the false- hoods you have told me, or the cruel callous arts of which you have been guilty. lam not now speaking of your first marriage," she went on, "but of the things you have done since we met." "I am unfortunate in possessing a hasty, uncontrollable temper," he replied. "I have lived much alone in my life, with no woman's influence to soften me, and I know I am lacking in the tender consideration to which you are accustomed, but if you will take .111) your life with me I will mend all that, and never offend you again. After all, it's hard luck on a man to marry him and Five him no chance of proving his repentance. "If you will leave me with Lady Mary for nioment," she said slowly, "I will try and make up my mind, but I shall have condi- tions which you must agree to before I can live with you tinder the same roof." He bowed, and when the door had closed upon him Stella reached out her hands to Lady Mary- "l see now—it is my duty. But though I will share his home, I can never really live with him as his wife. I cannot! I was mad not to have realised before what it meant." "I am glad you are going back, dear," Lady Mary said gently. "It is the only thing you can do now. Give him another chance!' Stella pressed her hand to her brow. "I will try, though I can't help feeling that• there is a mystery somewhere, that I shall learn far worse things about this man who is now my husband! Oh, if only I had waited," she broke out passionately, if only I had not given up hope, I should have been free to marry Jaspar now "Dear," Lady Mary said gravely, "if you want any peace in your married life you must put all these thoughts behind you and be brave. Though you cannot love your hus- band you can at least behave outwardly as though you were happy with the lot that has fallen to you. All the other arrangements of your life together lie only between you and Mr. Hawke; no third person can interfere between you." "I understand," Stella said wearily. "I will do my best, but promise me that you won't let Jaspar think I have ceased to love him," she went on with a sudden flush. "I shall always love him—always—though I shall have to lock it all away in my heart!" She paused a moment, then in a different voice said: "Call him in and tell him that I will go back, and as you say, we must settle how we shall live when we are alone."

week later Lady Mary was talking to Jasper Tennant in the room where she had last seen Stella patch up her quarrel with her husband. Jasper was better, though still weak, and as she looked at his pale face Lady Mary knew that he had learnt the news about Stella's wedding that she had kept from him all this time. "So you read it in the paper?" she said cranthr- " Um dear bor. YOU =lSt be brave,

Jaspar exclaimed, "hut I will. find 'out the truth, and when I am convinced that my suspicions are right then Clifford Hawke, successful financier as he is, will have to meet me face to face." "And Stella—what of her if she shourd learn that her husband, the man to whom she is tied for better and for worse, is the cause of your failure to keep, your word?" Lady Mary asked gravely. 'Whatever you dis- cover, Jaspar, whether rightly or. wrongly, for her sake you must keep silent now." "Yet.it may be for her sake that I shall have to speak one day," Jaspar answered slowly.

div.head: CHAPTER XVII. ISOBEL FRANT PAYS A VISIT.
div.p: CHAPTER XVII. ISOBEL FRANT PAYS A VISIT.

Isobel Frant was one of those women who, when they hate, do so with a thoroughness that might have been 'applied to a worthier object. There were two people whom she now hated with the full force of her strong, passionate nature, and they were her cousin Stella and Clifford Hawke—the girl for win- ning the man she wanted for herself, and the man for loving the girl. When Stella and her husband were on their honeymoon, Isobel spent her time as she liked, having absolute freedom given her by Mr. Traine, who never made any effort to control her actions. One morning she received a letter thatmade her smile with satisfaction, and after, breakfast she left the house, and walking down Park- lane, boarded a motor 'bus that ran out Ham- mersmith way. Presently she got out, and turning down a street past Hahimersmith- bridge, she walked down it, and stopped at No. 15. In answer to her request to see Mr. Smith the woman who opened the door stared at her curiously for a moment, in a way that brought a flush to Isobel's face, and said curtly: "What name, please, Miss?" "Just say a lady wishes to see him," she replied quietly, and there was something in her manner that checked further curiosity on the part of the landlady. In a few seconds she returned and said, "Come this way, please." Isobel followed her and found herself in a sitting-room facing the back garden. It was a pleasantly furnished room, plain and home- ly, and had communicating doors which evi- dently separated the bedroom from the sit- ting-room. As she stood gazing round curi. ously, tne door opened, and a man entered the room. As soon as he saw Isobel he flushed awkwardly beneath his sunburnt skin.
She held out her hand with a smile. You see I got your letter this morning, and_have come at once."

"It is good of you to be so prompt," be replied, holding her hand i second longer than was necessary before he released it. Then he went on quickly, "I 'saw the notice of your cousin's marriage the other day, and her photograph as well. She has a sweet face.' Isobel's lips grew straight. "You did not send for me to tell me of your admiration for my cousin, I presume," she said coldly. "Does this mean that you are not going on with our plans? I thought from your letter that you had some definite news to give me." "So I have," he answered, "only I hate hunting a woman. You see, Miss Frant, I am not naturally a blackguard, and though Hawke has done me about the dirtiest trick a man can do, I'd not like to drag down a woman who is young and beautiful, and might love him." She broke into a contemptuous laugh. "You need have no fear on that score. My cousin married Clifford Hawke because she was weak, and had not the courage to break off her engagement; but her heart belongs to another man. You are surely not going to be weak now that you have everything your own way!" she went On; "you have completely covered your tracks. Clifford Hawke thinks you are dead, and that his secret is buried with you in the Claverton-street fire. Now Is your chance to wreck him completely. You must remenyber," she added, "that had it not been for me you might have died." "I shall never forget that," he said quick- ly, while his face flushed. "I know that you have brought something new into iny life, an interest and eagerness it never possessed be- fore, and that is why I am so loath to hunt a woman who may not know how vac her hus- band

come or go. I only hope he escaped. So that is how it happened so strangely. Clif- ford Hawke hopes I have been burnt." Isobel looked at him thoughtfully. "You are not going to make yourself known to him as Paul Steinway yet?" He smiled.
"No, let him lull himself asleep with the idea that I am out of the way. I can afford to wait."

"I don't know," she replied. "Clifford Hawke is a clever man. Ho will trace any- thing that seems odd or out of the way at once, and if he suspected that the man who * " • ^-^4 ' still alive he would be cap- able of any trickery. 1 know him. lie has moro courage and cunning than any man I have ever met." "I don't think there is any fear of his trac- ing 'Mr. Smith' to me; I am not going into the city now, and I will not be seen in pub- lic even with you, Miss Frant. It was risky that other time when he was still in town.'

"I was stupid," she said, "but I could meet you no other way then." Then she said slowly, "You told me that his first wife died, but what became of the child?" "Probably it stied too," he answered. "I never knew anything about it. That is not the secret I held over his head, though it formed part of the chain of evidence." „ . „
"You 'won't tell me the real secret?" she asked. 'He shook his head.

"Not even you yet. It would be too dan- gerous. One never knows how things leak out; if you knew it I could not rely on your silence—even yours!" he repeated. "Don't ask me—you will know one day !" She looked at him curiously. "I suppose I must wait then. But you have told me that I shall know. You will keep your promise?" "I will keep my promise—you shall know one day," he replied, "the day that the rest of the world knows."

She shrugged her shoulders when she was sitting in a hansom on her way back to Park-lane. This man, rough, simple Colonial as he was, interested her immensely. She had met him twice before the day that Clif- ford Hawke had seen them together in Picca- dilly, and because she had hated the finan- cier as bitterly as he, they had struck up a bond of strange friendship, and though he had not revealed fully his hold over Clifford Hawke, he had confirmed her suspicion about the former wife in the past. She had not mentioned her real reason for asking—that she had seen Clifford Hawke start at the sight of a faded canvas. In the meantime Paul Steinway—or Mr. Smith '—waited till it was dark, and then went out for a walk. During his brief stay in Clifford llewke's office he had used his brains to some purpose, and had, by buying certain shares and selling them again, made a comfortable gum of money, and the unex- pected opportunity he had had of effacing himself had suggested a newer and more subtle form of revenge against the man who by now was probably congratulating himself upon being free from fear of the past. As he strolled along: the Fulham-road won- dering what it was that had made Isobel Frant, the society lady, seek him out and urge him on to crush Clifford Hawke, there was a sudden cry from a girl who stood In the middle of the road, hesitating in the midst of the throng of traffic. It was the work of a moment to dash forward and draw her on to the kerb, and as she turned to thank him he dropped her arm and stared at her stupidly. "Who—who are you, girl?" he said thickly, "tell me your name quickly !" "My name is Lottie Bond,"- she said with quiet dignity. "I don't understand why you should ask me." _

He flushed suddenly. "I beg your par- don," he said hastily. "You remind me of someone I once knew. I saw her last when she was a girl like you. But you must let me put you in a cab," he went on. "You are trembling all over. I am afraid you are shaken." "Please, I would rather go in a 'bus," she replied. "Don't trouble about me." He smiled gravely. "I must. For the sake of that someone you remind me of I must see that you run no further risk of be- ing hurt." As he put her in the hansom he had hailed, he glanced at her again. There was some- thing peculiarly fascinating in the sweet face in its frame of light brown hair and the

wistful blue' eyes itirred him stranViy. She was poorly but neatly dressed, and he won- dered whether he would ever see her again. "Where shall I tell the man to go to?" he said. "Vincent Buildings, Westminster," she re- plied, then added, "and thank you very much." He held out his hand. "May I post that letter for you? It will save you the trouble." She gave him the letter with a little smile. "Thank you. You won't forget it, will you? It is very important." As the cab drove off Paul Steinway glanced after it thoughtfully. "Vincent Buildings, Westminster, and her name is Lottie Bond," he murmured. "When I saw her I thought it was Alys Tennant, that blackguard Hawke's wife, come back from the grave after twenty years!" Then he glanced at the letter in his hand. "I'll post this at once; the poor little girl might be writing for a billet." He looked casually at the address as he slipped it into a neighbouring pillar-box, then uttered an exclamation. It was ad- dressed to "Mrs. Clifford Hawke, Hotel Ritz, Paris." "What has this girl to do with Clifford Hawke's second wife?" he. muttered. "Was it something stronger than accident that made me meet her to-might?" (To be Continued.)

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

A Match-making Bureau.—We are hearing much to the effect that " marriage is out of fashion " and it would appear that there is a good deal of discontent with prevailing conditions in the social world. We have lately had Miss Knowles lecturing on the unhappy lot of the unmarried daughters of the middle class, who had more or less useless and uninteresting lives at home, with little prospect before them but that of drifting into hopelees spinsterhood. The remedies puggested nearly always take the form of nnpracticable proposals for encouraging social intercourse. Such may be said of the proposed municipal match-making bureau in New York, promoted by Mrs Austin, the novelist and playwright. It is to maintain properly supervised dance halls, pleasure parks, gardens, tea rooms, and so en, all under excellent chaperonage, and the highest standard of social custom. Mrs Austin thinks that the very large unhappy marriagos, followed by divorces, in America' is due to a too limited choice of possible husbands and wives. Sha seems to think that young people would have the oppor- tunity of enlarging their circle of acquaintances at her Garden of Ed n, and thus stand a better chance of making the right seleotion. That might be no, but one is inclined to think that the match making bureau is I but a promise of distant fulfilment. Schemes of this kind have been suggested times ont of number, whilst some have been tried, with the invariable remit of failure. Cupid will not be tricked, and, if he were blamed, he would probably retort ttat the reason why marriage is out of fashion is mainly because young peoi.le of this unromantic age take broad and indepen- dent views of life, are content to be merely " pals," and indeed to laugh at his cld-fashioned " absurdly I sentimental " ways. The Restless Age.—The old slying that " familiarity hreeds contempt," applies to many of our interests in life. As time goes on we oiscover that our favourite autheirs, and the periodicals of which we used to think so highly, are "not so good as they were. "It is much the same with our recreations, our favourite holiday resorts, and the neighbourhood in which we live. None of these things, when we have known them for years, appear to be as good as they used to be. They have all gone down, especially the neighbourhood in which we reside. We discover that all the decent people, except ourselves, have died,er gone away, and there is nothing for it but to follow suit and move. That is the senti- ment at the bottom of the great houseshitting move- ments, which emir at the March, June, and September quarters. Not one in a hundred, owing as they say, to the general stupidity of builders, ever finds exactly the house wanted. After a lot of unsatisfactory hunting, the new house is, in many instances the one vihich was at first rejected as " too impossible for anything," but whether that is so or not, the malady of restlessness soon blots out any advantsges gained, and in a short time all has to be g.ine over once more. Inartistic Wall Papers.—An eminent artist laments the lack of taste on the part of the public in the selection of wall-papers, and one need not have a large visiting list to be reminded very often of this deficieney. It might be asked ally gaudy and hideous wall papers are ruannfactured, but the house-painters and decorators would probably say 'thatOt is not their business. They leave to you the tour points to be con- sidered—colour, patters' wearing qualities and price. There is much to be said in favour of the white room. It suggests coolness in summer, and is bright in winter, but light tints, although pleasantest and the most effective, are avoided by many people because "they show the dirt" and are expensive. Colours affect different reople in different ways, and medical opinion is inclined to think that they have an important bearing upon one's health. Red is commonly supposed to have an irritating effect upon a good many people. Blue, on the other hand, is said to have a restful and calming influence, and is generally to be preferred for bedrooms. The Searching Spring Sunshine.—The pre-Easter season is always a very busy time at the shops. With the first burst of real Spring sunshine, we discover that I clothes which we thought quite fresh and smart in the drab short days, have become shabby, and cannot be worn another day in the searching sunlight. That is ono of two misfortunes which Paterfamilias usually associates with Easter. The misery and trials of Spring cleaning, and large demands on the part of the family for new clothes. With the coming of Easter, this ' demand for now clothes is universal, and, as Pepys has left on record, it has existed in all ages. "My wife " he says," dressed herself, it being Easter day (1664) but I not being so well as to go out, she, though much against her will, stayed at home with me, for she had put on her new best gown, and this morning her tailor brought home her other new laced silk gown, and new petticoat, I bought the other day, both very pretty." Spring Millinery.—The choice of headgear is truly bewildering. A new flower toque has a high pointed crown, fittingly covered with violets, the leaves of which form the brim. Some new models turn up only on one side, or at the hack, but the hat with the fully draped crown and a drooping feather or aigrette on the under brim is among the newest styles. Drawn taffetas of the shot or chameleon kind is extensively used in 1 millinery, and is so decorative that very little trimming is considered necessary. The new taffetas I and straw hats, shaped without a wire foundation that admit of being folded in any wry, are both serviceable and pretty. The upturned brim will doubtless have a vogue. On this type of hat the trimming instead of resting on the crown is laid up on the brim. Crisply-curled ostrich feathers trim some of the new hats, on others big bunches of brush feathers droop beneath the brim, and touch the shoulder. Many of the most fashionable hat shapes have a lining of a contrasting colour. Chip straws will be much worn, so will crinoline in wide- brimmed shapes. A small hat has a high crown of coarse straw, round which a lace scarf is carelessly swathed, a big bow of lace—wired—standing up at right angles to the crown, being the only trimming. Lace scarves will be much used on hats, and as this is to be a lace year, millinery of every description will be decor' rated with this graceful trimming. The Corselet Skirt and Basque Blouses —ln tailored form, the corselet skirt is returning—if it has ever quite gone out of favour. The only novelty with

regard to it, consists in the cut at the xrsistt; now easy fitting, and in some instances VI Other types are much higher at the back than 11 Quite a welcome change from blouses wetn„lit corselet skirt are the new lace basqued effec"" present reign supreme, and are donned over the t skirt of taffetas, satin or Bilk. The blouse °I season is of exceptional merit, and made °tl possible material, is sometimes difficult to from an afternoon dress. Casement cloth of shade, trimmed with a bright colour, linen 110110 and white stripes, voiles, embroidered voiles cashmeres are all used for the confection popular and useful modes. Table Decoration.—For some time Prl— women have been showing the greatest possible", in their table decorations. arid nowadays it is„, 41' ordinary procedure for them to design, personally, all floral schemes for great occaso"sl less to soy, artistic knowledge of colours, blending of them are very necessary, 818° Arranging the blooms and foliage, if the scherst, be a success. High table decorations are to ; evidence. The whole arrangement is kept su low, to permit of cross table conversatioo,ol happily,any of the dodging, and neck.craniag by-gone days.

div.head: Penketh.
div.p: Penketh.

PRESENTATION TO MIL WATSON. -An interesting presentation took place in the Penketh Council Schools yesterday afternoon to Mr John Watson, who has for forty years been headmaster of the Council School, on the occasion of his retirement. The present took the form of a large oak easy chair handsomely upholstered which had been subscribed for by the manages. teachers and scholars of the school. Dr Murray pre- sided, and in making the presentation testified to the excellent capabilities of Mr. NVatson, and also spoke of the good feeling which existed between hint and all who had associated with him. Eulogistic speeches were made by many of the school managers and also by Mr Watson the assistant head- master. Miss Tinsley had always thought Mr Watson an ideal schoolmaster and Mr Midwood said that when Mr Watson first joined them in 1873 the schools were carried on by a voluntary system and independent of creed. At one time the Railway Company had helped to keep the schools going. He bad known Mr Watson for seven years and he was delighted to see the children had taken such a deep interest in their teacher. The new schoolmaster Mr. Griffiths was introduced by the chairman and made an interesting speech in which he said he hoped Mr. Watson's associations with them at the village would continue for marty years to come. (Applause.) The boys and girls of to-day were going to constitute the nationfof the future and they should all look after the education of the children. Mr. Watson made a lengthy response and thanked the subscribers most heartily, lie noped the good feeling which had existed in the past would prevail for all time. Mr. Foster also spoke.

div.head: PENKETH PARISH MEETING.
div.p: PENKETH PARISH MEETING.

The annual meeting was held on lVlonday evening in the Connell schools, Stocks-lane. The following Parish councillors were present :—Dr Murray (chairman), Miss Tinsley, Messrs William Davies, James Ditchfield, Richard Routledge, James Woodburn and Mr Ethelbert Foster (clerk to the Council). There was also a good attendance of ratepayers present, who brought up several things for discussion.

AG C OF CHILDREN ATTENDING DAY SCHOOL. I Mr E Marshall raised a question arising out of the minutes concerning children attending the Council School. He proposed a resolution to request the Parish Council to urse the local education authorities to admit the children to the Council School at the age of four years. He said they were aware that he had raised this question two or three times before and yet nothing had been done to fulfil the wishes of the rate- payers. He contended that it was far better for children at this age to be at school rather than running about the road and thus exposing themselves to the danger of beingiren over by motor cars. The argument put forward by RIS rue people was that it was not healthy for them to attend school at this age, but he said that the children were allowed to go to school at this age in the town and they had far more fresh air in the country. Mr. W. Moores said that if the admission of children at four years of age was not made compulsory, he should support the proposal. Mr. Faulkner said resolutions had been passed at three parish meetings and asked what was blocking the way as they had not been carried out. It was getting about time that the wishes of the parishioners were adhered to.

The Chairman said the resolutions had always been sent to the education authorities at Preston. The Clerk (Mr. Poster) read a letter with reference to the resolution sent last year and it stated that this matter was received too late to be dealt with for that year. Mr. T. Walker suggested that the resolution might be carried into effect if a petition was signed by the parents in the village. The Chairman said they must not forget that the managers were against the proposal. Mr. J. Leigh asked who appointed the managers? Had the ratepayers no voice in the appointments. The Chairman: The Parish Council appoint the managers.
After more discussion the resolution was carried. FEEDING OF SCHOOL. CUILDREN.

This matter was brought forward by Mr Marshall who asked the Chairman if anything had been done by the local Education Authorities to feed the school children In case of necessity. The Chairman said inquiries had been made he did not think there were any urgent cases at present. Did anyone in the meeting know of anyone who was really in want.

Mr J T Ambler said as a member of the Sankey and Penketh Old Folks Treat Committee he was pleased to tell them they had a balance its hand to the amount of about £lO and at a meeting held a few days ago the committee passed a resolution to help anyone who were in want. They had dealt with one case which had come under their notice. (Applause.) Mr T Walker said he knew a case that he thought was one of necessity.

div.head: BAD STATE OF WARRINGTON-ROAD.
div.p: BAD STATE OF WARRINGTON-ROAD.

..... Mr Marshall said the state of this road was dis- graceful. What with dust in the summer and the pools of water during the winter, it was out of all reason and he thought this meeting should impress on the Council to have this road seen to at once. Mr Ambler said he should like to have seen the County Councillor there so that this meeting could have impressed on him the urgency of the matter —Mr Mainley and Mr W Davies also criticised the state of the road, others followed, and the Chairman suggested that the best thing they could do would he to send a resolution trout that meeting to the County Council, expressing their grievances. Mr Marshall moved the following rssolution :—"That this meeting of parishioners of Penketh protest against this digraceful condition of the road through the Penketh village, and request the County Council at once to repsir the same with tar-macadam Mr Ambler, in supporting it, suggested that a copy might to be sent to Lord Wolmer and the County Councillor. This was agreed to unanimously.

ITOUSING QUESTIoN. Mr Marshall also brought forward the housing ques- tion arid the inspection of same. He said if the Inspector bad not time to inspect the Houses properly he should have some assistance. Mr C Wozencroft said from what be had seen a abort time ago in some houses which had been reoently cleaned through,he did not wonder that poor people had bad health when the walls inside were as wet as they could be. It certainly was hign time that the houses the working class had to live in were more healthy and sanitary. Mr Marshall moved, and Mr Wozencroft seconded, that the Parish Council take steps to urge the Urban District Council to remedy the conditions of the insanitary property in Peaketh and also that the'houses be reinspected. Others having supported this It was put to the meeting and carried. _

div.head: IiROOK POLLUTION.
div.p: IiROOK POLLUTION.

Mr. Faulkner put before the it.i-e;iing the question of pollution of the brook in Chapel-road and said that most of the villagers were aware that the cause of this was the over flush at times from the Penketh Tanning Company works. Although he admitted that they had tried to abate the nuisance, he thought they could do still more to improve the condition of the brook. He also said he could not relieve the Council from all blame in this matter as they might have given it better attention.
After further discussion it was agreed to write to the Penketh Tanning Campany with reference to It. FEDLERS FERRY FOOTPATH.

This was again discussed. Mr Faulkner asked the Chairman what had been done, with reference to this subject. The Chairman said the Clerk would read the corres- pondence received in reference thereto. After some discussion it was decided to write to the L. and N.-W. Railway Company for information with regard to their land adjoining the footpath dispute.

-THE RECREATION GROUND. Mr Ambler mentioned the shocking state of the recreation ground where the swings are placed for the children, and suggested that a few loads of cinders should be put there to fill up the places where the water lodged. A good number spoke on this question in rather strong tvrais, and it was decided to have the matter attended to.

div.head: _THE LOCAL POLICE.
div.p: _THE LOCAL POLICE.

Mr Mainley said he would like to call attention to the fact that the local constable was away on special duty, and there was no constables in the village and at a time like this they should have a constable in the village. It was agreed to write to the police authorities on this matter.

For the past three weeks the election fever has been growing upon the people of Lymm, Heatley and Broomedge and to-day tan crises have been reached. As the contests will be very keen, the results, which it is expected will be announced by Mr W Milliard, the returning officer, shortly after 9 o'clock to-night, will be eagerly awaited. The candidates and polling stations are as follows : Booth's Hill Ward: *Sir John Hardy Holt and Mr TB' W Dixon,Polling Station at tbe Zion Chapel school- room, Choi ry-lane. Ileatley Ward : *Mr Thomas Henry Warburton and Mr Peter Shorrocks. Polling Station in the Infants' schoolroom, Sandy-lane, Heatley. Lymm Ward: *Mr Richard Harry Gotobed and Mr Fred E Evans ; the Polling Station being the Boys' schoolroom, Pepper-street. *The retiring councillors in each case are given first.

LECTURE AT THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—A lecture on "A Trip to Nora ay " by Mr Parrott was delivered at the Grammar School, on Saturday evening last, and was thoroughly enjoyed by the large number of persons present. The lecture was enhanced by limelight views of some splendid slides of the lecturer's own manu- facture and were shown under the skilfal manipulation of Mr C MOSS. The Misses Shaw and Hiley adced further enjoyment to the gathering by their contri- bution of a pianoforte duet. BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.—The anneal public meeting of the British and Foreign Bible Society's Lynam Branch was held in the Wesleyan Chapel on Friday the 22nd inst. The chair was occupied by the Rev It W B Whitessay, the president, and was supported by the Rector, the Rev G B Thurston, M.A. After a hymn and prayer the Rector read a portion of scripture. This was followed by the Treasurer's (Miss Moston) report. Though regretting a slight decrease on Fast year's amount the securing of two additional collectors wes a good portent for the future. The Secretary, Mr D Mort read the miuutes of the com- mittee meeting which were confirmed in duo course The President after speaking of the blessings that the Bible has been to our land showed how that it was the aim of the Bible Society to give similar blessings to all the peoples of the world. After a short introduction the Rev T A Wolfendale. M.A., delivered a lecture on "Bible work in Malaysia." Tne lecture was a most interesting and instructive one and deserved a far larger audience to appreciate it. It was illustrated by Rome very flue slides which were shown to remarkable advantage by Mr C Moss. Mr Wolfendale brought his lecture to a close by a stirring appeal for help with the Bible Society's work and with the aid of a chart created a great interest among his audience. After the collection had been made the Rey • G B Thurston proposed a vote of thanks, during which, he said he reciprocated the chairman's remarks regarding the good fellowship that existed between the Established and Free Churches In this phase of God's work. The Rey R W B Whiteway seconded the proposition which having been carried,Mr Wolfendale suitably responded. The singing of the Doxology, and the Bendiotion concluded the meeting. LYMNI URBAN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council was held on Thursday evening. Mr 0 a Smith presided and the were also present :—The Rev G B Thurston, Messrs T II Warburton (vics-chairmati), W G Groves, U L Wel ford, 6 Davies, It H Gotobed, S W Gould, F Lockyer, W Mullard (clerk aid collector), Dr Edward Meyer de Jong (medical officer of health), Mr W L Donaldson (gas mMarnDageArf).ort (surveyor, tto.), NO LIGHTING DURING THE STRIKE. The Gas Committee bad passed a resolution that owing to the coal strike the lamos in the district with the exception of the automatic lamps, be not lighted uutil further notice.

_ DANGEROUS TELEGRAPH POLE. At a meeting of the Roads Committee, the Clerk was instructed to write a strong letter to the Postmaster- General, and cal i his atention to the dangerous position of the pole in Station road, with the request that the pole be put back in the wall where it was first placed. THE GRAPPENHALL AND DISTRICT SEWERAGE SCHEME. At a meeting of the Sanitary Committee a letter was read from Messrs R Davies and Co , solicitors, Warring- ton, on behalf of the Thelwall, Grappenhall and Latch- ford Without sewerage scheme as they were opposing it and asking for the co-operation of the Lymm Council if they considered that in the circumstances set out in their letter the Council ought to interfere ; further whether there could be any possibility of the terms being made with this Council for the Thel wall sewerage being dealt with at the Councils Sewerage Works. The Clerk was directed to communicate with Mr Hatto3 and ask him to meet the Council. OVERSEERS OF THE POOR. Messrs W G Groves and S W Gould were re-appointed overseers of the poor for the next twelve months. They

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March, 30,1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March, 30,1912.

Lymm. MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.—Asshown by the preliminary announcement given on our front paee, it has been decided to resuscitate theLymm May Queen Festival, which for various reasons was omitted last year. The ceremony is to take place on Whit Thursday. May 30th next. Strong committees have been formed, and given a fine day there is every prospect that as a spectacular demonstration the revival of this old English custom will leave nothing to be desired.

PRIMITIVA METHODIST RE-UNION —A re-union of old friends and scholars of the Primitive Methodist Church and Sunday school, was held in the schoolroom on Wednesday night and was well attended. After the singing of a hymm and a prayer by the Rev R W B Whiteway, Mrs Holt sang "Darby and Joan," and an encore "The swallows." The chairman, Mr G L Welford spoke of the beginnings and purpose of the gathering. Tracing the growth of prosperity of the Church and Sunday school he said the officials were still not satisfied and wished for further develop- ment ; it was their desire to see their old friends' and occasional visitors become regular worshipers, hence the invitation to this re-union. Refreshments,were provided by the ladies of the church and partaken of whilst Mr H Holt sppplied pianoforte music. Mr J H Brazendale sang *The animal's band " and,in response to the hearty applause he received he sang" The water melon." The Rev RW B Whiteway, the resident minister, then addressed the meeting. He asked the people to put the question to themselves as to whether they had not in past years obtained some benefits by the administration of God's Word either through the Ministers or Sunday School teachers, if so, then they ought to repay their debt to the Church by supporting and atteaaing the services. After Mrs Holt had rendered another solo, a hymn, followed by the Benediction brought a pleasant gathering to a close.
URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTION.

TOWN PLANNING.

At a meeting of this committee it was decided that a deputation, consisting of Messrs Welford, Groves and Holt, wait upon the owners of property in Newfield to discuss the possibility of enlarging certain cottages in Nevrfleld by building another bedroom, making in all three sleeping rooms to each house. All the minutes were opproved and the actions of the various committees confirmed.

THE EFFECT OF THE STRIKE. Mr. Warburton asked whether all the rate payers could receive a small quantity of coke. It was generally understood that it was only supplied to cottagers. He had given people who bad spoken to him about the matter to understand that all ratepayers could have coke in small quantities.

div.head: Grappenhall. GRAPPEN HALL SEWERAGE SCHEME.
div.p: Grappenhall. GRAPPEN HALL SEWERAGE SCHEME.
LATCHFORD RATEPAYERS STRONG OBJECTION.
MODIFIED SCHEME SUGGESTED.

The proposed sewerage scheme embracing Grappen- hall, Thelwall and Latchford is arousing much interest in the various parishes affected. At the meeting of the Grappenhall Parish Council a few weeks ago the scheme was bitterly criticised and opposed. At the annual meeting of the Parish of Latchford Without, held in the Baptist Chapel schoolroom on Tuesday evening, the scheme war again opposed and the ratepayers voiced their feelings in fighting speeches. A lengthy and interesting speech was made by Mr W Roberts, in which he said he thought it was not necessary to go to such an enormous expenditure for some years, as the requirements of Latchford Without had been met for ten years to come. Mr R T Fairclough who presided over a large attendance, said he had hoped they would have had a map so that they could have had a better explana- tion of the matter. Unfortunately they had not been able to get one, but the proposition was that a sewer should commence at the extreme point of Fairfield- road and continue through the parishes to Statham Bridge. They would be compelled to purify the sewage and he could not see how they were going to utilize the canal for that purpose, and they would therefore have to go to the place selected by the engineer—Statham Bridge. The Local Government Board were very loth to grant any scheme to any single parish ; their object being to try and combine two or three parishes so that the expense would not be so heavy as for one single parish. They had written to the engineer, and he had offered to meet the whole of the three parishes at any single place they might desire. In the meantime he would answer any questions they might ask. Mr Pilling said he had had several letters in con- nection with it and they had had one meeting of the three Councils and the engineer explained very plainly as to how the scheme should be carried out. The engineer bad promised that when the three districts met together he would be present and explain every- thing to them. Mr Ashton would also be in attend- ance. He was only sorry they not been able to let copies of the plans. Mr W Roberts wanted to know when it was likely that the Local Government Board inquiry for per- mission to grant the loan would take place. The Chairman believed that matter was left with the Local Government Board who would arrange the time Mr Pilling pointed out that they would have two o , three weeks' notice before the inspector came down. That was the only time they could make any objection. Mr Roberts said that was very important, because a very great deal would depend on that as to the form any opposition might take. Mr Browne wanted to know if he could take it beyond all doubt that the canal was included in the River Pollution Act. The CHAIRMAN : I think you will find it applies to anything except still water. Mr Browne !thought that prescriptive rights could have been established and they could not have stopped them. Mr Roberts said it had been stated by the Surveyor that they had made a suggestion to them and it was found hopeless to make any arrangements with the Ship Canal Company and that was why the scheme had been taken to Statham. Mr J Barker wanted to know if it was not in the Act that the bhip Canal Company had to provide full means. He was of tbe opinion that they in Latchford Without had just been brought in to make a sufficient rateable area. There was another strong objection, which was that the scheme was not let out by contract but the engineer was asked to send in his estimate, which was accepted. A scheme of such proportions could not be brought out in five minutes and he wanted to know why in 1912 they were first getting to know about it.
The Chairman: The engineer was asked to submit a scheme and he also gave an outside estimate.

Mr. Roberts: The contract is not let to anyone. Mr. Gorton said he was in the dark as to where the scheme originated from. They had been treated with the greatest discourtesy. He strongly protested against what bad been done at Runcorn and the way that Council had treated them. (Hear, bear). Mr. F. A. Jenkins as a member of the council quite coincided with Mr Gorton. He had hardly heard the sewage scheme mentioned and had never heard it dis- cussed. He was present at Grappenhall when the engineer estimated the scheme would cost £18,500 and at the end said "that's my little lot." (Oh!) The scheme would go very hard with some of them ,and he was afraid there would be some empty houses. Mr Gorton asked if they could not get the Ship Canal company to meet them in carrying the water up to_a 5 feet culvert.
• Mr Browne wanted to know who was the aotual initiator of the scheme.

Mr Pilling *Add the London and North-Western Railway Company had given them two years to take out the sewage from the Grappenhall district. That was about twelve months ago. They had entered into an agreement to do it in that time. Mr W Roberts understood they were all opposed to the scheme and he would be surprised if they were not. He was present at the Grappenhall meeting and he did not think that if they had searched the country through they would have found a more competent engineer than the one they had got. A Voice : Perhaps not more expensive. Continuing Mr. Roberts said that at that meeting they were all satisfied as to the ability of the engineer. He thought it was a council scheme and the only reasonable chance of success was that they should rake counsel with the other parishes and submit a modified scheme which would not entail anything like the estimated expense. (Hear, hear.)—A modified scheme which would commend itself to the Local Government Board and then they might have some chance of success The final decision would rest there. Personally, he did not think they should be put to such an enormous expense for some years to come. Their requirements at the present time were reasonably met and he would say without fear of contradiction that they could manage as they were for the next ten years. The effect of the scheme on a parish like theirs would increase the rates and it made one wonder if it would not pay them to be taken in by Warrington instead of submitting without protest to a scheme which would at leastiadd an increase of Is. 2d. on their rates. They bad not known much about the scheme. He was of the opinion that it would be worth their while to have legal advice on the matter. (Hear, hear.) They wanted a substitute that would meet their requirements. If there was good ground for believing that a satisfactory scheme could be submitted at a fourth of the cost of the proposed scheme then they would have a very good reason for going before the Local Government Board Inspector and try at any rate to stave off what, to his mind, was going to be a costly scheme and would have a bad effect on speculative building. They would not see the evidences of prosperity they had enjoyed in the past. Prosperity would he stopped to a certain extent and the next thing would be that they would be crying out to be amalgamated with the County Borough of War- rington. (Applause.) , A member of the Council said it was stated at Grappenhall that the District Council had promised them at Grappenhall that when the scheme was developed they would bring it before them before any- thing further was done. That had not been carried out. ' He thought that those who were going to pay the piper ought to have a say as to what the tune should be. (Hear, hear). Mr L Warburton asked if the District Council had any alternative scheme to offer? The Chairman : They have not prepared one. Mr 'Umber proposed that they should get the clerk and engineer down to propound the scheme, and have the whole plans laid before them. Mr Gorton seconded. The Chairman thought the Act of Parliament that had been passed with respect to tidal rivers would be overridden. The process of purifying he thought had to take place first. A member urged that no objections had been raised in the past, and he thought they would let, it run in as before.

Mr Pilling : It is the Railway Company. Mr Roberts thought that in view of the importance of the matter an opportunity should be given for every ratepayer to attend a meeting at which any questions would be asked as to the legality of the question. So far as tacking up to other parishes was concerned they had a snmple in the Stockton Heath Council school where there were only 20 children of theirs in attendance.(Hear,hear.)They had objected then but they might as well have talked to the moon. (Hear, bear). The Chairman said it would be better if they under- I stood the Ship Canal Act. Mr Bailey thought it was bad management on the part of the District Council in giving a job out to one man instead of inviting competition. Mr Pilling : You would not get men of that standard to come in if it was an open competition. Mr Bailey : I say we would. After further discussion it was decided that joint meeting of the three parishes be held to discuss the question and that the Clerk to the Runcorn District Council and the Engineer be asked to attend, and that Mr Arthur Browne be instructed to obtain counsel's adOice as to whether the sewage of the parish could be run into the Ship Canal. A subscription list to defray expenses will be opened if necessary.

div.head: Moore.
div.p: Moore.

WESLEY GUILD.—SOCIAL EVENING.-00 Wednesday evening the winter session was concluded with a very successful social evening when about SO members and friends were present. The first part of the evening consisted of a short musical programme social was pre- sided over by the Rev H Middlewood. Miss E Done opened with an excellent pianoforte solo ; Miss Eva Tanner contributed two songs, "Th. Merry Month of May" :Ind "The Nightingale" which were very much appreciated ; Mrs Ashley contributed two mandoline solos ; Miss Dutton quite riveted the attention of the audience with a very clever recital from Shakespeare's Henry V. depicting Henry's love-making to Catherine of France. Mr A G Dale is always well received at Moore and was quite up to his usual form. Mr J Gibson gave an excellent rendering of the two popular bass songs" Out on the deep "and" When the ebb tide flows." After this varied and excellent programme the refreshments were served under the well directed supervision of the ladies of the social committee. When the refreshments were over a very interesting competition was entered into with zeal, which consisted of estimating the ingredients of a pudding which was exhibited (these numbered 61). The winners were : Lady, Miss Eleanor Shaw, and gentle- man, Mr I Lawton. The remainder of the tine was spent in games, and a very enjoyable evening came to a close at 10.30 with the singing of the doxology.

Orford. DEATH OF MRS. HALLWOOD.—We deeply regret having to report the death of Mrs liallwood, of The Mount, Orford, at the age of 51, after only a very short illness. She was out on Friday, but was complaining of feeling unwell. Friday night she had a stroke, but Dr Fox did not consider it as being serious, but she developed pneumonia and she passed away, owing to that and heart treacle, on Sunday midnight. She will be missed by everyone in the village, as she had a kindly dispositTon and was always ready to help either the poor' the sick, or anything in connec- tion with the church or school. She did good deeds quietly, not seeking any thanks. The funeral, a private one, was held on Thursday morn- ing. The service was held in Orford Church at eleven o'dock conducted by the vicar, the Rev G Vale Owen. A number of the villagers assembled in the Church and afterwards proceeded to the cemetery, where the last rites took place. The deceased was followed to the grave by Mr Alfred Hallwood (widower), Mr J Hall wood and Mr A Hallwood (sons), James Hallwood and F %V Hallwood (brothers-in-law), J Longland, J Cann and A Thomas. Wreaths were sent from Mr and Mrs James Hallwood, Eagle Mount, " Daddy," "Her three bairns," "Mary," " Maggie,"" Maud and Fred," C Unswortb, Mr and Mrs Densham, " All at Brookfield. Padgate," Mr and Mrs Cann, Hilda Houghton, Mr and Mrs Joseph Houghton and Geoffry, Miss Stanier and Miss Horton' Mr and Mrs Charles Simpson and awis, Mr and Mrs Legge. Mr and Mrs Percival, "Teachers and scholars from Orford School," Mrs Fairhurst and Family, " Lily," Mr and Mrs Carpenter, " Fellow Wardens, Padgate Habitation Primrose League," Miss M Sutton, Miss Mary Lloyd Shotton, J G and L Dematn,Otley,Mr and Mrs James Warburton and Nancy. SUDDDEN DEAT3I.—On Thursday morning an elderly man named Mortimore, employed at Orford Tannery, was seized with sudden illness when leaving the Tannery at breakfast time, and died an hour after reaching home. The cause of death is thought to be a stroke.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
FEEDING THE HUNGRY.

Credit is due to Mr. Joseph Fairhurst (an insurance official) and his staff, for the manner in which they organized the feeding of 00 children last Saturday. This kindly effort was only made possible by the generous co-operation of the local tradespeople, for right heartily did they respond with gifts of meat, bread and vegetables. A willing band of lady workers prepared the wholesome soup, and the children met together in the assembly rooms, Hotel- street, and duly partook of a substantial meal. Thanks also are due to the proprietors of the rooms, so willing placed at the disposal of the workers. An effort is being made this week-end to feed some of the mothers who are most affected by the strike, LORD WOLNIER'S OUTBURST. "WICKED AND LAMENTABLE BLUNDER."

Speaking at a Tory meeting at Woolston, near Warrington, on Saturday night Lord Wolmer asked " What were they to think of Ministers like Mr Lloyd George, who made speeches of the Limehouse character 1 setting class against class, turning Englishmen against I each other, when they ought to be co-operating together to promote goodwill, peace, and patriotism? There were real economic causes at the back of all the terrible industrial warfare they were going through, and tbcse causes, to a large extent, were due to the fact that the Government still adhered to the obsolete theory of Free Trade, and refused to make tbe necessary reforms in their fiscal system, Prices were going up year by year, but wages did not go up in proportion. He bad great sympathy with the miners in their demand for a living wage, but all these great industrial problems —such as the railway and coal strike, and the cotton lockout—ought to have been dealt with before by the Government instead of wasting time on other measures. The coal strike was actually upon them, and after it had gone on for nearly three weeks Mr Asquith introduced his Minimum Wage Bill in a hurry and panic, and demanded that the House of Commons should pass it without proper consideration in order, as he (Mr Asquith) said, to allay the strike. There was nothing in the bill that would stop the strike or prevent a master locking his men out. The bill was introduced at the last moment to save the faces of the syndicalist leader, to enable them to take advantage of the Bill to withdraw from an untenable position. Such a thing would be purchased at a serious price. It meant that the leaders of organised labour or syndicalists bad only got to hold up England three weeks, to get bold of the country by the throat, and they could coerce Parlia- ment into getting them out of the mess. The Govern- ment, in giving way to such men, were laying in store for themselves and the people of the country a whole series of future troubles of a like nature. He thought it a wicked and most lamentable blunder to give such an incitement to syndioalists. Mr. Asquith had not i dealt with the bill n a statesmanlike manner.

ST. HELENS.

5,000 GL ASSWORKERS UNEMPLOYED. Between 5,000 and 6,000 of the employees at Messrs. Pilkington's sheet and plate glass works received notice on Tuesday night that the works would close the follow- ing day. This startling information, caused a tremen- dous sensation among the trading community. The industries of the town have come to a stop one by one during the past three weeks, but the town was saved from real starvation by the exertions of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, who kept all their people going. During last week-end the difficulties of the task increased tremendously. Still the works went on in the hope that a settlement of the coal strike would be brought about ; but as Tuesday's outlook was no brighter it was decided at half-past four in the afternoon to issue notices to close down. FEEDING THE HUNGRY. - - - - -

In the St. Helens district the distress caused by the coal strike is becoming very acute, but the Corporation and the townspeople generally are doing all that is possible to alleviate the uffering. Nearly .CBOO has been subscribed to enable the education authorities to teed the children, and in the different districts and wards of the town committees have been formed to raise funds so as to organise the supplying of coal. In Parr and Hardshaw a committee was tormed on the suggestion of Councillors Forsbaw and liamblett, under the direction of Messrs J Lydiate and E Cawley, and five depots have been :opened, at which 1,200 women and children were fed on Tuesday. A number of grocers and publicans have opened private soup kitchens.
EXPLOSIVES BY TRAMCAR. ST. HELENS MAN HEAVILY FINED.

Ralph Pennington, of 93, Greenfield-road, St. Helens, was summoned before the Liverpool stipendiary on Wednesday under sections 33, 39, and 40 of the Explo- sives Act (1875) for conveying to the Stanley Land and Brick Company a quantity of ammonite without affixing a label stating the kind and class of the contents. Evidence was given that the defendant admitted having conveyed 10Ib of ammonite, Ph of gunpowder, and six detonators from St Helens by tratnar on February Bth. The stipendiary observed that it was a wicked thing to convey such explosives by tramcar. If there had been a collision not only would the tramcar and every- one upon it have been blown to bits, but all the persons and houses in the neighbourhood. Under the circum- stances, in spite of the plea of ignorance, defendant must pay a fine of £2O and costs.

COUNCILLOR TOG Sir,—l was very much of the meeting in the To last, between the deputa Council and the Mayor, andparticularly respectiq Adult School and those -s

div.head: WHAT NEXT?
div.p: WHAT NEXT?

' A deputation from the Warrington Con- servative Council, consisting of MR. HAROLD SMITH, M.P., MR. J. FULTON SMITH, Mn. G. H. SMITH, AND OTHERS laid before the Mayor a complaint that the present unfortunate state of unrest and poverty was being made use of for politiecal ends by the Liberal Party in Be wsey Wald." Thus our Tariff Reform contem- porary on Wednesday in an article which might (a corresponuent suggests) appropriately have been headed "THE PUSHFUL SMITHS AND THE COAL STRIKE. " These disinterested and public-spirited politicians seem to have shed copious crocodile tears at the f.et of the Mayor over the perfidy of the Liberal party. The Member for the Borough explained that" a curious state of affairs had arisen in Bewsey, where an Adult School had begun to give out soup and act generally in a way that was distinctly opposed to the Mayor." Then he went on to suggest that because Mr New had written to the Editor of the' Examiner" supporting the efforts of the Adult School that the latter was a sort of branch organisation of the Liberal party acting under an assumed name. The sugges- tion is so preposterous that it is hardly worth our notice, particularly as there is ample repudiation from official sources in the letters printed below. Mr. Harold Smith must surely have for- gotten that he is Member for the Borough, and not merely the standard bearer of the Conservative party, or he would never have " put his foot "into such a grotesque piece of blunder- ing as the deputation has been guilty of. Instead of endeavouring to arouse the

indignation of Warrington people in refer- ence to the alleged disregard of the Mayor's wishes by the members of the Bewsey Adult School, would it not have been more seemly and in accord with the position he holds, to have commended the self-sacrificingrabours of these worthy people, and urged upon the Mayor that the time had surely arrived for action to be taken in alleviation of distress? Apparently he and his party are piqued at not being first in the field. The man in the street wants to know if Peter Walker and Sons, by opening a soup kitchen on a wholesale scale for the benefit "of any man, woman or child in the town who needs assistance" merit " the thanks of the public for their generosity " (vide the " Guardian ") why a few working men (whose sympathies have been so aroused by their daily contract with their less fortunate brethren in Bewsey that they have dared to open a small soup kitchen principally to feed the children and women should be held up to condemnation and publicly charged with attempting to make political capital out of the sad conditions which obtain? How sad and how shocking those conditions are—and how urgent was the need of such help as the Adult School has been giving—is amply proved by the letters which follow: To THE EDITOR OF THE "EXAMINER."

THE ADULT SCHOOL'S DIGNIFIED PROTEST- Sir,—With reference to the statements made before the Mayor, by the deputation from the Warrington Conservative Council on Tuesday last, as re?orted in the Warrington " Guardian " on Wednesday, we hasten to reply to the criticisms made against the action of the Bewsey Adult School in opening a soup kitchen. We are charged with disloyalty to the Mayor because we did not wait until cfficial sanction had been given. The position is as follows :—Several members of our school attended the Town's Meeting on March 18th, and one of them also attended at the adjourned meeting on the following day. As you are fully aware, the latter meeting decided to take no immediate steps in the direction of relief. As the members of our school, who are almost all residents in the neighbourhood, and, conseiuently, know far better than officials the condition of their neighbours, knew of many cases in need of assistance, they decided to commence soup kitchen in a small way on the following day. It is significant that at the Town's Meeting Mr. Bottomley (clerk of the Guardians) and Councillor Ashcroft both stated that Bewsey was the district most affected, and one of our members mentioned the same fact at the same meeting. In a neighbourhood like Bewsey there are many families whose position becomes precarious through the absence of one week's wages, and not infrequently does this happen when families are large. Also, there are many people—the honest poor—who shrink from seeking relief from the Guardians, and whose position is very trying. Delay is felt to be impossible. The claims of a COMMOD, suffering humanity were insistent in our ears and we felt that relief must be given ; and this relief was, and is, being given irrespective of political or religious associations. The Conservative deputation was labouring under a delusion in imagin- ing that our soup kitchen was a tool in the bands of the Liberal party. Men and women of all shades of political opinion are members of our school. Our movement is unsectarian and non-political. Several members of the local Conservative party frequently address our meetings, and some of our officials are members of the same party. We have been assisted, in regard to the soup kitchen, by members of all parties. It is, therefore, absurd "to connect this sectienal effort with the Liberal party." Mr. New's letter (of which we knew nothing until it appeared in the Press) was a purely personal one. He is in no way whatever associated with the soup kitchen, nor does he attend the school. He was anxious, like many others, to help us (hence his letter) and we welcome help, as we give relief, irrespective of politics or religion. Needless to say we are much grieved to think that the disinterested service of our members, almost all workingmen and workingworaen, shuld have been brought within the turmoil of party politics and party strife. We are quite ready—as we have been all along— to close the kitchen, if other steps are considered necessary by those in authority, and the services of our members would be gladly placed at their disposal. Vigilant measures have already been adopted to prevent overlapping, as others have subsequently found it necessary to take steps towards relief, but so long as our members know of cases of urgent need— provided those needs are not met elsewhere—so long will our efforts be directed towards relieving that distress.— Yours faithfully, on behalf of the school, AGNErS SIMPSON (President Women's School). H. GRAY (President Men's School). Catherine-street, Bess sey. March 28th.

COUNCILLOR DICKENSON'S POSITION. Sir,—As my name has been made use of in connec tion with the Bewsey Adult School and the work it has been doing during the last few days, may I be allowed throuph your columns to make clear mt position. I made very careful inquiries as to whethey the Adult School was non-political and was assured ir was. _ _

Knowing the acute distress that did and doesi pre- vail, particularly in the Betvsey Ward, I felt t my duty to -give my mite. I had not the least id ea of party advantages, and deeply regret the deputation should see fit to impute such base motives to myself. —Yours faithfully, JAMES DICKENSON.
Holly Bank, Fearnhead. 29. th March, 1912.

COUNCILLOR TOOLE'S STRIKING FACTS. Sir,—l was very much surprised to read the account of the meeting in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening last, between the deputation from the Conservative Council and the Mayor, re the distress in the town andparticularly respecting the action of the Bewsey, Adult School and those who are assisting it. The

deputation implied that what was being done was for party purposes. A more groundless assertion never was made, and seeing that my name was mentioned, I most strongly repudiate that any such motives prompted any little assistance of mine in the praise- worthy efforts of the Adult School. No matter what pious resolutions may have been passed at the Town Hall,and what official information ithe Mayor may be receiving, that distress does exist in Bewsey and the neighbourhood and has existed " acutely" for the past two weeks is patent to anyone troubling to enquire. That the Bewsey end of the town is most affected is proved by figures given me to-day by the Director of Education—who with his staff are doing admirable work coming within their province. I understand that under normal conditions from 30 to 40 children are in receipt of free meals from the Education Authority. On Monday last, 310 meals were distributed from six centres, Bewsey centre taking 160 of these meals ; Tuesday. total 407, Bewsey, 106 ; Wednesday. total 156, Bewsey, 212 ; to-day (Thursday), total 572 ; Bewsey, 255.—1 t will thus be seen that the Bewseyl centre accounts for nearly as many free meals for children as the whole of the other five centres of the town put together. I have before me particulars of 37 families residing in and about Bewsey who have applied here to-day for assistance. I personally investigated many of the cases and can vouch for their accuracy. In those 37 homes, besides the parents, there are 156 children. and from the inquiries I made I was Old that in only four of those homes had any money been received in the form of wages for the week, ending Saturday last, and the amount totalled 28a. 3d. for the four homes, or taking all the 37 together the wages earned last week were less than Is. per home. In many of the houses as many as six and seven small children (no money coming in) dependent entirely on vo:untary assistance. In one of the homes visited the father is out of work—neither food nrr coal—and a young child lying dead in the kitchen. This is the second death in that house in a week, and the poor mother's anxiety to-night is not about food or fuel bet the means of raising sufficient money to bury the little one. Some of the hardest cases are in the most respect- able families, who do not want to admit their privations. Official information that has been relied upon is the most unsatisfactory of all sources bemuse people will suffer to the end rather than apply for poor law relief. _

Surely the time has arrived when those of the town, best able and willing to bear the Cost of relief will not be debarred fuither from giving assistance so urgently needed. I offer no apologies to anyone for any little assist- ance I have been able to give to the Bewsey Adult School, and my only regret is that I have m t at my disposal sufficient means to enable me to subscribe to their fund, in a manner appreciative of their work. Far from the school being rebuked the ladies and gentlemen and working men and wamen attached to the school deserve the greatest credit for their ungrudging, unselfish and charitable efforts in dis- tributing the Lecessities of life to all needy cases irrespective of creed or politics. These people did not wait for red tape and sealing wax —and no matter what criticisms thsre may be from certain quarters, they have the blessings of scores of houses in Bewsey to-night for their timely help.—Yours sincerely. OWEN TOOLE.

div.head: TORIES' BAD BLUNDER.
div.p: TORIES' BAD BLUNDER.
The Examiner, Saturday, March, 30, 1912.
8, Frogball-lane, Warrington. March 28th 1912.
DR. BENNETT'S STRONG PLEA.

Sir,—l am amazed to learn from a report in the Warrington" Guardian" of Wednesday last that our civic authorities are under the impression that there is no acute distress in our midst. For a week at least my work has brought me in contact with cases of actual starvation and but for the noble generosity of small shop-keepers in giving credit—knowing only too well that the prospect of ever being paid is extremely remote—many, in the absence of other help, must by now have died of hunger. There is no neglect what- ever on the part of Poor Law Authorities who are doing all they can to find such cases as are herein referted to, but many of these people who will not notify the uuardians of their condition would gladly take advantage of a public fund. To-day (Thursday), I have seen women or more correctly " shadows " of women crying because they had no food for their children. One mother with infant in her arms and other children besides had not hdd a fire for a fortnight. Two families were crouching round one " so-called " fire, I am told that it is no uncommon thing for three or bur families to join at a fire, migrating from one house to another so that each gets a fire every third or fourth day, and this probably, only for a few hours. In another house there were husband, wife and six children, the husband's father and a man lodger and not a shilling had been earned by any of the men for three weeks and I was told that for days they had gone without food. Groups of children with basins and tins might be seen both in Bevvsey and Sankey Bridges districts eagerly asking to be directed to soup kitchens, whilst a continuous procession of men might be seen coming up Lodge-lane, many staggering and exhausted with an armful of crop wood, not enough to burden a boy who was properly fed. .

I visited in the course of my professional duties this morning eight houses in the Bewsey district and in five of these the occupiers did not know where to turn to get a bit of food, with the exception of the Adult School. In two others although they were 'not entirely without, they were distressed with the most intense anxiety as to the immediate future and in only one of the eight was the bread-winner winning bread. Now sir, these were not selected cases with a view to publishing harrowing details, but such as my ordinary avocation brought me in contact with, and unfortunately I have every reason to believe that the same proportion of aetual starvation would apply to the whole district. I write this because my heart has been aching for days for those who are slowly but surely dying in the midst of plenty, and every day I have been expecting a move on a large scale to be made by the authorities, and the first thing this morning I felt it my duty to let my experience be known in the right quarters. Not an hour must be lost ; famine is in the land; fathers and mothers are almost bereft of reason and children too weak to cry. This is no time for any political party seeking to gain party capital or taking umbrage because others have made themselves aware of the true facts of the case and have taken action accordingly. An appeal will surely be made at once for funds if the public health is to be saved from a dire calamity. I trust it may he only a matter of a very few hours before it is in nperation.—On behalf of the hungry, I remain yours faithfully, JAMES BENNETT, M.R.C.S. &c., D.P.H. Lynton Orange Padgate, March 28th, 1912.

THE LIBERAL ASSOCIATION'S POSITION. Sir,—Respecting the protest of the Warrington Conservative Council in regard to the Bewsey soup kitchen, which appeared in the " Warrington Guardian " of Wednesday last, allow me to at once assure every reader that no political capital has been attempted by the Liberal party, and as a matter of fact the soup kitchen referred to—which is doing extremely good work—is actually controlled by persons of various shades of political and religious opinion. The letter sent by Mr. New to the " Warrington Examiner" was simply a personal suggestion made only with a view to an early alleviation of the distress which is PO prevalent in the district. Might I impress the fact that the people who are being relieved are innocent of the cause of the present distress, and therefore all the more worthy of every possible assistance. ' Further, why pick out the Lewsey soup kitchen for criticism, when similar worthy efforts are being made in Whitecross Ward, St. Austin's Ward and Dallarn Brewery ?—Yours truly, JAS. T. LOCKER,

--- March 28th, 1912. Hon. See. Liberal Association. A further letter in support of, and the need for the good work being done by the Bewsey Adult school has been received from Mr. A. T. Hughes, 14, Bedford-street, Stockton Heath.

• 'Proposed' National Health Week. The Warrington Tradesmen's Association has fallen in with the idea of taking part in the proposed National Health week (April 2St6 to May 4th) and a resolution recommending all the tradesmen in the town to make suitable displays during this particular week will be sent out in due course.
