COAL STRIKE
MINIMUM WAGE BILL PASSED.
BALLOT OF MINERS TO BE TAKEN.

At noon yesterday, by Royal Assent, the Coal Mines (Minimum Wage) Bill became law. The epoch-making measure passed its third reading in the House of Lords on Thursday night, after a series of half-hearted attempts by Tory peers to carry amendments in the interests of the coalowners. _

All these .rmendments were firmly rejected by the Marquis of Crewe, who said emphatically that the Government would not have the Bill tampered with. Negotiations for a settlement by consent having failed, the Govgrnment pushed forward the Minimum Wage Bill, which passed the House of Comn:Cms on Tuesday by 213 votes to 4S. Both coalowners and miners' leaders hail grown "sick and tired" of tbe Downing-street conferenc,-s, the hope and purpose of vt hich were to gain the con- sent of the empleyers to the " Five arid Two" concession. In announcing to the C ,mmons the breakdown of the negotiations, Mr. Asquith was labouring under great emotion. Mr. Brace's amendment to include the 53. minimum for day wage men and the 2s. st.trting wage for boys of 14 secured 83 supporters ag-‘irtst 320. .

A noiahle r•peech' in tile —dehate was that of Mr. Stephen Walsh. the miners' member f,r Tone, who, in moving an amer.dment providing that the minima to be fixed by the district boar is should not he less than ths amount at present paid, declared that when I the Bill pis,ed it would he the duly of every well- wisher of the country to make the best of it, whatever

and Knowles works is that those workmen whose employment has not been interfered with by the strike have subscribed liberally for the assistance of their less fortunate comrades,and individual directors as well as the members of the office staffs, have also contributed their quota. Over £lOO has been raised in this way. Unfortunately, the opening of the works kitchens has been taken advantage of by unscrupulous persons to impose upon the charitable by representing themselves as collectors of subscrip- tions from the public for these relief measures. 'lt is, therefore, necessary to state that the efforts are confined entirely to the firms and their employees, no outside appeals having been anthorized. At the works of Messrs. Monks, Hall and] Co. Ltd. and the Whitecross Co. Ltd. we understand that the soup kitchens have been financed by balances from the works recreation club. Those of the employees of Messrs. Rylands Bros. Ltd. who are at present in work are subscribing for the benefit of their fellow-wizykmen who find themselves in distress and this (Saturday) evening a concert is being given to raise relief funds. The Education Committee are now feeding 000 necessitous children daily, and,under the exceptional circutukances, the provision of meals will not be suspended over the week-end but will be continued to-day and on Sunday.. With coal at famine prices—the amounts asked this week have ranged as high as 2s. per cwt.—there are many fireless grates in the town, whilst there has been an unprecedented demand for logs and firewood generally.

On Wednesday the Miners' Federation resolved to take a ballot of the whole of their members on the following question: Are you in favour of resuming work pending a settlement of the minimum rates of wages for the various grades of work by the district hoards to be appointed under the Coal Mines (Minimum Wage) Act ? YES. NO. The result of the ballot will be known by next Wednesday. While there is no general stampede of the men to the Fits, many mines are being prepared for work, and there ate indications that the ballot verdict will be favourable to an early ie-start of coal getting. In some districts this prdspect is being encouraged by the men's leaders, who, recognising in the Bill a distinct gain to Labour, though not all for which they fought, are already co-operating in the work of estab- lishing the district boards. EASTER ON THE RAILWAYS, Easter on the railway systems will be a time of probably unexampled dulness, since the customary excursion traffic will be almost entirely consnisu us by its absence. The London and North-Western Railway Company indicate their position by stating that " in consequence of the coal strike they will be unable to run excursion or other trains at less than the ordinary or tourist fares during the Easter holidays:" '
The'Ch. shire Lines Railway Company will have no rains on Sunday.

Binks supported the request, and it WHS pointed out that, while it would be impossible to suspend the rule without notice, it would be competent for the Board to relax its enforcement under the exceptional circumstances.—At a meeting of the Board of Management yesterday it was decided to meet the situation in that way.

div.head: RELIEF FUND OPENED.
div.p: RELIEF FUND OPENED.

The distress in Warrington has reached such an acute stage that a relief fund has at last been opened by the Mayor. The Dist! ass Committee met at the Town Hall last evening and decided to take immediate measures to deal with necessitous cases. A temporary scheme was approved and will remain in force until Tuesday morning when lit is hoped a more complete scheme will be inaugurated. It has been decided to make use of the soup kitchens already opened at the works. Full particulars of the arrangements, together with the first subscription list, will be found in our advertising columns. The special sub-committee en- trusted with the details of the work will meet this (Saturday) morning at ten o'clock and a meting of the executive Committee will follow at 11-30. The reports received from the various works and charitable organizations of the town showed that the situation had quite altered since the first meeting called by the Mayor and that during the last few days there had been a great increase in the distress caused by the strike. The Mayor stated that he had kept himself in constant touch with the conditions prevailing and that in consequence he had called last evening's m eating.

div.head: POSITION IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE POSITION IN WARRINGTON.

The closing down of the principal works in War- rington must of necessity have produced a con- siderable amount of privation but this has been mitigated by voluntary effort, chiefly in connection with the firms whose employees have been thrown idle by the shortage in coal. It is now nearly a month since the services of some of the workmen bad to be dispensed with, and their resources have by this time been completely exhausted. Those who are brought into close touch with the poorer quarters of the town, particularly the Bewsey area, speak of acute distress,approaching starvation in some instances, and every day makes such conditions of extreme poverty more widespread. It is, however, unpleasant to contemplate the dire straits to which large numbers of workingclass families would have been reduced, but for the private benevolence which has helped to keep the wolf from the door. We are informed that the applications to the Guardians for relief, while showing an appreciable inorease on tae normal demand, have not reached the alarming pro- portions usually associated with times of stagnation in the labour for bour worbly a certain reticence in d. This may, however, be accounted seeking Poor Law assistance. Each day there is a distribution of soup and bread at the kitchens opened at the works of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co.. Ltd. ; the Whitecross Co., Ltd. ; Messrs. Mon ks, Hall and Co., Ltd. ; and Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd. Some thousands of people have been provided with at least one substantial meal per day in this way. While the three first-named firms cater only for their own workpeople and dependents, Messrs Walker, whose works are running as usual, have opened their kitchen for the benefit of any man, woman or child in the town who needs assistance. Another independent effort which has been much appreciated by the po T is that of the Be wsey Adult school, where the workers have for almost a fortnight been ilia- tributing food to several hundred applicants daily, at their soup kitchen in Catherine-street. A gratifying , feature of the effort in connection with the Pea•son

div.head: Picturedrome Soup Kitchen.
div.p: Picturedrome Soup Kitchen.

During the present itidustrial upheaval, the manage- ment of the Picturedrome bavearninged to open a soup kitchen which will be open during the whole of nen week, Good Friday excepted. There will be no distinc- tion of religion or politics. The kitchen will be open from 10 to 12 noon and those desiring soup are to apply betueen those hours at the Picturedrome. It there is any bad weather applicants will be accommodated in the Picturedrome.

A splendid series of pictures have been depicted on the screen during the week and an exceptionally strong programme has been arranged for next week in one of which the principle actress is Madam Sarah Bernhardt.

div.head: NO RELIEF FOR COLLIERS. Interesting Discussion by the Warrington Guardians.
div.p: NO RELIEF FOR COLLIERS. Interesting Discussion by the Warrington Guardians.

The position of Colliers with reference to the distribution of out-relief during the strike was under consideration at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday and it transpired that it is illegal for Guardi,ns to telieve men who are out on strike. When the minutes of the House Committee were submitted, The REV A M MlTcliku. asked whether colliers who were in need of relit would be treated as cases of sudden on urgent necessity ? He had been told that it was the intention not to give any relief to a collier out on strike or supposed to be on strike The CHAIRMAN : Mr Mitchell The Rev AM. MITCHELL : I want to know how we stand. Is it so, or is it not?
'me CIAIRMAN : his is out of order altogether. . . .

The Rev AM M ITCH KLL : No, it is not out of order, I submit. I want to know whether it is within the power of the Guardians to grant relief. (Cries of • Chair.") The CHAIRMAN : You are out of order, Mr Mitchell, at the present time. The Rev A 34 Murcitut.r. : It is a simple question. The CHAIRMAN : But it is not one for the House Committee.

The matter then dropped. At a later stage, the CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board as to the action which may have to be taken by Guirdians in view of the shortage in coal supply due to the dispute in the coal trade and the consequent stoppage of aork in various industries. If the present situation should continue it must be antici- pated that the throwing out of employment of many workers would lead to the number of applicants to the Guardians for relief becoming very considerable. In such circumstances it would be desirable for the Guar- dians to consult with other local authorities in the Union as to what help or facilities the latter could render to the Guardians and generally as to the ways in which the authorities could co-operate. The Board could not doubt that in many places action by the local authorities would be assisted or supplemented by voluntary efforts designed to provide with the necessaries of life those who had been deprived of their livelihood by the results of a trade dispute in which they were not themselves directly concerned. The Guardians would no doubt consider that it would be imprudent in affording them relief to relax the usual conditions The Board would be prepared to agree, if the necessity arose, to the appointment for a temporary period of assistant relieving Lacers or other necessary officers, and to the hiring of relief. stations for the purpose of distributing relief in kind. The Rev A M MITCHELL : Are we to understand that that means that any man out on strike is nut to receive any assistance,no matter what his state may be? If he happens to be in a state of sudden or urgent necessity I take it that, notwithstanding he may bea strik-r or identifkd witu the strikers, it is the duty of the Guardians to afford such a person relief. As I understand it. any man who is a collier at the present time is practically" black balled" and no matter how urgent his casa may be, he is to receive no relief,eacept it comes under the head of medical relief. Continuing he said a woman came to see him the other ;day. Her case was certainly a bad one and she told him that the relieving officer bad distinctly informed her that no relief would be given to any collier who was out on strike. He asked the relieving officer about it that 1 morning because he knew his natural kindness of heart and he (Mr Mitcleell) understood him to say that if relief was given it would be on the understanding that there would be a prosecution either for the. recovery of the money or because the man would not work. There were a number of colliers who were out, who were not actually in sympathy with the strike, but putting that on one side, every man who was on the verge of starvation, no matter what be had done, ought to be fed. There was another law besides the law of the land. There was the

LAW OF GOD AND HUMANITY. He did not know that the Local Government Board was a true exponent of the law of the land. He had it from a barrister that the Local Government Board was a law practically unto itself, and if they went back as far as the Act of 1832. The CHAIRMAN: Do you think it is quite in order to tell us what the Local Government Board can or cannot do ? It is for us as Guardians.—.

The Rev A M MITCHELL: I think it is well for the Guardians to know that the Local Government Board is not a true interpreter of the law. You and I have to obey the law first of all, and if the law gives us power and authority to help people who are in need and necessity, it is for us to obey the law and to set the Local Government Board aside. The CLERK said the question of relief was governed not by An order of the Local Government Board, but by the common law. In 1899 there was a large strike in the Merthyr Tydvil Union. Three thousand persons were on strike and the Guardians relieved them by setting them to work at the workhouse. The proprietors of the colliery thereupon took action to restrain the Guardians from giving relief on the ground that the men had work to go to but had refused to work. The case went to the Court of Appeal which decided that under those circumstances it was . .

illegal on the part,of the Guardians to give relief t; strikers. Then came the question of the relief of the families of strikers. He (Mr. Bottomley) had told the relieving officers that before any relief could be granted he should certainly get a medical certificate in each case stating that the applicants were actually suffering and that that suffering had been caused by destitution. He would then be prepared to give relief. It was, however, undoubtedly illegal for the Guardians to give relief to persons who were on strike. If the Guardians took that step it would be open to colliery proprietors in the Union to take action to restrain them, although that would not upset the power of the Local Govern- ment Board to remit any surcharge in respect of illegal payments that the Guardians might make. With regard to what had been done in that Union, he attended the town's meeting at which it was stated that there was not sufficient reason to open a public fund to relieve the destitute. Several firms had opened soup kitchens and he sent a list of applicants for relief to the different works where the men were employed to see if anything could be done for them. That, of course, did not interfere with the relief given by the Guardians. In every case where the relieving officers considered there was need, relief had been granted. Every attention had been given to the cases that had come before them, arid they had been promptly and satisfactorily dealt with. .

The Rev A NI MITCHELL: But in Warrington you have not the colliers to deal with. I want to know whether in a case of sudden or urgent necessity relief would be refused to a collier said to be on strike. The CHAIRMAN : take it that the clerk has answered you that it is not legal by common law to help a striker. The Rev A M MITCHELL : That is the ruling, is it? The CLERIC: It is the ruling of the Court of Appeal that it is illegtl to give relief to a striker.

div.head: WHO PAYS FOR MOUNTED POLICE?
div.p: WHO PAYS FOR MOUNTED POLICE?

When the precept of the Lancashire- County Council to cover the expenditure for the coming half year was under consideration, the Rev A M Mitchell asked who was going to pay the expense of bringing mounted police into the colliery district. The CHAIRMAN ; That has nothing at all to do with us.
The Rev A M MITCIIELL : Win it be included in that estimate ?

The CHAIRMAN: We don't know. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : I want to know. The CHAIRMAN : 'Chat may be, bat you must ask the County Council. The Rev. A. M. MITCifELL : I want to know, arising out of that.
The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Mitchell, you ought to know that we don't know what is in that precept, except what has been read out.
The Rev. A.M. MiTcHELL : It is for you to ascertain, not me.
The CHAIRMAN : We don't want to know. We are satisfied with that.

div.head: STRIKE RIOT.
div.p: STRIKE RIOT.

THREE MINERS COMMITTED FOR TRIAL. Much interest was centred in a case at the Warrington Occasional Court on Tuesday when, before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair), and Mr. C. E. Parker, three miners named John Crawford (21), 17, Bramwell-street, James Gibson (22), 18, Hargreaves-street, and William I lancock (16), 436, Fleet-street, all of Parr, St. Helens, were charged with riotously assembling at Burtonwood on the 19th inst. Mr. Steel, instructed by the Chief Constable, of Lancashire, prosecuted and Mr Haslam Fox represented the prisoners. The proceedings commence at 10.30 and lasted until about 7 o'clock in the evening. The interest which the case had aroused was evidenced by the large crowds which assembled outside the Court house during the day. Mr T S Steel, in opening for the prosecution, said the Collins Green colliery was situated in the township of Burton Wood. There was a large coal tip on the premises and he understood the excuse had been made for those men on strike assembling there that the colliery company had declined to allow them to search the tip for coal. The company had good reason for that refusal because there was a great danger to the people who scraped the tip to get coal. At Wood Pit, Hayclock rioting took place and there the people were allowed to pick coal and that did not stop them from rioting. For over a week prior to the disturbance of March 19th men had been congregating in the vicinity of the colliery, and the company inconsequence of their menacing attitude obtained police assistance. On the day prior to the alleged offence the crowd was so threatening that it was deemed advisable to draft in an extra force of officers, because it had been stated that rioting would take place ; in fact a notice had been chalked on a bridge leading to the colliery reading "Rioting will begin at 2 o'clock." Mr. Fox : That is not evidence against us unless you can prove that we had any hand in the writing of it. _

Mr. STEEL : I hold that it is evidence. The CHAIRMAN said collateral matters of that kind could not be brought in unless there was direct associa- tion with the men charged. It was not evidence unless it could be proved that the prisoners wrote the notice. Mr. STEEL submitted that where there was an unlawful assembly those who took part in the proceedings took the consequences of all the acts of that assembly, and surely the general conduct of the crowd could be mentioned, or no riot could be proved. He had no desire to be unfair, but at the same time he had a duty to the public to discharge. On the day of the disturbances a crowd numbering between 1,000 and 2,000 people gathered in the vicinity of the colliery and seemed to divide themselves into two sections, one of which was led by the prisoners, and the police to the number of 20 were keeping the crowns off the colliery premises. One section stationed itself on the bridge, and there was a considerable amount of stone- throwing at the offices and the police in charge of the offices. The other section was on the St. Helens side where the tip was situated. The police on the Burton- wood side were in charge of Inspector Bannister, and those on the St. Helens side were in charge of Sergeant Smith, ,4 Sankey. Stone-throwing began in the morn- ing, and at two o'clock it grew so severe that the police were compelled to charge the crowd Irom time to time. Towards four o clock Inspector Bannister drove the crowd from the bridge, but the people worked round, joining fcrces with the people at the Parr end. The attitude of the rioters was so threatening that it was anticipated some further danger would arise, and as a result the police, thirteen in number, stationed at the Bold Colliery, were telephoned for. Those men hurried to the assistance of their comrades at Collins Green. From two o'clock until 5.45 the crowd were constantly throwing stones at the police and the colliery. A great number of the rioters were armed with slings, with which they threw the missiles. whilst many more were provided with sticks and rails taken from the fences in the surrounding fields. The three prisoners were in the front ranks of the crowd and were shouting" Come on, we have the -- beaten " and " Let us rush the colliery." They threw stones at the police as they came along. The crowd did not confine themselves to the roadway and a number got on the tip and did considerable damage. Crawford was unable to get away when the police made their charge and he WBS calling on the crowd to rush the colliery premises. He was in charge of one of the sections and had bean under observation for two hours. He was arrested and taken into one of the offices of the company. The other two prisoners took a leading part in the riot. In one of the baton charges at 545 five men rushed into a house in Broad-lane. The police followed and three of the men escaped but Hancock and Gibson were captured. When Gibson was arrested five macadam stones were found in his pocket. During the whole afternoon the district was held up. People were unable to pass and a great number were turned back. Carts and vehicles were kept standing for a considerable time, and when any tried to run the gauntlet they were stoned. Material which was deposited on the roadway for repairs provided ammuni- tion for the rioters. A number of women were rendering assistance by carrying supplies of stones in their aprons to the men in the field. About 33 con- stables were on the scene in the afternoon, t.nd every one was struck, some of them being severely injured. Sergeant Smith sustained a contused wound on the nose; Sergeant Mitchell was cut under the eye and a constable had his wrist injured. One of the colliery clerks was hit on the face with a stone. Superintendent Strickland sent for the mounted police who arrived at 5.45, and along with the foot police they charged and dispersed the crowd. The riot was undoubtedly AN ORGANIZED ATTACK ON THE COLLIERY and the prisoners were taking part in it. John Greaves Thompson, Bank House, Burtonwood, the manager of the colliery, gave evidence bearing out the statements of M Steel. He said that the colliery premises which contained a lot of valuable machinery were in great danger. In answer to Mr Fox witness said that he had no knowledge of the colliery company having given per- mission to people to pick coal on the tips, nor did he know that only one policeman Was required to protect 400 yards of property nearer to St. Helens. He had had to apply to the Chief Constable of St. Helens for extra officers. George A Burgoine, under manager at the colliery said be heard the crowd say" Let us rush the colliery" and he also heard allusions to the police. Inspector Bannister, of Widnes, who was in charge of the police, said the fall of stones was like HAILSTONES IN A STORM. He, witness was struck by some of the missiles. He
got within 15 yards of Gibson and saw him stones. The crowd was in a furious and attitude.

The cross-examination by Mr •'ox was di showing that the prisoners were not in the the times sworn to by the witnesses for ti cution, and that they were elsewhere. Sergeant Smith said he was positive of his tion of the prisoners, whom he charged u arrest. Crawford replied "I was there," and 1 both answered " I have nothing to. say." In the course of cross-examination by Sergeant Smith said that all the three prise throwing stones with the right hand. Several police officers gave evidence to that they saw the accused throwing stones c disturbances. Constable Millman said that was knocked down and he arrested him, F. said be arrested Gibson in a house in Broad-Is were five stones in his pocket. Sergeant MITCTIELL said Crawford was a spicuous personage on the day in question and that account that be was finally arrested. inciting the others to raliy round. Witness Hancock throwing stones at the police. Mr. Fox stated that so far as Hancock was there was little or no evidence. Sergeant S said that Hancock was a right-handed thrs was left-banded, and it was only by little— t as that that they could say whether the indet was correct. Hancock, who was a boy of flf working with his father on the surface Havannah Pit at 3.30 p.m. He went beano had his tea, and afterwards worked. garden. About 5.15 his mother told hi to look for his sister, who was at went to the colliery for a rightful purpose to sister away. COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON RELIEF OF DISTRESS CAUSED BY THE STRIKE. At a Meeting of the Distress Committee held at the Town Hall last evening, it was decided "that the Mayor be requested to open a fond for the relief of persons in distress owing to the Coal Strike." I therefore appeal to the inhabitants of Warrington for their support and help in raising a fund for the purpose. Subscriptions may he paid to the Borough Treasurer, Bank House, Sankey Street, or into any of the Banks. Town Hall, Warrington, G. W. JOSEPH, 29th March, 1912. Mayor. LIST OF SUBSCRIPTIONS. s. d. COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON RELIEF OF DISTRESS CAUSED BY THE STRIKE. WORKPEOPLE who have been thrown out of work through the Strike may make application for relief to their own works for a recommend, which, when obtained must be taken to the Education Office, between the hours of noon and 5 p.m., where an order for food or fuel will be given in exchange. CASUAL WORKERS in distress owing to the Strike may apply for tickets to one of the following persons or places:— Education Office Sankey Street. Guild of Help, Office, Street. Office of Clerk to the Guardians, Bewsey Chambers. To one of the following Relieving Officers:— Mr. Gidman, 26, Arthur Street. Mr. Cotterill, 40, Thewlis Street. Mr. Aukland, 42, Church Street. To any of the Clergy or Ministers of Religion. The District Heads of the Citizens Guild of Help for tbe following Wards : Bewse7 Ward, Whitecross Ward, St Austin's Ward, Fairfield and Orford Wards, St. John's and Town Hall Wards, Howley Ward, Latchford Ward, Town Hall, Warrington, G. W. JOSEPH, 29th March 1912. Mayor.

GREAT WESTERN RAILWAY. COAL STRIKE. GOODS TRAFFIC ARRANGEMENTS. The Great Western Railway Company hereby give notice that in consequence of the continuance of the General Coal Strike their Goods Train Service after THURSDAY, MARCH 28th, 1912, will be further curtailed, and excepting Foodstuffs, for human or animal consumption, Coal and other descriptions of fuel, Patent Manures, Pulp for paper making, and Paraffin and Petroleum Oils, they will not accept any oommoditios specified in Classes A. B, and C, of the General Railway Classification of Goods, including any of the same commodities that are in the higher Classes and all desoriptiovs of Empty Packages other than those used for the conveyance of Foodstuffs. Copies of this Classification can be inspected at any Great Western Goods Station. , FRANK POTTER, Paddington Station, General Manager. London, March, 1912.

OXO CINEMA FILM. Included in our programme this week is a. film which all our patrons will enjoy. It is entitled " Life on the OXO Cattle Farms," and shows beautiful living pictures of some of the 350,000 ONO cattle, including a grand march past of one herd counting cattle -a novice opening a gate on horse-back—a cow- boy breaking-in his horse—branding calves —a parade of pedigree Hereford MO bulls worth 5-1,000 each—great bulls weighing over a ton plunging into a bath and swimming through it —cowboys separating big bulls from a herd and galloping across the plains. There is a very big demand for this film all over the country and we consider cur- selves fortunate in having obtained it for our patrons. It will form part of an excellent programme. This week the OXO film will be shown at EMPIRE THEATRE, BROOKFIELD ST., EARLESTOWN.

It is said by those who should know, to be one of the best 18 hole courses on the Continent, and has that additional charm for all lovers of the health-giving garne of being close to the shore, where there is a beautiful beach of fine white sand some fifty yards wide at low tide. and ' extending about twenty-five miles along the coast, running by Ostend and Illankenberght land along to the frontier of Holland, only a short distance from Le Zoute-Knocke. Owing to the tine beach and good bathing, this golfing station is a great favourite with the children.
